## tips letter
Tip: Ctrl+B, Ctrl+I and Ctrl+U toggle bold, italic and underline in nearly every word processor. Your mouse can rest.
Tip: In LibreOffice Writer, Ctrl+Alt+Shift+V pastes as unformatted text. Handy when the source font looks like a ransom note.
Tip: Ctrl+Enter inserts a page break in Writer and in Word. Far better than pressing Enter forty times.
Tip: Ctrl+Z undoes, Ctrl+Y redoes in Writer and Word. Regret is only a few keystrokes deep.
Tip: Ctrl+Home jumps to the top of the document and Ctrl+End to the bottom. Scrolling is for people with time.
Tip: Ctrl+Backspace deletes a whole word at once, backwards. Great for undoing a sentence you regret starting.
Tip: F7 starts the spell check in Writer and in Word. Do it before you send the letter, not after you spot the typo.

## tips writing
Tip: Ctrl+A selects everything, Ctrl+C copies, Ctrl+V pastes. You know this. Everyone knows this. Do it anyway.
Tip: Ctrl+Left and Ctrl+Right move a word at a time. Add Shift to select as you go. Surgical.
Tip: In LibreOffice Writer, Ctrl+1, Ctrl+2 and Ctrl+3 apply Heading 1 to 3. Ctrl+0 goes back to body text.
Tip: Ctrl+K inserts a hyperlink in Writer and Word. Link the source instead of writing "click here".
Tip: Ctrl+L, Ctrl+E and Ctrl+R align left, centre and right in Writer and Word. Ctrl+J justifies.
Tip: In LibreOffice Writer, F5 opens the Navigator. A long report is easier when you can jump by heading.
Tip: In LibreOffice Writer, double-click selects a word and triple-click selects a sentence. Quadruple-click gets the paragraph.

## tips spreadsheet
Tip: Ctrl+Arrow jumps to the edge of a block of data. Ctrl+Home goes back to A1. Scrolling 10,000 rows is optional.
Tip: F2 edits the selected cell in Excel and in Calc without wiping its contents. Typing over a formula is how tears begin.
Tip: While typing a formula, F4 cycles a reference between A1, $A$1, A$1 and $A1. In Excel and in Calc.
Tip: Ctrl+; enters today's date and Ctrl+Shift+; the current time, in Excel and in Calc. No calendar needed.
Tip: Ctrl+D fills the cell above down into the selected cells. A new line inside a cell is Alt+Enter in Excel and Ctrl+Enter in Calc.
Tip: Ctrl+Space selects a whole column and Shift+Space a whole row. Works in Excel and Calc.
Tip: Select a range of numbers and the status bar shows their sum, no formula needed. Excel and Calc both do it.

## tips slides
Tip: F5 starts the slideshow in Impress and in PowerPoint. Esc ends it. Rehearsing in the editor is how you present with a sidebar showing.
Tip: During a slideshow, type a slide number and press Enter to jump straight to it. Handy when someone asks about slide 14.
Tip: Ctrl+M adds a new slide in Impress and in PowerPoint. Fewer words per slide helps more than new slides, though.
Tip: In PowerPoint, B or the full stop key blackens the screen during a show. Press it again to return. Great for a pause.
Tip: One idea per slide. If it needs scrolling, it is a document, not a slide.
Tip: Export your deck as a PDF before sending it. The fonts will look the same on every screen.

## tips email
Tip: Ctrl+Enter sends the message in Thunderbird, Gmail and Outlook. Read it twice before you press it.
Tip: Ctrl+R replies and Ctrl+Shift+R replies to all, in Thunderbird and in Outlook. Choose with care.
Tip: Ctrl+N starts a new message in Thunderbird and in Outlook.
Tip: In Thunderbird, Ctrl+Shift+V pastes as plain text. No more mystery fonts in the middle of your email.
Tip: Fill in the To field last. An email that cannot be sent by accident cannot be sent to the wrong person.
Tip: Attach the file first, then write "see attached". The attachment is the most forgotten thing in email history.

## tips inbox
Tip: In Thunderbird, A archives the selected message and M toggles read and unread. Inbox zero is a keystroke away.
Tip: In Gmail, switch on keyboard shortcuts in the settings. Then E archives, C composes, J and K move between messages.
Tip: Shift+Delete removes a message for good in Thunderbird and in Outlook, without sending it to the trash first. Use with care.
Tip: In Outlook, Ctrl+Q marks a message as read and Ctrl+U as unread.
Tip: Open your inbox at fixed times, not all day. Constant checking is just a very slow game of Whack-a-mole.
Tip: Unsubscribe at the bottom of a newsletter you do not read. The link counts as a gift to your future self.

## tips code
Tip: In VS Code, Ctrl+P opens any file by name and Ctrl+Shift+P opens the command palette. The mouse is optional.
Tip: Ctrl+/ comments or uncomments the current line in VS Code. Select several lines and it does them all.
Tip: In VS Code, Alt+Up and Alt+Down move the current line. Shift+Alt+Down copies it below.
Tip: Ctrl+D in VS Code selects the next occurrence of the highlighted word. Press it repeatedly, then type once to edit them all.
Tip: F2 renames a symbol in VS Code everywhere it is used. Better than find and replace and hope.
Tip: F12 goes to the definition of the thing under the cursor in VS Code, and Alt+Left takes you back.
Tip: Ctrl+` toggles the built-in terminal in VS Code. Ctrl+Shift+K deletes the current line.

## tips terminal
Tip: Ctrl+C stops the running command and Ctrl+L clears the screen. Ctrl+D on an empty line exits the shell.
Tip: Ctrl+R searches your command history as you type. Press it again for older matches.
Tip: Ctrl+A and Ctrl+E jump to the start and the end of the line in bash and zsh. Ctrl+W deletes the word before the cursor.
Tip: Most Linux terminals paste with Ctrl+Shift+V and copy with Ctrl+Shift+C, since Ctrl+C means stop. Windows Terminal does that too.
Tip: Tab completes file names and commands. Press it twice to see the options. Typing full paths is for the brave and the bored.
Tip: In bash and zsh, !! repeats the previous command. sudo !! repeats it with admin rights, which is the classic fix for "permission denied".
Tip: Ctrl+Z pauses a running program and fg brings it back. The program is not harmed. It is merely inconvenienced.

## tips howto
Tip: Ctrl+F searches the current page. Long tutorials usually hide the one step you need on the third screen.
Tip: Ctrl+D bookmarks the page in Firefox and Chrome. Do it before you close the tutorial you will need again.
Tip: Ctrl+Shift+T reopens the tab you just closed, in Firefox and in Chrome. Repeat for older ones.
Tip: Middle-click a link to open it in a new tab. Ctrl+W closes the current tab.
Tip: Ctrl+plus and Ctrl+minus zoom the page, Ctrl+0 resets it. Useful for tiny screenshots in a tutorial.
Tip: Search the exact error message in quotes. Somebody has already had your problem, and wrote about it in 2014.

## tips search
Tip: Ctrl+L or F6 focuses the address bar in Firefox and Chrome, ready for a search. No clicking required.
Tip: Put a phrase in quotes to search for it exactly, and a minus sign before a word to leave it out. Works in Google and DuckDuckGo.
Tip: Add site:example.com to a Google search to restrict it to that website. Handy when a site's own search is hopeless.
Tip: Add filetype:pdf to a Google search to find only PDFs. Great for manuals and reports.
Tip: Ctrl+Shift+R reloads a page and ignores the cached copy in Firefox and Chrome. Useful when a page insists on being old.
Tip: Alt+Left goes back a page and Alt+Right forward in Firefox and Chrome. Your trackball days are over.

## tips video
Tip: On YouTube, Space or K pauses, J and L skip 10 seconds back and forward, and the arrow keys skip 5.

Tip: On YouTube, the number keys 0 to 9 jump to 0 to 90 percent of the video. 0 goes back to the start.
Tip: On YouTube, T switches to theatre mode and I opens the miniplayer, so the video can sit in a corner while you work. Mostly work.
Tip: On YouTube, while the video is paused, the comma and full stop keys step one frame back and forward.

## tips image

## tips error

## tips qa
Tip: On Stack Overflow, check the date of an answer. A 2012 solution may not work on today's software.

Tip: A good question includes what you tried, the exact error, and a small example that reproduces it.

## tips git
Tip: git status shows what changed, and git diff shows how. Run both before every commit.
Tip: git switch -c name creates a branch and switches to it. git switch - returns to the previous one.
Tip: git stash puts your changes aside and git stash pop brings them back. Handy when you must switch branches in a hurry.
Tip: git restore file throws away your uncommitted changes to that file. There is no undo, so check git diff first.
Tip: git commit --amend fixes the last commit message, as long as you have not pushed it yet.
Tip: git add -p lets you stage a file chunk by chunk, so one commit does one thing.
Tip: git reflog lists where HEAD has been, including commits that vanished from the log. Often that is how you get lost work back.
Tip: git log --oneline --graph shows the history as a compact tree. Much easier to read than the full log.

## tips updates
Tip: On Debian and Ubuntu, sudo apt update then sudo apt upgrade installs updates. On Fedora, sudo dnf upgrade.
Tip: On Arch and CachyOS, sudo pacman -Syu updates everything. Do not run -Sy without -u. Partial upgrades break systems.
Tip: On Windows, Win+I then Windows Update checks for updates. Restart when it asks, not three weeks later.
Tip: Save your work before you install updates. A restart will close your programs.
Tip: Update when you are not in a hurry. Updating five minutes before a presentation is a bold choice.
Tip: Restart after a kernel update to actually use the new kernel.

Tip: Win+V opens clipboard history on Windows, once you have turned it on. I keep mine for you: say "clipboard history".

## tips general
Tip: Press Ctrl+S often. Autosave is a nice idea, but it has never loved you the way you love your document.
Tip: Back up with the 3-2-1 rule: three copies, on two kinds of storage, with one copy somewhere else.
Tip: Use a password manager and turn on two-factor login for your important accounts. One strong password for everything is one weak link.
Tip: Name files with the date as year-month-day, like 2025-03-14. They sort in order that way.
Tip: Lock your screen when you leave, even for a minute. A minute is plenty for a colleague with a sense of humour.
Tip: Restarting fixes a surprising number of problems. Save first. Then ask why afterwards.
Tip: Ctrl+Shift+T reopens a tab you closed by mistake in Firefox and Chrome. Ctrl+Z undoes almost everything else.
Tip: Every 20 minutes, look 20 feet away for 20 seconds. Say "timer 20m break" and I will remind you.

## welcome hello
I'm Clipster, the paperclip who lives on your desktop. I help with the office side of computer life: reminders and to-dos, writing, focus, tidying files and looking after the computer.\n\nEverything runs on this computer, on rules, not AI. Click Next to set me up (it takes a minute), or Cancel to skip.

## welcome name
I'll use it now and then. Leave it empty if you'd rather stay mysterious. You can change it later by telling me "call me Sam".

Same help either way. You can switch any time in Settings, or by saying "be boring" or "be unhinged".

## welcome notice
I only read these to comment on them, and nothing leaves this computer. You can change each one in Settings.

## welcome startup
The version check asks GitHub once a day whether a newer Clipster is out. Nothing else is sent.

## welcome calling
• Click me, or press Meta+C anywhere.\n• Meta+Shift+C opens my Desk.\n• Right-click me for a menu: the Desk, Settings, a quiet hour.\n• Double-click me for a trick.\n• Type in plain words, typos and all. The up arrow repeats what you typed.\n• "help" shows everything I can do, by topic.

(from window titles, which stay on this computer).

• "plan my day": pick today's top 3 in the morning.\n• "wrap up my day": what got done and what's left (move it to tomorrow), then lock or shut down. I offer it after 5 pm on busy days.\n• "my week in review": on Friday afternoons I offer a summary you can copy.

## welcome upkeep
• "computer checkup": free space, the trash, temporary files, system updates, battery health, apps that start with the computer, the last backup. ## program acrobat
> acrobat | acrord32
@ read
A PDF reader. The one document you can always open and almost never edit.
Acrobat is open. A good time to remember that Print to PDF is free and "Export" is a trap with a price tag.
Fill & Sign is the secret hero here. You can sign a form without a printer, a scanner or a mild panic.
PDFs: the format that looks the same everywhere and is editable nowhere. Be gentle with them.
Searching with Ctrl+F works in most PDFs. Scanned ones are just photographs of text, and need a bit of OCR first.
A very long PDF is opening. Click the bookmarks panel on the left. Scrolling 200 pages is a choice, not a requirement.

## program sumatrapdf
> sumatrapdf
@ read
SumatraPDF: a reader about the size of a nice photo. It opens before you finish clicking.
SumatraPDF reads PDF, EPUB, MOBI, comics and more. It has no ribbon, no sidebar tour, no account. Refreshing.
Press Backspace or Alt+Left to jump back after clicking a link in a PDF. Few readers do this so smoothly.
A reader that doesn't want your attention. It wants to show the page and get out of the way.
It also reloads a file automatically when it changes. Good news if you write documents and export them again and again.
Light, fast, and a bit yellow in the background. Sumatra is the lemon of PDF viewers.

## program 7zfm
> 7zfm | 7zg
@ carry
7-Zip. Free, fast, open source and about as flashy as a brick. A very good brick.
The .7z format usually squeezes files smaller than ZIP does. Use it for your own backups, ZIP for everyone else.
Right-click a file, 7-Zip, Add to archive. That is the whole feature. It does it for the price of nothing.
7-Zip can also show a CRC or SHA checksum for any file from the right-click menu. Great for downloads you're not sure about.
Opening a RAR, ISO or TAR file? 7-Zip does that too. It is the great translator of archives.
If the archive asks for a password and you don't have one, no tool in the world will help. Not even this one.

## program winrar
> winrar
@ sly
WinRAR. The famous 40-day trial that has been 40 days long for twenty years. A very patient app.
"Your evaluation period has expired." You have heard this before. WinRAR says it every time and does nothing about it.
Still using WinRAR? ZIP works natively and 7-Zip is free. But WinRAR is a classic, and classics get to stay.
RAR archives can be split into volumes (part1, part2, part3), which made sense when files had to fit on discs.
WinRAR can add a recovery record to an archive, so a damaged one can be repaired. Underrated, and very useful for old backups.
A progress bar reading "Calculating..." is the oldest joke in computing. WinRAR does not mind being the punchline.

PowerToys has more tools than a shed. Pick one, learn it, then pick another. Do not try them all today.

## program everything
> everything | everything64
@ search
Everything: a file search that finds files before you finish the word. It reads the file index directly, so it's nearly instant.
Everything is open. Type three letters and watch every file with them appear. Windows Search could not feel less seen.
Tip: Everything shows your files only by name, so name them well. "final_FINAL_v7" is a cry for help.
You can sort by size or date in Everything. The biggest file on your drive is usually a video you forgot.
It indexes your drives in seconds the first time and then stays out of the way. A tool with manners.
Right-click a result and choose "Open Path". You get a folder and, at last, the answer to "where did I save it?".

## program putty
> putty | puttygen | pageant
@ cool
PuTTY: a blue window to a faraway server, drawn like it's 1999. It works anyway.
In PuTTY, selecting text copies it and right-click pastes it. It has done this forever. Nobody told you.
Save your sessions under a name in PuTTY. Typing a server address every time is a chore of your own making.
Use SSH keys instead of passwords. PuTTYgen makes them, and Pageant remembers them for you.
If the terminal freezes, close it and connect again. A silent connection is not a thinking connection.
Be careful on a server: the commands you type run for real. Double-check before pressing Enter on anything with "rm".

## program winscp
> winscp
@ carry
WinSCP: two panels, your files on one side, the server's on the other. Drag across. Done.
Use SFTP in WinSCP, not plain FTP. Plain FTP sends your password in the open. It's not 1995 anymore.
WinSCP has a built-in editor: double-click a remote file to change it, save, and it uploads by itself. Dangerous, convenient.
The sync feature compares two folders and copies what's different. Check the direction arrow before you press go.
A transfer queue in the corner shows the slow upload you started. It is patient. You should be too.
Check twice which side is the server. Dragging a folder the wrong way around is a rite of passage.

## program wmplayer

Visualisations. A moving colour show for your music. Best enjoyed with nothing else to do.
The Library view is where all your albums live. It also remembers the ones you forgot you had.

## program microsoft.photos

## program regedit
> regedit
@ shock
The Registry Editor. A big tree of settings with a thousand tiny switches. Export a key before you change it.
Everything in Windows keeps its settings in here, in a tree with names like HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE. Nobody enjoys the names.
Nothing in the registry has an undo button. File, Export saves a copy first. That is your undo button.
If a tutorial tells you to change a value here, check the source first. And then check it again.
Searching with Ctrl+F is slow here, but it works. The F3 key finds the next match. Very 1995.
The registry is the attic of Windows. Interesting, dusty, and full of things whose purpose nobody remembers.

## program mmc

@ think
The Management Console is open: Device Manager, Disk Management or Services lives in it. Admin stuff, in grey boxes.
Services. A long list of things that start by themselves. Some of them you need. Some of them you'll never meet.
In Disk Management, check twice which disk you right-click. The one labelled "Disk 1" is not always the one you expect.
Device Manager. A yellow triangle means a driver wants attention. A very polite little cry for help.
Right-click, Properties. Right-click, Properties. This is the whole control panel philosophy.
This window is for the grown-up jobs on your computer. Tread slowly and read what you click.

## program msinfo32
> msinfo32
@ read
System Information. A page that knows everything about your computer and tells you in a boring table.
Handy for support calls: it lists your processor, memory, BIOS version and more. Just don't read it all out loud.
Use File, Export to save the report as a text file. Attach it to the support request. They will love you.
Search at the bottom of the window is useful. Type "bios" and jump to the right row.
Your BIOS date is here. If it says 2013, your computer is doing very well. Or has been ignored for a decade.
A lot of facts, and no jokes. I'll provide the jokes.

## program dxdiag
> dxdiag
@ search
DirectX Diagnostic Tool. It tests your graphics and sound, then lets you save everything in a text file. Support loves that file.
dxdiag shows which graphics card you really have. Useful for games that ask for system requirements politely.
Click "Save All Information" and attach the text file when you ask for help. It saves a lot of back-and-forth.
There's a note at the bottom of each tab saying "No problems found." It is a very gentle sentence.
The Display tab lists your video memory and driver date. An old driver is an old friend. Maybe too old.
The Sound tab has a test button. Press it only when the volume is not at 100 percent.

## program cleanmgr
> cleanmgr
@ carry
Disk Cleanup. It shows how much space temporary files are hogging. A lot, usually.
Click "Clean up system files" for the bigger savings, like old update leftovers. Look at the list first.
Cleaning the Recycle Bin and temp files here is safe. Reading the checkboxes before you press OK is safer.
The numbers look dramatic. Four gigabytes! Of what? Of leftovers. Of nothing you'll miss.
A spring clean for your disk. Doing it twice a year beats doing it in a panic once.
"Calculating how much space you will be able to free" is a message that can take a long time. It's a mood.

> dfrgui
@ think
Optimize Drives. On a hard disk it defragments. On an SSD it sends a "trim" instead. Same button, different job.
Don't defragment an SSD by hand. Windows already does the right thing for it on a schedule.
The tool reports "OK (0% fragmented)" on healthy drives. That is a pleasant sentence to read on a Monday.
A spinning hard drive still benefits from a defrag now and then. It makes the file pieces closer together, like a tidy desk.
There's a schedule button. Weekly is fine. You'll forget it exists, which is the point.
The defragmenter in the 90s had a block map you could stare at for hours. This one has a table. Society has progressed.

## program msconfig
> msconfig
@ fix
System Configuration. The Startup tab here sends you to Task Manager now. The Boot and Services tabs still do real work.
Use "Hide all Microsoft services" on the Services tab before you disable anything. Otherwise you're switching off Windows.
msconfig is how people do a "clean boot" to find what's making the machine misbehave. Method, not magic.
Selective startup is a good troubleshooting step. Change one thing at a time and restart. Changing five is just chaos.
Don't tick "Safe boot" and forget about it. You'll boot into a very small, very beige Windows.
Change something here only with a reason and a way back. It is a control room, not a toy panel.

## program osk
> osk
@ think
The On-Screen Keyboard. A real help if a key is stuck, and a very slow way to write a letter.
Handy for when a physical key has stopped working. Press it with the mouse and carry on. A noble last resort.

Not many programs have a keyboard that can be dragged around the screen. This one does. It deserves some respect.
If you're here because of a broken key, now is a good time to clean the keyboard. The crumbs you'll find are a surprise.

## program charmap

Character Map. Pick a symbol, press Select, Copy. Great for © and ™ and other things the keyboard won't give you.

## program onedrive

## program anydesk

## program mstsc

@ cool
Remote Desktop Connection. Type a computer name, press Connect, and your office desk appears in a window. Not your office chair, sadly.

## program vncviewer
> vncviewer
@ search
A VNC viewer is open. It shows another computer's screen and lets you click on it. Remote desktop, the old-fashioned way.
VNC sends pixels, not much else, so it works on most systems. It's also a bit slow and, by default, not encrypted. Tunnel it through SSH.
Never expose a VNC port to the internet. Put it behind a VPN or an SSH tunnel and sleep well.
Scaling the remote screen to fit your window makes text unreadable. Use a one-to-one view and scroll. It's an honest view.
VNC stands for Virtual Network Computing. It doesn't stand for "Very Nice Connection", though it can be, on a good day.
A black screen after connecting often means the remote machine is locked or asleep. Wake it up and try again.

## program parsecd
> parsecd | parsec
@ cool
Parsec is running: low-latency screen sharing, famous for streaming games to another computer or a friend's. Works best on a wired connection.
Use Parsec to play from your couch on a laptop while the game runs on your desktop. The laptop's fan will thank you.
Share your Parsec link only with people you trust. Guests can see the screen, and even play, if you let them.
Wi-Fi works, 5 GHz works better, an Ethernet cable works best. Latency doesn't care about your optimism.
Hardware encoding helps. If the stream stutters, check the settings for the hardware decoder before blaming the router.
It's also nice for remote work: a fast desktop in another room, a quiet laptop in your lap.

## program moonlight
> moonlight
@ cool
Moonlight streams games from a PC to another device. It's the open-source client for game streaming, and surprisingly good.
Wired beats wireless. If you must use Wi-Fi, use 5 GHz and sit near the router like a plant by a window.

## program remmina

Remmina, the remote desktop client for Linux. RDP, VNC, SSH and more, with saved connection profiles.

## program keepass

KeePass: a password manager that keeps everything in one encrypted file on your own computer. No cloud, no subscription.

## program dashlane

@ alarm
Dashlane is running. A password manager that fills in logins and warns you about reused passwords. The warnings are fair.
A password health score is only useful if you act on it. Change the three worst ones today, the rest on another day.

## program enpass
> enpass
@ alarm
Enpass: a password manager that keeps your vault on your own devices and syncs it through a cloud you choose.
Use a long master passphrase. Four or five unrelated words beat any clever eight-character mess.
Enpass can fill logins through its browser extension. Always glance at the address bar before you let it.
Keep an emergency copy of your vault in a place you won't forget. A forgotten backup is the same as no backup.

## program nordvpn
> nordvpn | nordvpnd | nordvpn-gui
@ cool
NordVPN is running. A VPN hides your traffic from the network you're on and shows it to the VPN company instead. Pick one you trust.
A VPN is great on public Wi-Fi and for reaching another country's websites. It won't make you anonymous, and it won't speed things up.
Turn on the kill switch. If the VPN drops, it cuts the internet instead of quietly leaking.
Choose a nearby server for speed, a far one for geography. Distance costs milliseconds, not your soul.
Streaming services often block VPN servers. You'll hear "this content isn't available". It's not you.
Don't run two VPNs at once. They argue, and the winner is "no connection".

## program expressvpn
> expressvpn | expressvpnd
@ cool
ExpressVPN is running. One big button turns it on. That one button is most of the product, and the speed.
A VPN encrypts your traffic between your computer and the VPN server. After that, it's as public as ever.
The network lock feature blocks the internet if the VPN drops. Leave it on and don't be surprised by a sudden silence.
Split tunnelling lets some apps use the VPN and others not. Good for work: your office tool stays local, your browser goes global.
If a website says your VPN is "detected", try another server or turn it off for that site. It's rarely worth the argument.
A VPN does nothing about phishing links. You still have to look before you click.

## program openvpn
> openvpn | openvpn-gui
@ cool
OpenVPN is connecting. It reads a .ovpn config file, which your IT department or your provider sent. Keep that file private.
A small tray icon turns green when you're connected. Until then, nothing is protected. Wait for the green.
The log window shows what's going on. "Initialization Sequence Completed" is the line you want. It's the only one you have to remember.
If it keeps failing, check the date and time on your computer. Certificates hate a wrong clock more than you do.
Don't share your .ovpn file. It often contains a key, and keys are meant to be carried by one person.
Disconnect when you're done, or the VPN keeps sending your traffic home for the day.

## program wireguard
> wireguard
@ cool
WireGuard: a VPN that does its job quickly, with a config file you can read in one sitting. Few lines, few surprises.
A tunnel in WireGuard is a config with a private key, a public key and an endpoint. Never share the private one.
It connects almost instantly. If you flip it on and the page loads, it's working. No fanfare required.
Turn the tunnel off when you're at home on the same network as what you're reaching. Sometimes the tunnel is the detour.
WireGuard is built into the Linux kernel. That's why the Linux version is so lean.
If the handshake never completes, check the endpoint address and port first. Nine out of ten times, it's a typo.

## program tailscale
> tailscale | tailscaled | tailscale-ipn
@ cool
Tailscale builds a private network between your own devices. Your laptop can reach your desktop at home as if they were in the same room.
Each device gets a stable name and address. SSH into "homeserver" and don't think about routers again.

Proton VPN is running. It has a free tier with no data limit, which is rare and polite.

## program rufus
> rufus
@ fix
Rufus makes bootable USB sticks from ISO files. Pick the ISO, pick the stick, press Start. It will erase the stick, so check the device name twice.

## program balena-etcher

## program crystaldiskinfo
> diskinfo64 | diskinfo32
@ read
CrystalDiskInfo reads your drive's health data. A blue "Good" means all's well. Yellow "Caution" means back up soon.
The temperature of a drive should stay moderate. If it's hot, check airflow before you worry about the disk.
"Reallocated Sectors Count" climbing is the number to watch on a hard drive. It means the disk is moving data from sick spots.
Power-on hours tell you how old the drive really is. A 40,000-hour drive has done a lot of work.
A "Good" status is not a backup. A backup is a backup. Do the second, even when you see the first.
Check the drive once in a while, not every ten minutes. Staring at SMART values won't improve them.

## program diskmark64
> diskmark64 | diskmark32
@ search
CrystalDiskMark measures how fast your drive reads and writes. The big number on top is sequential speed, great for large files.
Everyday use feels more like the random 4K numbers, which are much smaller. A fast drive is fast in both rows.
Run the test with nothing else going on. A download in the background will spoil the score.
The benchmark writes a test file to the drive, then deletes it. It doesn't harm anything, but a full drive makes slower numbers.
Don't run it over and over on an SSD for fun. It's built to last, but there's no prize for the highest score.
A fast SSD is great. A fast SSD with no backup is a race car with no seat belt.

## program hwinfo64
> hwinfo64 | hwinfo32
@ search
HWiNFO shows every sensor in your computer: temperatures, voltages, fan speeds, clocks. If it has a number, HWiNFO has it.
Run it in "sensors-only" mode to watch temperatures while you play or render. The CPU package temperature is the one to watch.
A processor at 90 degrees under load isn't unusual, but staying there warrants a look at fans and dust.
Dust is the sworn enemy of fans. A can of compressed air costs less than a new cooler.
Cleaning the intake filter every few months does more for your temperatures than any software setting.
Don't panic at a spike. Look at the average. Computers spike for fun.

## program msiafterburner

## program windirstat
> windirstat | wiztree64 | wiztree | wiztree32
@ search
WinDirStat or WizTree: a map of your disk where every file is a coloured block. Big blocks are big files. The picture is the answer.

## program autoruns

## program procexp

## program irfanview

Small, fast, free for personal use, and still updated. A model citizen of the desktop.

## program foobar2000

## program jdownloader2

@ carry
JDownloader handles bulk downloads: paste a link and it finds every file on the page and queues them. Be sure you're allowed to download them.

## program utorrent

A BitTorrent client is open. Perfectly legal for Linux ISOs and other open files, and for sharing things you made.

## program veracrypt
> veracrypt
@ alarm
VeraCrypt encrypts a drive or creates an encrypted container file. Pick a long passphrase and remember it, because nobody can recover it for you.
Back up the volume header after you create a container. It's the one file that could save you from a bad day.
A forgotten password means the data is gone for good. That's not a bug. That's the whole point of the thing.
Dismount the volume when you're done with it. An open volume is just a folder anyone at your keyboard can read.
A small container file is a good way to keep a few sensitive documents safe. It's easier than encrypting a whole drive.
Keep the recovery files and the passphrase in separate places. Two locks, two keys, two rooms.

## program freefilesync
> freefilesync | freefilesync_x64
@ carry
FreeFileSync compares two folders and shows what's different before it changes anything. A sync you can read before you press go.
Choose "Mirror" to make the target identical to the source, or "Two way" to merge both. Check which you picked before you sync.
Deleted files are moved to a versioning folder if you set it up. That small setting is your safety net.
A backup is a copy somewhere else. A sync is a copy that follows your deletions. They're not the same, so choose the right one.
Run a comparison first and look at the arrows. If a big pile of files is about to be deleted, stop and breathe.
Save the job as a .ffs_batch file and schedule it. A backup that runs without you remembering is the best kind.

## program lightroom

## program cura
> ultimaker-cura | cura
@ fix
Cura slices a 3D model into layers for your printer. Load the model, choose the profile, press Slice, save the file.
Check the first layer before you leave the printer. Most failed prints are lost in the first five minutes.
Supports are for overhangs. If you can avoid an overhang by rotating the model, do that instead. Less plastic, less sanding.
Lower layer height gives a finer surface, and a much longer print. For a functional part, 0.2 mm is a fine compromise.
Keep your filament dry. A hissing, stringy print means the plastic has absorbed water from the air.
Slice, preview, then print. Don't skip the preview. The layer view shows the problem before the plastic does.

## program prusa-slicer
> prusa-slicer
@ fix
PrusaSlicer turns a 3D model into instructions for a 3D printer. It has simple and expert modes. Start simple.
Use the preview tab before you print. Scrub through the layers and look for gaps and stringy bits.
Orient the model so its flattest side faces down. It's the oldest tip, and it's still the best.
The "seam" setting decides where each layer begins. Put it at the back, and the front of your print stays tidy.
Print a small test cube when you change a filament. A 20-minute cube beats a 9-hour disappointment.
Cleaning the bed with isopropyl alcohol helps the first layer stick. Fingerprints are the enemy of adhesion.

## program bambu-studio

@ fix
Bambu Studio or OrcaSlicer: slicers for 3D printers. Pick the printer, pick the filament, press Slice.
Look at the preview for the estimated time and filament use. A 14-hour print deserves a second look at the plan.

Take a break. Your real farm, the one with the laundry, also wants a visit.

## program terraria

## program ksp_x64

## program radeonsoftware

@ cool
AMD Software: Adrenalin Edition is open. It handles your graphics driver, game profiles and performance tuning.

## program icue

@ fix
iCUE is open. It controls the lights and fans on Corsair gear. Rainbows are a setting, and you may turn them off.
Fan curves matter more than colours. A quiet computer under load beats a glowing one that sounds like a hairdryer.

## program scummvm

## program dosbox
> dosbox | dosbox-x | dosbox-staging
@ happy
DOSBox runs old DOS programs and games on modern computers. Mount a folder as C: and the 1990s come back, including the sound card setup screen.
Type "mount c ~/dos" then "c:" and run the game. Three lines, and a lost afternoon.
Press Ctrl+F12 to speed up and Ctrl+F11 to slow down. Some old games were meant for a gentler time.
Alt+Enter toggles full screen. Ctrl+F9 closes the emulator when everything freezes.

## program wesnoth

## program mame
> mame
@ party
MAME emulates old arcade machines. The ROMs are your problem, and the legal ones are few. The software is free.
Insert a coin with the 5 key and start with 1. Nostalgia is that simple, and it still costs nothing.

## program hexchat
> hexchat
@ cool
HexChat is open. IRC, the chat protocol from 1988 that never quite left. Type /join #channel and you're in.
Pick a nickname you like. Register it with NickServ so nobody takes it. In IRC, a nick is a name and a promise.

Many open-source projects still answer questions in IRC channels. Say what you tried, then ask. Don't ask "is anyone here?".
Logs are saved on your computer. Remember that the chat history is yours.

## program irssi

Claws Mail is open. A fast, lightweight email client that has been quietly doing its job for many years. No fuss, no cloud, no pop-ups.

Check the "Send later" option to avoid sending angry emails at 11 p.m. A draft is an excellent place for feelings.

## program betterbird

## program todoist

Todoist is open. Type "call mum tomorrow at 5pm" and it understands the date. A small bit of magic for your task list.

## program clockify

## program rescuetime

## program zim

@ write
Zim is a desktop wiki: a notebook of linked pages stored as plain text files. Old-school, quick and very much your own.

## program cherrytree

@ write
CherryTree is a hierarchical notebook. Nodes in a tree, with rich text, code and images on each one. A tidy way to keep a lot of notes.
Use sub-nodes to group related notes. A tree with fifty branches and no structure is just a bush.

The code boxes keep their formatting and highlight syntax. A handy place for the commands you always forget.

## program nano
> nano | pico | micro
@ write
A terminal text editor is open. In nano, Ctrl+O saves ("write out"), Ctrl+X exits and the shortcuts are listed at the bottom, to save the guesswork.
In micro, the keys are the ones you already know: Ctrl+S saves, Ctrl+Q quits, Ctrl+C and Ctrl+V copy and paste. A very polite editor.
In nano, press Ctrl+W to search and Ctrl+\ to search and replace. It's all in the help at the bottom.
Unlike Vim, nano doesn't have modes. You open it, you type, you save. Everybody gets out alive.
If you're editing a system file, use sudo. Otherwise your changes disappear with a confusing "permission denied".
Check the file name before you save. "Untitled" is not a good name for a config file.

## program texstudio

@ read
A LaTeX editor is open. Beautiful documents, a gentle learning curve shaped like a wall, and the joy of a perfect equation.
Compile twice (or let the editor do it) when you add references or a table of contents. The first run collects, the second one fills in.

## program webstorm64

## program thonny

@ happy
A beginner-friendly Python editor is open. Thonny shows variables as you step through code, which makes "why is x 3?" a visible question.
Press F5 to run, F7 to step through. Watching the code run line by line is the best way to understand a loop.
Spyder has a variable explorer and a console side by side. A good fit for data work and experiments.

## program arduino ide
> arduino ide | arduino-ide | arduino | processing
@ fix
Arduino IDE is open. Ctrl+R verifies your sketch and Ctrl+U uploads it to the board. The two buttons that decide your evening.
Select the right board and port under Tools. "Failed to upload" is usually "wrong port" or a charge-only USB cable.
A charge-only cable is the cause of half the world's "my Arduino isn't detected" questions. Use a data cable.

## program sourcetree

## program winmergeu

## program bruno
> bruno | fiddler | mitmweb | mitmproxy
@ search
An API or traffic tool is open. Bruno stores requests as plain files you can commit to Git, which is a pleasing idea for a request tool.

## program ssms
> ssms | heidisql | tableplus | beekeeper-studio
@ search
A database client is open. Run queries, browse tables, and remember which server you're connected to before you press F5.
Always check the connection name before running a query that changes data. "Production" in the corner is a quiet warning.

## program sqlitebrowser
> sqlitebrowser | db browser for sqlite | sqlite3
@ search
DB Browser for SQLite is open. Edits aren't saved until you click "Write Changes" or press Ctrl+S. Everyone forgets once.
A SQLite database is a single file. Copy it, back it up and email it. Simple and portable, like a tiny filing cabinet.
In the sqlite3 command line, .tables lists tables, .schema shows how they're built and .quit gets you out.
Use the "Execute SQL" tab to try queries before you put them in code. It's the fastest way to learn what the data looks like.

## program mongodbcompass
> mongodbcompass | mongodb-compass | redisinsight | mongod | redis-server
@ search
A document or key-value database tool is running. MongoDB stores JSON-like documents, Redis keeps data in memory for speed.
In Compass, filter with a JSON query like {"name": "Ada"}. The documents answer back in order.

## program postgres
> postgres | postmaster | mysql | mariadb
@ coffee
A database server is running in the background. It's the quiet engine behind a lot of apps. Don't stop it mid-write.
Back up with pg_dump or mysqldump regularly, and test the restore at least once. An untested backup is a nice story.

## program nginx
> nginx | caddy | httpd | apache2
@ fix
A web server is running. It receives requests and sends back pages. In the best case, nobody notices it at all.
In nginx, run "nginx -t" to test the configuration before you reload it. It takes a second and prevents a bad evening.

## program php

PHP or Ruby is running a script. Both languages power a surprising part of the web, quietly and mostly reliably.

## program go
> go | dotnet | msbuild | javac | dart
@ think
A compiler or build tool is running. Go, .NET, javac or Dart. A quiet moment while the machine turns text into something that runs.
In Go, "go fmt" formats your code the one true way. No more arguments about tabs.

## program adb
> adb | scrcpy | fastboot
@ fix
ADB or scrcpy is running. adb talks to an Android phone over USB, and scrcpy shows and controls the phone's screen on your computer.
Turn on USB debugging in the phone's developer options. Only connect phones you trust, and accept the key prompt with care.
"adb devices" lists connected phones. If yours isn't listed, check the cable, the mode and the authorisation prompt on the phone.
scrcpy needs no root and no app on the phone. Plug in, run, and the screen appears. The kind of tool you wish had been invented sooner.
"adb logcat" shows the phone's log. A river of text. Add a filter, or you'll drown.
Turn USB debugging off again when you're done. A door you don't use should be closed.

## program kubectl

## program wsl
> wsl
@ cool
Windows Subsystem for Linux is running. A real Linux inside Windows, for the shell and tools without a dual boot or a virtual machine.
Keep your project files inside the Linux file system, not under /mnt/c. File access across the border is much slower.
"wsl --shutdown" restarts the whole subsystem. It's the "turn it off and on again" of WSL, and it works.
WSL can run Linux graphical apps in Windows 11. Yes, really. A tiny Linux window on your Windows desktop.
Update your Linux distribution inside WSL, too. It's a computer inside a computer, and both need updates.
If disk space vanishes, the virtual disk file has grown and doesn't shrink on its own. A compact job is in order.

## program git-bash
> git-bash | mintty | conemu64 | tabby | termius | mobaxterm | securecrt

## program testdisk
> testdisk | photorec | ddrescue | recuva | recuva64
@ fix
A recovery tool is running: TestDisk, PhotoRec, ddrescue or Recuva. If you're here because something got deleted, stop writing to that drive right now.
Every new file written to the drive can overwrite what you're trying to rescue. Recover onto a different disk. This is the one rule.
PhotoRec finds files by their content, so it recovers pictures and documents even when the folder structure is gone. Filenames are not coming back.
ddrescue copies a failing drive carefully and keeps going over the bad bits. Make an image first, work on the image.
Recovery takes patience. Let it finish, and sort the results afterwards.
Once you're done, set up a backup. The best recovery tool is the thing you didn't need.

## program ffmpeg
> ffmpeg | ffplay | ffprobe
@ spin
ffmpeg is running. It converts, trims and squeezes nearly any audio or video. The fans are about to find out how much you asked of them.
Add "-c copy" to cut or rewrap a video without re-encoding. It takes seconds and loses no quality. The best trick it knows.
"-crf 23" is the quality dial for H.264: lower is better and bigger. 18 is nearly invisible, 28 is visible if you look for it.
Put the input file first and the options before the output name. Order matters in ffmpeg, as in many things.
Long encodes are a good time to stand up. The progress line shows the speed: "1.0x" means real time.

## program rsync
> rsync | grsync | luckybackup
@ carry
rsync is copying. It only transfers what's changed, which is why the second run is so much quicker than the first.
Use "-n" or "--dry-run" first. It shows what would happen without doing it. The cheapest insurance in Linux.
A trailing slash on the source folder changes the meaning. "dir/" copies the contents, "dir" copies the folder itself. Everyone gets this wrong once.
"--delete" makes the target match the source, including removing extra files. Powerful, and worth a pause before pressing Enter.
"-avh --progress" is a good default: archive mode, verbose, human-readable sizes and a bar to watch.
rsync over SSH is a nice way to back up to another machine. Fast, encrypted and boring in the best way.

## program dd
> dd | dcfldd
@ alarm
dd is running. It copies raw bytes from one place to another and doesn't ask if you're sure. Check "of=" twice. Then once more.
dd is nicknamed "disk destroyer" by people who got the "of=" wrong. The command is fine. The typing was the problem.
Add "status=progress" to see how far it is. Without it, dd says nothing until the end, like a very confident cat.
Use "bs=4M" for faster copies to USB sticks. The default block size is tiny and the copy is slow.
Run "lsblk" first and be certain which device is which. /dev/sda is not always the one you think.
Don't unplug the stick until "sync" is done, or the command says it's finished. Patience is part of the command.

## program tar
> tar | gzip | xz | zstd | bzip2 | zip | unzip | 7z | 7zz
@ carry
An archiver is working. tar bundles files into one, and gzip, xz or zstd squeeze it. Two steps, one noise: .tar.gz.
"tar -xzvf" unpacks: extract, gunzip, verbose, file. "tar -czvf" packs: create instead of extract. The letters spell nothing, but you'll remember them.
Use "tar -tf" to list what's inside before you extract. Some archives explode into the current folder like a confetti cannon.
xz squeezes harder, zstd works faster. Pick by whether you're in a hurry or have an evening.
Don't tar up your whole home folder without excluding the junk. Browser caches and node_modules make heavy suitcases.
Test an archive after you make it. A backup you can't unpack is a very heavy paperweight.

## program wget
> wget | curl | aria2c | axel
@ carry
A downloader is running: wget, curl or aria2c. No browser, no fuss, just a file and a progress bar.
"wget -c" resumes a half-finished download. Everyone's patience is limited, but a download's should not be.
"curl -O" saves a file under its own name and "curl -L" follows redirects. Two flags that explain most of the web.
Check the checksum of a download if the site offers one. A tiny mismatch means something went wrong on the way.
Don't pipe a script from the internet straight into a shell without reading it. It's convenient, and so is a stranger offering you a drink.
aria2c can download from several connections at once. A kind of turbo mode, for when the server allows it.

## program pandoc
> pandoc | latexmk | pdflatex | xelatex | lualatex

pandoc or LaTeX is converting a document. Pandoc turns Markdown into Word, PDF, HTML and back. A document translator with a very large vocabulary.

## program fsck
> fsck | e2fsck | fsck.ext4 | xfs_repair | btrfs
@ fix
A file system check is running. Do it on an unmounted drive, and let it finish. It's a medical for your disk, and nobody likes being interrupted.
If it asks whether to fix something, "y" is usually right. If you're unsure, run it with "-n" first for a look without changes.
A file system check after a crash is normal. Things were interrupted, and the disk is tidying up the mess.
Lots of errors on a healthy-looking drive is a reason to check the drive itself with smartctl, and to make a backup now.
Don't run it on a mounted disk. The check and the system will disagree about who's in charge.
Files that turn up in "lost+found" afterwards are rescued fragments. Open them and see what's left.

## program smartctl
> smartctl | gsmartcontrol
@ search
smartctl reads your drive's health data. "PASSED" is nice, but it's only the summary. The attributes below tell the real story.
Watch "Reallocated_Sector_Ct", "Current_Pending_Sector" and "Offline_Uncorrectable" on a hard drive. Non-zero numbers mean the drive is struggling.
On an SSD, look at "Percentage Used" and "Available Spare". Those say how much life is left.
A "PASSED" drive can still die next week. A backup is the only reliable test of anything.
Run a short self-test with "smartctl -t short /dev/sda". It takes two minutes and doesn't hurt a bit.
Temperatures above 50 degrees for a hard drive are worth a look at airflow.

## program sudo
> sudo | su | doas | pkexec
@ alarm
sudo is running a command as the administrator. Read the command before you type the password. It's the one moment of the day that deserves your full attention.
"sudo !!" repeats the last command with sudo. It saves you from retyping and from thinking. Use it sparingly.
Avoid "sudo" for things you don't understand. If a tutorial says to run it, check what it's about first.
Don't run a graphical program with sudo. Files it creates in your home folder end up owned by root, and you'll be fighting them later.
The password isn't shown while you type. It's not broken. It's being discreet.
Use the least power you need. A user who can do everything can also break everything.

## program crontab
> crontab
@ alarm
cron is running a scheduled job. Five fields for time, then the command. "*/5 * * * *" means every five minutes, if you can read it.
The fields are minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week. A cheat sheet saves a lot of "why did it run at 3 a.m.?".
cron runs with a tiny environment. Use full paths for commands, or your script will say "command not found" to a silent inbox.
Send the output of jobs to a log file. A job that fails silently is a job nobody knows is failing.
Test the script by hand first. Then schedule it. Not the other way around.
A systemd timer is the modern alternative. It has logs, and it knows if the machine was off. cron has charm.

## program journalctl
> journalctl | systemctl | systemd-analyze | dmesg
@ search
The system's log or service manager is being read. "journalctl -xe" shows the most recent errors with explanations, and it's usually where the answer is.
"journalctl -b" shows this boot only. "-f" follows the log live. "-u name" shows one service. Three flags that cover most of it.
"systemctl status name" tells you whether a service is running and shows its last log lines. Start there.
"systemctl --user" manages your own services, without sudo. A tidy way to run things in the background.
"systemd-analyze blame" shows what slowed your boot. Often it's something you didn't know you had.
Read the first error, not the last. Everything after it is usually fallout.

## program ping
> ping | traceroute | tracepath | mtr | tracert | pathping
@ search
ping or traceroute is running. Ping asks "are you there?" and times the answer. Traceroute asks every router on the way. Press Ctrl+C to stop.
If you can ping an IP address but not a name, the problem is DNS. If you can't ping either, it's the connection.
Pinging 8.8.8.8 tests whether the internet is reachable. Pinging your router tests whether your own network is fine.
High or jumpy ping times mean a busy or weak connection. A steady 20 ms is lovely, a ping of 400 ms is a slideshow.
mtr combines ping and traceroute into a live view of every hop. The best tool for "where is the slowness".
A few lost packets are normal. A lot of them are a reason to check the cable, the Wi-Fi or the provider.

## program nmap
> nmap | zenmap
@ search
nmap is scanning. Only scan networks and machines you own or have permission to test. A port scan on someone else's network is rude, and sometimes illegal.
"nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24" lists the devices on your home network. It's a nice way to find out what's actually on your Wi-Fi.
Open ports aren't bad. Open ports you didn't know about are. Close what you don't use.
"nmap -sV" tries to identify the services and versions. Old versions with known problems are the ones to update first.
A scan takes a while on a big range. Be patient, or narrow the range.
Keep a list of what's expected on your network. The surprises stand out against a list.

## program iperf3
> iperf3 | speedtest | speedtest-cli
@ search
A speed test is running. iperf3 measures the real speed between two machines on your own network. A very honest test, since nothing else is in the way.
Run iperf3 with "-s" on one machine and "iperf3 -c address" on the other. Two commands, and your Wi-Fi's secrets come out.
A speed test measures the moment you ran it. Test at different times, and the real picture emerges.
Wired is faster and steadier than Wi-Fi. If you can plug in, do. A cable is a tiny, honest tunnel.
Close downloads and video calls before a test. A fair measurement needs a quiet network.
A speed far below what you pay for is worth a call. Have the numbers ready, with the time and date.

## program ufw
> ufw | iptables | nft | firewalld | firewall-cmd | gufw
@ alarm
A firewall tool is running. "ufw status" shows the rules, and "ufw enable" turns on the default: block incoming, allow outgoing.
Allow SSH before you enable the firewall on a remote machine. Otherwise you'll lock yourself out and meet the console.
Open only the ports you need. Each open port is a door you have promised to keep an eye on.
Write down what a rule is for. "Port 8080 allowed" tells nothing in a year.
Test from another machine after changing a rule. A rule that looks right and a rule that works are different things.
A home computer behind a router is already fairly safe. A firewall is one more layer, not the whole house.

## program ssh-keygen
> ssh-keygen | ssh-add | ssh-agent | gpg | gpg-agent | pass
@ alarm
A key tool is running. "ssh-keygen -t ed25519" makes a modern SSH key. The private one stays secret, the public one goes to the server.
Protect the private key with a passphrase. A key without one is a house key under the doormat.
ssh-agent remembers the passphrase for your session, so you don't retype it for every connection. A small, trusted butler.
Never send the private key (without .pub) anywhere. Not by email, not in a chat, not to support.
Use a different key for each important job, or at least for work and for personal use. One key to rule them all is a lot of rule.
Back up your keys in an encrypted place. Losing one is an afternoon of regenerating access.

## program certbot
> certbot | lego
@ cool
certbot is requesting a certificate. HTTPS for your site, for free, issued by a machine that checks you own the domain.
Let's Encrypt certificates last 90 days, and certbot renews them automatically. Check that the renewal timer is actually set up.
"certbot renew --dry-run" tests the renewal without changing anything. Run it once and sleep better.
The domain has to point to your server first. A certificate for a name that goes nowhere is a very formal letter to a wall.
Keep ports 80 and 443 reachable during validation. The check knocks, and wants an answer.
An expired certificate is a very visible mistake. Set a reminder as a backup to the automation.

## program snap
> snap | snap-store | appimagelauncher
@ carry
Snap, Flatpak or AppImage is handling an app. Each packs the app with its own libraries, so it runs the same on any Linux.
"snap list" shows installed snaps, "snap refresh" updates them. They also update by themselves, quietly, in the background.
Flatpaks live in their own sandbox with their own permissions. Flatseal is the tool to look at them and adjust.
An AppImage is a single file you make executable and run. No install, no uninstall, no questions. Delete the file and it's gone.
Packaged apps are bigger on disk, because each brings its own libraries. Disk space is cheaper than dependency arguments.
Prefer your distro's own package when there's a good one. Use these when the app you want is only there, or newer.

## program zypper

@ carry
A package manager from another family is running: zypper, Nix, Portage, makepkg, pamac, xbps or apk. Every distro has its own spells for installing things.
Read the list before you confirm the transaction. A change of 200 packages deserves a pause, not a reflex "y".
Refresh the package lists before you install. An old list wants a version that no longer exists.
Update regularly, in smaller steps. A system two years behind is a very long trip with a very long list of broken things.
Nix keeps each package in its own isolated path, so you can roll back. A time machine for your software, if you'll learn the language.
On Arch, read the news before a big update. A pacman -Syu without reading is a roll of the dice with a prompt.

## program mkinitcpio
> mkinitcpio | dracut | update-initramfs | grub-mkconfig | update-grub | grub-install
@ fix
The boot image or the boot loader is being rebuilt. It happens after a kernel change, and it's the one part you really want to finish.
Don't interrupt this. A half-written boot image is the kind of failure that turns an evening into a rescue-stick night.
Keep a fallback kernel or a rescue stick around. The day you need it, you'll be extremely glad you made it earlier.
After editing GRUB's config, regenerate it. The file is generated, so edit the source, not the output.
A power cut during an update is the main danger. A laptop on mains and with a good battery is half the safety.
If it boots, thank it quietly. It's done this a thousand times without a word of praise.

## program krdc

## program k3b
> k3b | brasero | xfburn
@ gift
A disc burning tool is open. Burn at a lower speed for reliability, and tick "verify written data". Slow and sure beats fast and a coaster.
Use CD-R for audio and one-off data, DVD-R for bigger things. Most players like them, and they're cheap.

## program partitionmanager

Back up anything important before you resize or move a partition. It's usually safe and, once in a long while, dramatic.

## program deja-dup

A backup tool is running: Déjà Dup, Pika Backup, Back In Time, Borg, restic or Duplicati. Good. The best time to back up was yesterday, the second best is now.

## program hardinfo

Choose "Custom" instead of "Typical" when a program offers it. You see what's coming along for the ride.
Reboot if the installer asks for it, and don't postpone it for three days. The half-installed state is a bad place to live.
Keep the installer file if the program matters. The website might not have that version in a year.

## program sfc
> sfc | dism | chkdsk | robocopy | defrag
@ fix
A Windows repair command is running: sfc, DISM or chkdsk. These take a long time, and interrupting them is the one wrong move.
"sfc /scannow" checks system files and repairs them. It takes ten minutes and often says it found nothing. "Nothing" is a good result.
If sfc can't fix everything, run "DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth" first, then sfc again. The two work as a team.
chkdsk checks the disk for errors. On a big drive it can take hours, so start it before bed.
robocopy copies folders robustly: it resumes after interruptions and logs every file. Use it for big moves instead of drag and drop.
Run these from an administrator window, and read the summary line at the end. It's the only line that matters.

## program winget
> winget | choco
@ carry
A Windows package manager is running: winget, Chocolatey or Scoop. Install or update programs by typing a name instead of hunting for download pages.
"winget upgrade --all" updates everything in one go. A modest miracle, and a good Saturday-morning habit.
"winget search name" finds it, "winget install name" gets it. Three words, and you've bypassed twelve ads.
Keep a text file of your install commands. A new computer is then an evening, not a weekend.
Check what's being installed before you say yes. A package manager is convenient, not magic.
Updating everything at once is great until one thing breaks. Do it when you have the time to fix it.

Updates are boring, necessary and the reason the news is not full of your computer.

## program stress-ng
> stress | stress-ng | prime95 | occt | furmark | memtester
@ alarm
A stress test is running. It pushes the CPU, memory or graphics card as hard as it can, to see if the machine holds up. The fans are about to have their moment.
Watch the temperatures while it runs. A CPU that goes over 95 degrees is a CPU asking for a break. Stop the test if it gets silly.

## program cinebench
> cinebench | geekbench 6 | 3dmark | aida64 | userbenchmark
@ search
A benchmark is running. It gives your computer a score, which is a number to compare with other numbers. Fun for an evening, meaningless for everything after.
Run it a few times and take the average. One run is a mood, three runs are a pattern.
A laptop on battery will score lower. Plug it in and set the power mode to maximum for a fair result.
Compare your score with others who have the same hardware. If yours is 20 percent lower, something's wrong: cooling, settings or background tasks.
A benchmark doesn't tell you how your computer feels to use. A computer with a lower score and a fast SSD can feel quicker than a raging beast with a slow disk.
Don't buy anything because of a single number. Think about what you actually do with the machine.

## program ngrok
> ngrok | cloudflared

A tunnel tool is running. ngrok and Cloudflare Tunnel make a local server reachable from the internet, with a public address that points to your own computer.

## program kleopatra
> kleopatra | kgpg | gpa
@ alarm
Kleopatra is open. It manages encryption keys (OpenPGP and S/MIME) and lets you sign and encrypt files and email.
Create a key pair, then share only the public key. The private key never leaves your computer, and it needs a strong passphrase.
Back up your private key and the revocation certificate. If you lose the key, the revocation certificate is the only way to say "please ignore this identity".
Verify a person's key fingerprint over a different channel, like a phone call. A key you've never checked is a stranger's key with a nice name.
Set an expiry date on your keys. A key that expires is a key that doesn't get stolen for decades.
Encrypting an email protects the content, not the fact that you sent it. It's a locked letter in a transparent envelope.

## program gdb

@ search
A debugger or tracer is running: gdb, lldb, valgrind, strace or perf. Time to find out what the program is really doing, as opposed to what you think you wrote.

eSpeak reads text out loud. It sounds like a robot with a cold, and it's very useful for testing.
Keep an uncompressed or lossless master. You can always make a small copy. You can't un-squash one.
Check the volume before you play the result. A "normalize" step can make a file much louder than you expect.

## program sensors
> sensors | sensors-detect | lm-sensors
@ search
The sensors command prints temperatures, fan speeds and voltages. It's a quick check on whether the machine is warm, hot or dramatic.
Run "watch -n 2 sensors" to see the numbers update live. Open a heavy program and watch the CPU temperature rise.
Idle CPU temperatures around 30 to 50 degrees are normal. Above 90 degrees under load for a long time deserves a look at the fans and dust.
A fan reading of 0 RPM might be a fan that stops on purpose at low temperatures. It might also be a fan that stopped.
Don't chase the lowest number. A computer is meant to be a little warm. A sudden change is the thing to notice.
Clean the dust out every year or two. A can of compressed air and ten minutes beat any software fix.

## window design
> figma | canva | illustrator | indesign | penpot | lunacy | affinity designer | affinity publisher | scribus | adobe xd | coreldraw | gravit designer

Design work. The most useful skill in this room is knowing when to stop moving things by one pixel.
"{title}" is open. Save a version before you try the bold idea. Bold ideas deserve a safety net.

Use components, styles or symbols for repeated things. Change it once and everything follows. Much better than fixing it forty times.
Align and distribute with the tools, not with your eyes. Your eyes are brilliant, but they get tired around four o'clock.
Export for the right use. PNG or SVG for the screen, PDF for print, and the right resolution for each.
Feedback early beats polish late. Show the rough version to someone and listen to their first reaction.
Take a break and come back. Fresh eyes spot the crooked line in the first second.
Don't use a font you can't license for the project. It's a very common and very avoidable mistake.
A design is done when removing anything makes it worse, not when adding anything makes it better.

## window editing
> davinci resolve | premiere pro | after effects | kdenlive | shotcut | openshot | clipchamp | camtasia | vegas pro | filmora | capcut | lightworks | avidemux
@ party
Video editing. The first cut is always too long, and so is the second. The third is usually fine.
"{title}" is open. Save the project and use auto-save. Editing software crashes with a flair for timing.
Cut on action. A cut in the middle of a movement hides the join and makes the edit feel invisible.
Audio matters more than picture. Viewers forgive a soft image, and not a crackly voice.
Add music after the edit is locked, not before. The beat will want to drive, and it shouldn't.
Use proxies if the timeline stutters. Edit with small files, export from the big ones.
Name and sort your clips into bins. A project of 400 files named "C0042.mp4" is a very long Tuesday.
Export a short test clip before you render the whole thing. Five seconds of output reveals a lot of mistakes.
Keep a copy of the original footage somewhere safe. The edit is the sculpture, the footage is the stone.
Don't use every transition in the list. A hard cut is a transition, and the best one.
Watch the final cut once without touching anything. If you want to fix something, write it down, then fix it.
Rendering takes a while. Go and look at a tree.
If it's for a deadline, export a draft early. A draft on time is better than a masterpiece that's still rendering.
Check the volume at the end. Loudness jumps between clips are the quickest way to annoy your audience.

## window database
> dbeaver | pgadmin | mysql workbench | datagrip | heidisql | sql server management studio | db browser for sqlite | mongodb compass | redisinsight | tableplus | beekeeper studio | phpmyadmin | navicat
@ search
Database work. Before you run anything that changes data, check which server you're connected to.
"{title}" is open. If the connection says "production", slow down. Everyone who has ever deleted the wrong rows was in a hurry.
Write a WHERE clause before you write the rest of an UPDATE or DELETE. It's a seat belt you put on first.
Wrap risky changes in a transaction. If the result looks wrong, ROLLBACK is the best button of the day.
Run a SELECT with the same WHERE first. If it returns the rows you expect, the change will touch the right ones.
Limit your queries when exploring. "SELECT *" on a table of ten million rows is a very long coffee.
Back up before changing structure. Adding a column is easy, and removing one is permanent.
Index the columns you search and join on. A slow query is often a missing index and a faint sense of guilt.
Use EXPLAIN to see how the database plans to run a query. It's the difference between guessing and knowing.
Keep your queries in files under version control. A great query typed once and lost is a great query that has to be invented again.
Don't use the admin account for everyday work. A normal user can't drop the whole database by accident.
Names matter. "tbl_final2_new" is a cry for help, "customers" is a table.
Dates and time zones are the quiet source of most data bugs. Store them in UTC and convert at the edges.
When a result looks surprising, check for NULLs. They're the lurkers of the data world.

## window diagrams
> draw.io | diagrams.net | visio | lucidchart | excalidraw | whimsical | xmind | freeplane | freemind | mindmanager | staruml | plantuml | umlet | yed graph
@ write
Diagrams. A box and an arrow can say more than a page of text, as long as the arrows point the right way.
"{title}" is open. If the diagram needs a legend of its own, it needs a rethink.
Start with a rough sketch on paper or in the tool. The first draft of a diagram is usually a tangle, and that's fine.
Keep to one idea per diagram. A picture that explains three things explains none of them.
Use consistent shapes. If a rectangle means "service" on one page, it shouldn't mean "database" on the next.
Align the boxes and distribute the space. A neat diagram is believed more easily than a crooked one, which is unfair and true.
Flow goes from left to right or from top to bottom. Pick one direction and stay with it.
Label your arrows. An unlabelled arrow is a mystery with a point.
Limit the colours. Two or three with meaning, rather than five for decoration.
Keep the file as editable source next to the exported picture. A diagram you can't edit is a diagram you'll redraw.
Zoom out and look at it as a stranger would. If you can't see the point in five seconds, simplify.
Don't put every detail in one diagram. Make a big one and a detailed one, and link them.
Date your diagram. Systems change, and an old diagram is an ancient map of a country that moved.
When in doubt, delete a box. Most diagrams survive it.

## window remote
> remote desktop | anydesk | teamviewer | rustdesk | remmina | vnc viewer | tightvnc | realvnc | krdc | moonlight | parsec | chrome remote desktop | nomachine | citrix workspace | vmware horizon
@ alarm
A remote session is open. Be careful: what you do now happens on another computer, and it feels exactly like your own.
"{title}" is the window to look at. Check which computer you're on before you shut anything down.
Close the session properly when you're done. A forgotten session is an open door with a light on.
Only accept remote connections you asked for. If a stranger calls and wants to "help", the answer is no.
Don't enter personal passwords in a session on someone else's machine. It's their computer, and their keyboard.
A slower connection benefits from lower colour depth and a smaller window. Pixels cost bandwidth.
In a full-screen remote session, move the pointer to the top to find the toolbar. It's hiding, politely.
Copying files over a remote session works, but a cloud folder or a proper file transfer is faster for big ones.
Don't leave a remote desktop signed in on a laptop you take away. Lock it or log off.
Tell the person on the other side what you're about to do. It's polite, and it avoids a heart attack at the mouse pointer.
A remote connection is only as safe as its password. Long, unique, and not on a sticky note under the monitor.
Two screens, one keyboard, one brain. It's easy to type into the wrong window, so look before you press Enter.
Update the remote software on both sides. An old remote tool is the very thing that visitors with bad manners look for.
Shut the session when the work is done. The server can be very patient and very bored.

## window audio
> audacity | fl studio | ableton live | reaper | ardour | lmms | cubase | studio one | bitwig | garageband | cakewalk | musescore | hydrogen | qtractor | tenacity | ocenaudio | adobe audition | pro tools | mixxx
@ music
Making sound. Check the input level before you record. A clipping take can't be fixed, a quiet one can.
"{title}" is open. Save a new version regularly: song_v1, song_v2, song_v3. "final_FINAL" is a trap, and a tradition.
Record the best take you can instead of fixing a bad one later. "Fix it in the mix" is a rumour.
Use headphones when you mix and speakers to check. The two tell different truths.
Turn the monitor volume down before you press play. A project that opens at full blast is a very short career.
Listen to your mix at a low volume. If it sounds good quietly, it will sound good loudly.
Take a break every hour. Your ears get tired before you do, and tired ears lie.
Name your tracks. "Audio 14" is not a drum.
Back up the whole project folder, not just the project file. The samples are in there, and so are your Sundays.
Don't layer fifty sounds if three will do. Space in a mix is an instrument.
Use a reference track. Compare yours to a song you love, and see what's different.
If it hums or hisses, check the cables first. Digital audio is great, and a loose plug still wins.
A finished track is better than a perfect loop. Export it, name it, and hit send before you start the next one.
Check the buffer size. A small buffer gives low latency and sometimes crackles. A larger one is safer when mixing.

## window modeling
> blender [ | .blend | freecad | openscad | sketchup | autocad | fusion 360 | solidworks | tinkercad | ultimaker cura | prusaslicer | bambu studio | orcaslicer | meshlab | zbrush | autodesk maya | cinema 4d | houdini | rhinoceros | librecad
@ fix
3D modelling. Everything is a shape, and the shape is always almost right.
"{title}" is open. Save a new version before a big boolean or a scary modifier. Undo is brave, backups are braver.
Save often and in increments. 3D programs crash with a flair for the moment after the hardest part.
Work in real-world units from the start. A table that's 2 metres or 2 kilometres wide is a very different table.
Keep the model simple until you need detail. A million polygons is easy to make and very slow to move.
For 3D printing, check that the model is watertight and has walls thick enough to print. The slicer will tell you, with feeling.
Name your objects. "Cube.003" is a cube, "Wheel_left" is a wheel.
Apply your scale before you export or modify. A hidden scale factor is a source of very strange problems.
Use reference images. A good model starts with a good look at the real thing.
Check the model from every angle before you call it finished. Your front view is lovely and your back view is a hollow shell.
Take a break and rotate the model in your mind. Spotting a wonky proportion often needs a rested brain.
Back up the project folder, including the textures. A model without its textures is a grey statue.
Render settings take time. Test at low quality first, then raise it for the final pass.
If it's for printing, print a small test version first. Failing at 20 percent size costs 20 percent of the plastic.

## window virtual
> virtualbox | [running] | oracle vm | vmware workstation | vmware player | vmware fusion | virt-manager | virtual machine manager | gnome boxes | hyper-v manager | qemu | parallels | windows sandbox | multipass | proxmox | esxi | docker desktop | podman desktop
@ spin
A virtual machine is open: a computer inside a computer. A very good place to be brave.
"{title}" is the window to look at. Take a snapshot before you try something risky. That's the whole point of the thing.
Check the "host key" so you can release the mouse. In VirtualBox it's usually the right Ctrl, and everyone has once been trapped.
Don't give the virtual machine more than half your memory. The real computer still has to breathe.
Install the guest tools or guest additions. They make the mouse smooth and the screen resizable. It feels like a luxury, and it's mandatory.
A snapshot isn't a backup. If the disk file is damaged, so are all its snapshots.
Don't store anything precious only inside the VM. It's a sandbox, and sandboxes are meant to be swept.
A virtual machine uses real battery. Plug in for long experiments.
Use a shared folder to move files in and out. It's the least fiddly door.
A sandbox is perfect for installing the odd program from a website you don't know. Look at it, close it, and everything's gone.
Disk files grow and rarely shrink. A year-old VM may weigh more than you remember.
Keep an updated base image and clone from it. Setting up the same VM from scratch every time is a charming way to lose a weekend.
Close the VM properly, or save its state. Pulling the plug on a virtual machine is just as rude as on a real one.
Remember which window you're in. Typing a password into the host instead of the guest is an eternal slip.

## window passwords
> keepassxc | keepass | bitwarden | 1password | lastpass | dashlane | enpass | proton pass | nordpass | password safe | passwords and keys | kwallet | seahorse | roboform | yubico authenticator
@ alarm
A password manager. It's open, which means you're doing the right thing. Please leave it open at exactly the right moments and not a second longer.
Use a long, unique master password: four or five unrelated words work better than one clever one.
Turn on two-factor authentication for the manager itself. A lock for the safe, not just for what's inside.
Let the manager generate passwords. A random 20-character one beats anything you can think of, and you'll never need to remember it.
Never reuse a password. One leak in one place opens every door you used it on.
Check the address before you auto-fill. A look-alike site will happily accept your credentials.
Lock the vault when you leave your desk. Auto-lock after a few minutes is a setting, and it's your friend.
Back up the vault and keep an emergency copy somewhere safe. Losing the master password usually means losing the lot.
Use the built-in breach check if it has one. Learning that an old password leaked is a little unpleasant and a lot useful.
Clear the clipboard after copying a password. Most managers do it automatically after a few seconds. Leave that on.
Update your recovery details. An email you no longer use is not a recovery plan.
Save the codes for two-factor in a safe place too. A phone in a lake takes your codes with it.
Change your most important passwords first: email, then banking, then everything else. The order matters.
Don't share a master password. If someone needs access, there's a sharing feature for that.

## window ebooks
> calibre | kindle | .epub | .mobi | .azw3 | kobo | foliate | fbreader | adobe digital editions | thorium reader | sigil | libby | readest | koodo reader
@ read
Reading a book on a screen. Settle in. The best feature of an ebook is that it doesn't mind you reading at two in the morning.
"{title}" is open. Adjust the font size and margins to what your eyes like. A comfortable page is a page you finish.
Use night mode in the evening. White on black, or a warm sepia, is kinder than a lit-up white rectangle.
Highlight the sentences you love, and note why. A year from now, the notes are the book.
Use the search to find a name you've forgotten. Reading a thriller with fifty characters is easier with Ctrl+F.

Take a break and look at something far away. Screens, even gentle ones, tire the eyes.
Keep your library backed up. A thousand books on one disk is a very big shelf in a very small house.
