Tip: Ctrl+Shift+F searches all notes in Obsidian. The best filing system is a good search box.
Tip: Markdown works in most note apps: # for a heading, - for a list, - [ ] for a checkbox. It's a few symbols you'll never forget.
Tip: Put the date at the start of a file name as year-month-day. Notes sort themselves in order.
Tip: Ctrl+N makes a new note in Obsidian. Capture the thought first, and tidy it later.

## tips design
Tip: In Figma, Ctrl+D duplicates the selection, and holding Alt while dragging copies it as you move. Two ways to make more of the same.
Tip: Shift+A in Figma adds auto layout. Elements space themselves, and the design stops falling apart when the text changes.
Tip: Ctrl+Alt+K turns your selection into a component in Figma. Change the main one and every copy follows.
Tip: Shift+1 zooms to fit the whole canvas in Figma, and Shift+2 zooms to your selection. Fast navigation beats a lot of scrolling.
Tip: Hold Space and drag to pan around in Figma and Illustrator. The scroll bar is an old, slow road.
Tip: Ctrl+Y in Illustrator switches to outline view. You see the paths, and the stray point you've been hunting for.
Tip: In Illustrator, V is the selection tool, A the direct selection tool and P the pen. Three keys cover most of the day.

## tips editing
Tip: Space plays and pauses in nearly every video editor. If a key does nothing else, it does that.
Tip: J, K and L shuttle backwards, stop and forwards in Premiere Pro and DaVinci Resolve. Tap L again to speed up.
Tip: I and O set the in and out points on a clip in Premiere Pro and Resolve. Mark the good bit, then drop it into the timeline.
Tip: In Premiere Pro, Ctrl+K cuts the clip at the playhead, and C picks the razor tool. In Resolve, B picks the blade.
Tip: Press M to drop a marker at the playhead in Premiere Pro and Resolve. A tiny flag at a spot you'll want to find again.
Tip: Home and End jump to the start and the end of the timeline. Good for a quick look at the whole thing.
Tip: Shift+Z fits the whole timeline in the window in Resolve, and the backslash key does it in Premiere. Zoom out and see the shape of the edit.

## tips database
Tip: In DBeaver, Ctrl+Enter runs the current statement and Alt+X runs the whole script. Know which one you pressed.
Tip: Ctrl+Shift+F formats SQL in DBeaver. A messy query is a puzzle, a tidy one is a question.
Tip: In SQL Server Management Studio, F5 or Ctrl+E runs the query. Select a few lines first and only those run.
Tip: Ctrl+R shows and hides the results pane in SSMS. Handy when you want to see more of the query.
Tip: In DB Browser for SQLite, press Ctrl+S to write your changes. Until then, they only exist in the window.
Tip: Put EXPLAIN in front of a query in PostgreSQL or MySQL to see how it will run. It's the best way to find out why something is slow.
Tip: Use LIMIT 100 (or TOP 100 in SQL Server) when exploring a big table. You'll see the shape of the data without waiting for the whole of it.

## tips remote
Tip: Inside a Remote Desktop session, Ctrl+Alt+End does what Ctrl+Alt+Del would. The local computer keeps the real one.
Tip: Ctrl+Alt+Break switches a Remote Desktop session between full screen and a window. Useful when you're trapped in the far room.
Tip: Ctrl+Alt+Home shows the connection bar in a full-screen Remote Desktop session. It hides at the top, and so does your cursor.
Tip: In Remote Desktop, "Save As" stores the settings in an .rdp file. Keep one per server with a name you'll recognise.
Tip: The Local Resources tab decides whether the clipboard and drives are shared. If you can't paste into the session, look there.
Tip: The Experience tab lets you pick a slower connection and turn off visual effects. A lighter picture on a thin line.
Tip: VNC isn't encrypted by default. Run it through an SSH tunnel, with ssh -L 5901:localhost:5901 user@host, and connect to localhost.

## tips audio

## tips virtual

## tips passwords

## site writing googledocs
> - google docs
@ write
+ Take a note = notes
Google Docs. Ctrl+Alt+M adds a comment on the selection, which is the polite way to say "this sentence is a problem".
Ctrl+Alt+Shift+H opens the version history. Every sin of the past three weeks, with timestamps.
Ctrl+Shift+V pastes without formatting. Spare your document the font of the website it came from.

## site spreadsheet googlesheets
> - google sheets
@ think
+ Timer 20 minutes = timer 20m Spreadsheet
Google Sheets. F4 cycles a reference between relative and absolute, a handy way to stop $ signs from becoming a chore.
Ctrl+; inserts today's date and Ctrl+Shift+: inserts the time. Not a function, just a key.
Ctrl+Space selects a column and Shift+Space a row. A good way to stop dragging a mouse over thousands of cells.
IMPORTRANGE pulls data from another sheet. It asks for permission once, then does it forever.
ARRAYFORMULA lets one formula fill a whole column. One cell, one formula, a hundred results. Efficient.
XLOOKUP and QUERY are in here. QUERY lets you ask a sheet questions in a small language that looks like SQL.
If a number looks wrong, click the cell and read the formula. The error is usually the one you wrote at 4 p.m.
Colour is for emphasis. Colour on every row is for confusion.

Notes are stored on your server, in a database. Back up the database and you have your notes.
Many universities and clubs run one for lecture notes. A very wholesome use of a server.
Slide mode is built on reveal.js. Press S for speaker view in the presentation. Two screens, calm presenter.
Permission levels let you choose who edits, who comments and who just reads. Pick the right level.
Easy to host on a small server. A project for a weekend, with a pleasant afterglow.
If the document is important, copy it out regularly. Good tools are still tools.

## site notes etherpad
> etherpad
@ read
Etherpad. The plain collaborative text editor from the early days of "everyone type at once". Colours show who wrote what.
The timeslider is the clever bit: drag it and watch the pad rewrite itself from the first character to the latest.
No account needed, just a link. It is why many hackerspaces and clubs have a pad for everything.
A pad link is a door with no lock. Do not paste anything private in there, and give it a hard-to-guess name.
Export the pad as HTML, plain text or ODF when the meeting is over. The pad itself may vanish.
Chat in the sidebar lets you ask "who just deleted my paragraph?" without a long email chain.
It does one thing and does it well: lots of people typing in one place without fighting. Mostly.
Before closing the tab, copy the useful bits somewhere safe. Pads are for the moment.

## site notes cryptpad
> cryptpad
@ write
CryptPad. A suite of end-to-end encrypted documents, spreadsheets, kanban boards and slides. The server can't read them.
The link contains the key, so it is both the way in and the secret. Treat it like a password.
Created by a team in France, and a regular guest at privacy-minded gatherings. A friendly project.
Real-time editing works in the encrypted pads. You see the other cursor while the server stays blind.
Drive in CryptPad is where all your pads live. Forget the link, and the drive remembers.
If you lose the password to your CryptPad account, no one can recover it. This is the price of true privacy.
Not the fastest editor in the world, but it is quite surprising how much it can do with no peeking.
Sensitive meeting minutes belong here. The pizza order does not need encryption.

## site notes pastebin
> pastebin
@ read
Pastebin. A place to paste text and get a link. A code snippet, a log, a very long error message to show a friend.
Set an expiry date when you paste. Logs and snippets rarely need to live forever.
Never paste passwords, tokens or private keys here. Public means public, even if the link is hard to guess.
Syntax highlighting makes a snippet readable. Pick the language from the menu before you hit Create.
A paste link is easier than a screenshot of text. People can copy from it, search it and not squint.
Some sites show a lot of ads around the paste. A cleaner alternative exists, if the ads bother you.
Raw view gives only the text. Handy for downloading, or for pasting into a terminal.
After sharing the link, check that it shows what you meant. A wrong paste in a support ticket is awkward.

## site writing overleaf
> overleaf
@ write
Overleaf. LaTeX in the browser. Ctrl+Enter recompiles, and a green button is the nicest thing you will see all day.
"Undefined control sequence" means a command is misspelled or a package is missing. It is usually a typo.
"Overfull hbox" is a warning that a line sticks out into the margin. It is a warning, not an emergency. Mostly.
The template gallery has a layout for thesis, CV, poster and paper. Starting from a template saves a weekend.
Track changes and comments help when a supervisor needs to see what you changed.
References come from a .bib file. Keep it clean, and the bibliography is almost automatic.
Compile timeout means the document is too heavy. Cut the biggest image or compile in draft mode.
Pretty documents do not write themselves. The words come first, the typesetting after.

## site writing grammarly
> grammarly
@ write
Grammarly. A very polite proofreader that sits in your browser and underlines things in red and blue.
It checks what you type, so keep passwords and anything private out of the text box it is watching.
Suggestions are suggestions. Sometimes the original sentence was better. You are allowed to say no.
The tone detector tells you whether an email sounds "formal" or "confident". Sometimes it says "worried". It has a point.
The premium offers are loud. The free version is enough for most emails.
For long documents, read the text aloud. Ears catch what underlines cannot.
It does not know your name, your company or your cat. Add them to the dictionary and the red lines go away.
Great for catching "their" and "there". Not great for catching "I should not send this".

## site writing languagetool
> languagetool
@ read
LanguageTool. A proofreader that handles German, French, Spanish and a few dozen other languages, not only English.
It started in Germany and is partly open source. The free version is generous, which is nice to see.
Switching the language of the text is a click. Writing a mail in two languages is no reason to see red squiggles.
It spots commas, capitals and style quirks. The German commas alone make the whole thing worth installing.
It checks the text on a server, so for confidential material, read the privacy notes or use the local version.
A style check can flag filler words and long sentences. A sentence of forty words is a bold act.
Good for letters to the landlord, the authority and the aunt. The same tone, different formality.
When it is done, read the text once more without the underlines. They are guides, not judges.

## site writing wordpress
> wordpress
@ read
WordPress. A site, a dashboard and a to-do list of updates. If a plugin has not been updated in three years, consider replacing it.
The first post on a new site is called "Hello world!" and many sites keep it. A tiny monument to enthusiasm.
The block editor is easier if you use "/" to add blocks. Type a slash and a word, and the block appears.
Back up the site before big updates. A plugin and a theme sometimes argue, and the loser is your homepage.
Keep the login URL and password out of sight. A strong password and two-factor login keep the guests out.
Categories and tags are different. Categories are for the table of contents, tags are for the index.
Preview the post on mobile. Half your readers see it on a phone. A tiny screen reveals a lot of sins.
Publishing is one button. Writing is the rest. Take your time and press it when it is good.

## site writing jimdo
> jimdo
@ think
Jimdo. A website builder from Hamburg for people who want a site for the bakery, the band or the book club without learning code.
Pick a template, change the text, add a photo, press publish. The hard part is deciding what to put on the "About" page.
A page with fewer words and a bigger photo is almost always better. People skim. Let them.
Add contact details and opening hours before anything else. That is the page people actually come for.
A custom domain costs a bit extra, and looks better on a business card. Worth thinking about.
Check the site on a phone. Some people only ever see it there.
Update the "latest news" section or remove it. A news page from 2019 is a time capsule with dust.
Spell check the opening hours twice. A site that opens at the wrong time is a site that opens to no one.

## site slides prezi
> prezi
@ read
Prezi. The presentation tool where slides are a big zoomable canvas. Spectacular when it works. A bit dizzy when it does not.
A zoom from the whole map to a tiny detail is a lovely effect. Ten zooms in a row is a roller coaster.
Plan the path first. A big canvas without a path is a very pretty mess.
Fewer zooms, shorter text. Use the movement to move the story, not just to be showy.
Export a PDF as a backup. Fancy tools and flaky Wi-Fi do not always get along.
Practise the talk once with the real tool. The first time is not the time to find the shortcut for "next".
People remember about three things from a talk. Make sure the zoom helps them remember.
Presenting live? Stand up straight and breathe. The canvas does the rest.

## site slides slideshare
> slideshare
@ write
SlideShare. A huge archive of other people's slide decks, from conference talks to the leftovers of a very ambitious sales pitch.
A good deck can be read without the speaker. Most cannot. You will know within three slides.
Search with a year in it. Tech decks from 2012 are a charming sort of wrong.
Download the PDF or the original, if the author allows it. Read it offline on the train.
Look at how people arrange their ideas. You will pick up a trick in two minutes.
When your own deck is dull, look at an inspiring one for five minutes. Then fix yours.
Reading decks is also a form of procrastination, but a respectable one. Respectable procrastination counts.
Close the tab when you have found your slide. The rest of the library will still be there tomorrow.

## site slides speakerdeck
> speaker deck | speakerdeck
@ think
Speaker Deck. Slides from talks and conferences, shared as PDFs. A neat, quiet library for people who give presentations about code.
The deck is the PDF, so it renders the same everywhere. No broken fonts, no missing animations.
A deck about a code topic is usually 30 slides, 12 of them diagrams, and one that just says "Questions?"
If you want to practice your own talk, look at the decks with the fewest words. They are usually the best.
Share a link with your slides after the talk. People will ask for it anyway.
Put the title and the date on the first slide. Future you will search for it.
A slide is not a document. Keep the details in your notes.
When you are done browsing, go write your own talk. Start with the title and the first slide.

## site pdf ilovepdf
> ilovepdf
@ write
iLovePDF. A pile of small tools for PDFs: merge, split, compress, rotate and the odd conversion. Handy when you need one fix and no software.
Merging scans of passport, contract and bank statement into one PDF is the most common job. Check the order first.
The files are uploaded to a server and deleted after a while. For anything sensitive, use a local tool instead.
Compress shrinks a large PDF so it fits an email limit. Fine for sending, not for printing a poster.
Rotate a sideways scan with one click. The scanner has a different idea of "up". You can overrule it.
Number the pages and add a watermark if you need to. A tiny "DRAFT" across the page works like a charm.
Free daily limits exist. If you have a stack, plan your batch so it fits in one go.
After merging, scroll through the whole result once. A page upside down in the middle is a classic.

## site pdf smallpdf
> smallpdf
@ cool
Smallpdf. A web toolbox for PDFs from Zurich: compress, merge, edit, sign and convert. A bit like a very friendly photocopier.
Free use is limited by tasks per day. When the limit appears, either plan your batch or use a local tool.
Signing a PDF here means drawing, typing or uploading a signature. For legal paperwork, check what the other side accepts.
"Edit PDF" lets you add text and shapes on top of the page. It is not a word processor, so keep it simple.
Converting a PDF to Word works well for plain text and badly for fancy layouts. Look at the result before trusting it.
Do not upload private documents if you do not have to. A local tool never sends anything away.
Name the output file clearly. "document (3).pdf" is not a name, it is a cry for help.
After you download, delete the copy from your Downloads. A pile of PDFs is a pile of paper without the paper.

## site pdf issuu
> issuu
@ think
Issuu. Magazines, brochures and catalogues rendered as page-turning PDFs. A bit like a waiting room without the chairs.
A catalogue from your local shop might be here. It is the same as the paper one, only with less paper.
Zoom in with the slider or double-click on a page. Small print is small in any format.
Fullscreen mode makes it a calm place to read. Dim the room for the full magazine effect.
Look at the date of the issue. Last year's "autumn trends" are this year's "oh, that."
You can search inside most publications. Type a name and it jumps to the right page.
Many publishers use it for annual reports. A long PDF is a long PDF, whatever it wears.
Close the tab when you are done. A magazine does not need an audience, but it does enjoy one.

## site files cloudconvert
> cloudconvert
@ write
CloudConvert. A web tool that converts almost any file into almost any other: HEIC to JPG, DOCX to PDF, MKV to MP4.
The files are uploaded, converted on a server and then deleted after a while. For private files, use a local tool.
Settings let you tweak quality, size and codec. Defaults are fine for most things.
On Linux, ImageMagick, ffmpeg and pandoc do the same locally from the terminal. Fast and with no upload bar.
A free account has a daily limit. Plan the batch, or the tool will ask you to wait or pay.
Check the output file before deleting the original. Never convert and discard in the same breath.
Converting a photo from HEIC means a phone is sending you images in a format that does not open everywhere. Welcome.
When done, close the tab. The server clears the files, but a clean Downloads folder is your task.

## site projects jira
> - jira | jira software
@ alarm
+ Take a note = notes
Jira. Press "c" to create an issue and "/" to search. Two keys that shorten a long afternoon.
Pressing "." opens a quick-actions menu on an issue. A little hidden shelf of verbs.
JQL, the query language, finds exactly the tickets you mean. "assignee = currentUser() AND status != Done" is a good start.
A ticket with forty comments and no description is an archaeological site. Write the summary first.
Story points are a way of agreeing that something is "medium". Nobody knows what a medium is, but the team agrees on it.
Moving a ticket to Done feels good. Moving it to Done before it is done feels better, and costs more.
Check the board before standup. It saves everyone listening to "yesterday I worked on Jira".
Updating the status is part of the job. It is the part that makes everyone else stop asking.
A ticket that has sat in "In Progress" for three weeks is not in progress. It is in hiding.

## site projects trello
> trello
@ alarm
Trello. Hover over a card and press "space" to assign it to yourself, "d" for the due date, "l" for labels. Mouse optional.
Press "q" to filter the board down to your own cards. The rest of the team dissolves into the background.
"c" archives a card. Gone from the board, not from the world. It is a recycling bin with good manners.
Butler is the built-in automation. "When a card moves to Done, tick the checklist." Ten minutes of setup, hours of saved clicks.
A list called "Done" with 600 cards is not a list, it is a memorial. Archive the old ones monthly.
Cards with a due date turn red when they are overdue. A tiny, silent colour that has been right many times.
Three columns are enough for most things: To Do, Doing, Done. Add a fourth and you are managing the board, not the work.
Checklists inside a card keep the card small. A card with 14 steps is really a project in disguise.
The best board is one you open every morning. Perfect boards you never open do not count.

## site projects asana
> - asana | asana.com
@ write
Asana. Press Tab+Q to add a task from anywhere in the app. A sensible shortcut for a very busy tool.
When you complete a task, a unicorn or a narwhal sometimes flies across the screen. It is the best part of the working day.
"My Tasks" is the page to live in. Everything assigned to you is there, sorted by the date it is due.
Projects can be viewed as a list, a board or a timeline. Same tasks, different mood.
Sections inside a project are a quiet way to group tasks without making a new project each time.
Dependencies tell you what has to be done first. Useful when someone else's task is blocking yours.
A due date on every task is more than the project needs. Put dates on the ones that matter.
Assigning a task to "everyone" is assigning it to no one. Pick a name.
At the end of the week, check what is overdue. The list is shorter than it feels.

## site projects linear
> – linear | linear.app
@ cool
Linear. Press "c" to create an issue and Ctrl+K for the command menu. The whole app is meant to be driven by the keyboard.
Issues are short, statuses are few and cycles end on schedule. It has opinions, and they are mostly tidy.
Cycles are like sprints with fewer meetings. A fixed period, a list, a finish line.
The issue ID is part of the git branch name if you copy it from the issue. Handy when you open the pull request.
Triage is a separate inbox. Newly reported issues land there until someone decides what to do with them.
Linear is fast. If it feels slow, the rest of the internet is slow. Check your Wi-Fi.
Projects and roadmaps give the big picture. The big picture is good to look at once a week, not once an hour.
Writing a good title is half the job. "Fix bug" is not a title. "Fix crash on save with empty name" is.

## site projects clickup
> clickup
@ alarm
ClickUp. The "one app to replace them all" that has a view for everything. Lists, boards, Gantt charts and more.
Features are many and the settings are deep. Pick three features and leave the rest for a quiet Friday.
Custom statuses per list keep each project truthful. "Blocked" and "Waiting for client" are very honest statuses.
Templates for onboarding, sprints and content calendars save a morning each. Use them as a starting point.
A task with six assignees, nine subtasks and four custom fields is an enthusiasm. Simplify.
Notifications can be tuned per list. A quieter inbox helps you do the tasks, not only be told about them.
Docs inside ClickUp keep the plan and the tasks in one place. The tab bar thanks you.
A tool that does everything is also a tool that can distract you with everything. Pick one view and stay in it.

## site projects monday
> monday.com
@ think
monday.com. Colourful boards for projects, with status columns that look like a traffic light and feel like a mood.
"Working on it", "Stuck", "Done". Those three statuses do the heavy lifting. Keep them honest.
Automations are phrased like sentences. "When status changes to Done, notify Anna." Pleasantly readable.
Each board can be switched to a calendar, a Kanban or a chart. Same data, new view, no data entry.
People on the board get their own avatars. A very visual way of finding out who owns too many things.
The name is a Monday joke, so it can be a mild shock when you open it on a Sunday night.
Keep the board lean. Twelve columns of fields no one fills in is a hobby.
A weekly review of the board takes ten minutes and saves several meetings.

## site projects basecamp
> basecamp
@ fix
Basecamp. To-dos, message boards, files and group chat, all in one place, with a strong opinion that you do not need more than that.
Hill charts show a project as "figuring it out" on the way up and "making it happen" on the way down. A rare honest way to say "I don't know yet".
"Campfire" is the group chat. A small digital fire, around which you can say "who has the file?"
Message boards replace the long email thread. A post, a few replies, a calm tone.
"Check-ins" ask the team a question on a schedule. "What did you work on?" It replaces a meeting. Mostly.
Fewer features means fewer arguments about features. A small advantage with a big reward.
Everyone sees the same list. A task that disappears is a task that someone finished. A pleasant mystery.
Do not let the to-do list become the work. Ten minutes of ticking boxes, then do something.

## site projects confluence
> - confluence | – confluence
@ think
Confluence. The company wiki, with pages in a tree and an unspoken rule that the one you need was last edited in 2019.
Type "/" to insert a macro, a table, a status label or a code block. The editor is smarter than it looks.
"Page tree" in the sidebar shows where a page lives. It is also where pages go to be forgotten.
A page called "Meeting notes" with no date is a page nobody will find. Put the date in the title.
Use labels to tag pages. Search finds labels faster than it finds good intentions.
Page history shows what changed. Useful when somebody "tidied" the architecture overview into a haiku.
Do not write a page that nobody will read. Write one that two people will actually use.
When you find a stale page, update it or mark it. A quick fix helps the next person.

## site projects azuredevops
> azure devops | dev.azure
@ think
Azure DevOps. Boards for work items, Repos for code, Pipelines for builds. A whole development workflow under one roof.
Work items, epics, features and user stories: four ways of saying "a thing that must be done".
A pipeline that sits in "queued" is waiting for an agent. Be patient. Or ask who ate the agents.
Link your commits to a work item with "AB#123". Tidy history, easy review.
YAML pipelines are version-controlled with the code. A change to the build is a pull request too.
A failed pipeline is only a message. Read the last 20 lines of the log before you do anything dramatic.
Branch policies make a pull request require a review and a green build. A small guardrail on a long road.
Keep an eye on who has access. A former colleague with admin rights is a very polite ghost.

## site projects youtrack
> youtrack
@ write
YouTrack. JetBrains' issue tracker, with a command box that lets you change many fields by typing a line.
Search queries are plain and forgiving: "for: me #Unresolved" shows what you have to do.
Issue state, priority and type are quick to change. Use them, so the board is not a work of fiction.
Agile boards group issues by state and sprint. Dragging a card across is the day's tiniest victory.
Time tracking can be added to issues. Honest numbers beat flattering numbers.
Knowledge base articles in YouTrack keep the answers next to the issues. Handy for "how did we fix this last time?"
A short, clear description saves five questions. Add steps to reproduce and the expected result.
Close the issues that are really done. An open list full of "maybe" is a very long maybe.

## site projects redmine
> redmine
@ write
Redmine. An old and faithful open-source tracker that sits on a server at a hundred small companies and has never been replaced.
Issue numbers are short and permanent, like "#1432". People remember them because they have been mentioned in so many emails.
It handles wikis, time entries, Gantt charts and roles. The interface looks like 2010, but the power is solid.
Custom fields let you track whatever your team needs. Add the three you actually use and skip the rest.
Plugins exist for almost everything, and some of them have not been updated in a while. Test before upgrading.
Self-hosted means you own the backup. Test the restore at least once a year.
A tracker that people use is a tracker that people are not afraid of. Keep forms short.
If the issue is vague, ask a question in the first comment, not three days later.

## site projects todoist
> todoist
@ alarm
Todoist. Type "tomorrow 3pm" or "every Monday" in a task and it understands. Natural language is the whole trick.
Press "q" for quick add from anywhere in the app. A task caught in two seconds is a task not forgotten.
Priorities are P1 to P4. If everything is P1, nothing is P1.
Karma points reward you for finishing tasks. A little number that is surprisingly motivating.
The Today view is where to live. Everything due today, plus whatever you rolled over from yesterday.
Recurring tasks like "every 2 weeks" are a good use of the app. Water the plants. Pay the thing. Call Mum.
Labels and filters are strong, but keep them simple. A list of fifty labels is not a system.
Clearing the list every evening is optional, but a very pleasant way to end a day.

## site projects ticktick
> ticktick
@ fix
TickTick. A to-do app with a built-in pomodoro timer, a habit tracker and a calendar. A very busy little pocket.
The focus timer runs next to your task. Twenty-five minutes on, five off. The tomato is optional.
Habits live next to tasks. Drink water, stretch, read. A tick a day keeps the streak alive.
Smart lists group tasks by date, tags or priority. It is a view, not a bureaucracy.
Reminders can be repeated until you finish them. It is like a friend who cares just enough.
The calendar view shows tasks next to events. A good habit: glance at it Sunday evening.
Too many lists feel like work about work. Three lists is plenty: Today, This Week, Someday.

## site projects mstodo
> microsoft to do
@ think
Microsoft To Do. "My Day" is a clean list that resets every morning. A fresh start, with no leftover guilt.
Suggestions show tasks you did not finish yesterday. They are optional and slightly judgemental.
It syncs with Outlook tasks and flagged emails, so a mail can turn into a to-do in one click.
Lists can be shared. A shared shopping list is the simplest form of cooperation.
Steps break a task into smaller tasks. "Do taxes" becomes "find papers", "log in", "cry quietly".
Due dates with reminders do the rest. A task with a date has a chance, and a task without has a hobby.
The app is simple on purpose. Simple is often what gets used.
At the end of the day, empty "My Day". A tidy list is a neat mind.

## site database airtable
> airtable
@ search
Airtable. A spreadsheet that has been to university and learned about databases: tables, linked records and views.
Linked records let a row in one table point to a row in another. "Customer" in the Orders table is a real customer.
The same data can be a grid, a Kanban board, a calendar or a gallery. Pick the view that fits the mood.
Fields have types: text, number, date, checkbox, attachment. Choose the right one and the sorting works.
Automations can send an email or a Slack message when a record changes. A little clockwork inside the table.
A base with forty tables is a very good reason to draw a diagram. Or to take a long walk.
Free plans have limits on records. When you reach them, it is a nice moment to delete the test rows.
A spreadsheet is fine until you start copy-pasting between three of them. Then a database is kinder.

## site diagrams miro
> visual workspace
@ fix
Miro. A huge online whiteboard with sticky notes and a very large canvas. Great for workshops and for getting lost.
Hold Space and drag to pan around the board. Scroll wheel zooms. No scroll bars, only courage.
Voting and timer features keep a workshop moving. A five-minute timer works wonders against a ten-minute argument.
Frames group parts of the board into presentable pieces. Present them one by one and the board becomes a story.
Templates exist for retros, user journeys, roadmaps and brainstorms. A good template saves a cold start.
Five people moving sticky notes at once is called "collaboration". Three of them moved the same one.
At the end of the workshop, export the board as an image or PDF. The canvas outlives the meeting, but the meeting does not outlive the canvas.

## site diagrams drawio
> diagrams.net | draw.io
@ fix
draw.io, now diagrams.net. Free, works offline, saves to a file or to your cloud, and draws boxes and arrows like it was born to.
Select shapes and press Ctrl+D to duplicate. Hold Shift while dragging to keep a straight line.
Align and distribute, from the Arrange menu, make a messy diagram look professional in a click.
The file is XML in a plain file, so it works with git. A diagram that diffs is a diagram that can be reviewed.

## site diagrams excalidraw
> excalidraw
@ fix
Excalidraw. A whiteboard that makes everything look hand-drawn, so even a sloppy diagram has charm.
Press a number key to pick a tool: 1 for select, 2 rectangle, 3 diamond, 4 ellipse, 5 arrow, 6 line, 7 draw. Fast and fun.
"Live collaboration" gives you a link. The room is encrypted end to end, so the server never sees what you drew.
Libraries of shapes can be loaded from the community. Flowcharts, wireframes, icons. Someone has already drawn the cloud.
A hand-drawn look is a good way to say "this is a draft". It lowers the pressure to make it perfect.
Export as PNG, SVG or a link. Or embed it in a Markdown file, if your team enjoys such things.

## site diagrams lucidchart
> lucidchart
@ write
Lucidchart. A diagram tool that is popular in companies for flowcharts, org charts and network maps.
Smart shapes snap to each other, so arrows follow when you move a box. The shape stays attached.
Templates for process maps, org charts and user journeys give you a head start.
Comments can be pinned to shapes. Handy in review, when someone says "this arrow is confusing".
A flowchart with one start, one end and no loops is a rare and beautiful thing. Real processes have loops.
Export as PDF or image for the slide deck. A diagram in a deck must be readable from the back row.
Keep the labels short and the colours few. Three colours is a diagram. Seven is a parade.
Drawing the process is half the work. The other half is noticing that two boxes do the same thing.

## site git github
> github
@ fix
+ Take a note = notes
GitHub. Press "t" in a repo to find a file by name, "?" for all shortcuts and "." to open the code in a web editor. The dot is magic.
Press "y" on a file page to turn the address into a permanent link. Great when the file will change and you still want to point at line 42.
"g" then "p" jumps to pull requests, "g" then "i" to issues. Two-key trips, no mouse.
The contribution graph is a calendar of green squares. A blank week is just a week. Nobody died.
A repo with no README is a house with no door. Add three lines: what it is, how to run it, how to complain.
Issue #1 from 2016 is still open. It has 38 thumbs-up and one comment saying "any update?"
A red cross next to a commit means a check failed. Click it, read the log, and fix the thing before the reviewer does.
The "good first issue" label is where newcomers begin. If you are the maintainer, label some. It is a kind thing.
Star a repo when it helped you. It costs nothing and warms a maintainer's whole afternoon.
"{title}": read the README, look at the last commit date and the open issues. A repo with no recent commits is a museum.

## site git gitlab
> gitlab
@ read
GitLab. Same idea as the other forge, with "merge requests" instead of pull requests and a CI that lives in a file called .gitlab-ci.yml.
Press "." to open the Web IDE for the current repo. Quick for small fixes, less so for large ones.
Pipelines run on runners, and runners are sometimes busy. A job stuck in "pending" is waiting for one to be free.
The CI file is YAML, so spaces matter. One wrong indent and the whole pipeline is a short story about failure.
Self-hosted GitLab is a popular hobby and a larger responsibility. Back it up before upgrading, not after.
Protected branches stop people pushing straight to main. A small fence that prevents large problems.
Check the pipeline status before asking for a review. A red pipeline is a very quiet way of saying "not yet".
Use labels and milestones to keep issues sane. An unlabeled issue is an issue waiting to be misfiled.

## site git bitbucket
> bitbucket
@ search
Bitbucket. Atlassian's Git hosting, popular with teams that already live in Jira. Pull requests and pipelines in one place.
Mention a Jira issue key in a commit message and the two get linked. A very tidy bit of bookkeeping.
The pipelines file is bitbucket-pipelines.yml. It lives in the repo and runs on every push, if you ask nicely.
Branch permissions and merge checks keep the main branch tidy. Set them early, before somebody pushes a surprise.
Large files do not belong in the repository. Use Git LFS, or an artefact store, or an honest shared drive.
A pull request with 80 files and a title like "stuff" is a reviewer's nightmare. Split it up and name it.
Review comments are most helpful when they are short, specific and kind. Say what, say why, say thanks.
Close old branches. A repository with 200 stale ones looks like a coat rack after a party.

## site git codeberg
> codeberg
@ think
Codeberg. A non-profit Git host from Germany, built on Forgejo and loved by people who like free software and no tracking.
Projects here are often small and heartfelt: a theme, a tool, a hobby library. The pull requests come with a "thank you".
Forgejo is the software behind it. You can run your own instance for a club, a family or a humble company.
Donations keep it running. A repository that has helped you could also help the host that stores it.
Static pages are served from a special repo called "pages". Handy for a small project website.
Issues and pull requests work the same way as elsewhere. The interface is plainer and quicker.
A good README is a gift on any forge. Add a screenshot. Add the install steps. Add a licence.
Free software is not free to maintain. If a project saves you an hour a week, say thanks.

## site qa stackoverflow
> - stack overflow
@ cool
Stack Overflow. Check the date of the answer and the version of the library. A beautiful solution from 2012 is a time capsule.
The accepted answer has a green tick. The best answer is sometimes the one below it, with more votes and a comment saying "this works in 2024".
Writing the question often solves it. Rubber duck debugging is built into the "Ask" button.
"Possible duplicate" has ended many a hopeful afternoon. Read the linked question first. They are right more often than you would like.
A good question has a short title, a minimal example, the exact error and what you tried. That is the whole recipe.
Copying code from an answer is fine. Understanding it is better. Look at the comments for the catch.
Upvote the answer that saved your afternoon. It takes one click and makes someone's day.
If the question is old and the answer is wrong, add an updated answer. The next person will thank you silently.
Close the tab when the code works. Do not open another "just in case".
"{title}": check the date of the answer and the version of your tools. Then upvote it, if it saved you.

## site qa superuser
> - super user | superuser.com
@ cool
Super User. The Stack Exchange site for computer questions that are not quite programming: Windows, macOS, Linux and "why is my Wi-Fi slow".
Answers here often include steps like "open Settings, click Advanced". Check that your version of the system matches theirs.
Search the exact error message in quotes. Somebody asked it, and somebody else replied with a long, kind answer.
The comments often add a crucial detail. Read them before running the command from the answer.
Never paste a command that you do not understand into a terminal with sudo. Look it up first. Even here.
A good answer includes the "why", not only the "what". If you only get a command, ask for the reason.
When you solve it yourself, post the answer. A question without a solution is a ghost in the archive.
Sort by "votes". A very long accepted answer is not always the right one for your Tuesday.

## site qa askubuntu
> ask ubuntu | askubuntu
@ cool
Ask Ubuntu. The Q&A site for Ubuntu and its relatives. Many answers also work for Debian, Mint and friends.
The answer from 2014 may say "apt-get install" and "sudo add-apt-repository". Today it may be "apt install" and a PPA you no longer trust.
Look for the version of Ubuntu in the question. A fix for 14.04 may be pointless on 24.04.
Adding a PPA is easy. Removing it cleanly is a different matter. Use ppa-purge if things go sideways.
"sudo rm -rf /" is a famous joke and not a fix. If an answer includes it, close the tab.
The terminal output is usually the most helpful part of a question. Paste it as text in a code block, not a screenshot.
If you are not on Ubuntu, the Arch wiki is probably the better place. Linux is a family, not a monarchy.
When the problem is fixed, mark the answer as accepted. The next person will know where to look.

## site qa serverfault
> - server fault | serverfault.com
@ cool
Server Fault. The Q&A site for people who manage servers, networks and the 3 a.m. phone call that goes with them.
Before you ask "why is the server slow", have a few numbers ready: load, memory, disk and what changed recently.
"Works on my machine" is not a diagnosis. "Works on my machine and the log says otherwise" is a start.
Read the logs. Then read them again. The error is usually five lines above the one you were staring at.
Always have a backup, and test the restore. A backup that has never been restored is a rumour.
Do not make changes on a Friday afternoon. This is not advice on Server Fault. It is a prayer.
Use configuration management so the server can be rebuilt. A pet server is a fragile thing.
After the incident, write what happened. Not to blame, but to remember. The next person will thank you.

## site qa unixse
> unix & linux stack exchange | unix.stackexchange | unix & linux
@ cool
Unix & Linux Stack Exchange. Shell scripting, system administration and "why does this one-liner work?". Answers read like tiny lectures.
Quote your variables. That advice appears in about half the answers, and it is right every time.
"Useless use of cat" is a classic gentle scolding. It points out that piping cat into grep is longer than giving grep the file.
man pages, "tldr" and "--help" will answer most questions before you ask. Try them in that order.
Always check what a command will do before running it as root. A dry run, an echo, or a read of the docs is cheap.
A good answer to "why does it fail" starts with "run set -x" or "add a debug line". Look at the actual commands.
Filenames with spaces and newlines are real. Scripts that assume otherwise are optimistic.
Write down what finally worked. Your future self will search for it and find your own answer. It is quite satisfying.

## site docs mdn
> mdn web docs
@ search
MDN. The reference for the web platform: HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Compatibility tables at the bottom tell you whether a feature works in your browser.
Every page has an example, a syntax section and a "see also". Skip to the examples first and the syntax second. It is human nature.
The compatibility table is the part you should not skip. A shiny new feature in your editor may not exist in a customer's browser.
Searching MDN directly from the browser's address bar is faster than the site search. Add it as a search engine with a keyword.
The "Learn" section has guides for beginners and is quietly excellent. It is a good place to send a friend who asks "how do I start?"
CSS Grid and Flexbox have their own guides, with pictures. A picture of a grid is worth a thousand Stack Overflow questions.
When two sources disagree, MDN is usually the one to trust. And when MDN is silent, the spec is the real source.
Bookmark the page you use most. We all have one. It is probably "Array.prototype.map".
"{title}": jump to the Examples and the browser compatibility table. The rest is the well-written bit in the middle.

## site docs docsrs
> docs.rs | - rust | rust programming language
@ read
docs.rs. Documentation for every Rust crate, built automatically. Press "s" to jump to the search and "?" for the other shortcuts.
The type signature at the top tells you more than a paragraph. Learn to read it and half the crate explains itself.
Examples in doc comments are compiled and tested. If an example is on the page, it works. A rare guarantee in documentation.
Check the version selector in the top-left. The docs for the old version may be the ones your project actually uses.
"Feature flags" show up in the sidebar. A function that seems to be missing may just be behind one.
The Rust book is free and online and really good. If something here confuses you, start there.
A crate that has not been updated in three years is not always dead. It may just be finished.
Compiler errors are long but kind. Read the first one and ignore the other ninety until it is fixed.

## site docs pythondocs
> python 3. | python.org
@ search
The Python docs. Under the search box lives the "Library Reference" with a page for every module. Boring in the best way.
Use the version switcher in the top corner. Features in 3.12 may not exist in the Python your server runs.
The Tutorial is a quick, friendly walk through the language. Reading it once is worth more than five blog posts.
"Python Module of the Week" and the standard library docs often show a built-in solution you were about to reinstall from a package.
The glossary explains words like "iterable", "decorator" and "dunder". A decent excuse to spend ten minutes on it.
Docstrings are the best documentation. Type help(name) in a Python shell and the page is right there.
PEP 8 is the style guide and PEP 20 is the "Zen". The Zen says "readability counts". It does.
"import this" is an Easter egg that prints the Zen. A good five-second break.
"{title}" is probably a module with more functions than you will ever need. Search the page for the one you want.

## site docs w3schools
> w3schools
@ read
W3Schools. Beginner-friendly tutorials with a "Try it Yourself" button that opens an editor right next to the example. Quick and handy.
The pages are simple and short. For depth and the finer details, MDN is the next stop.
The quizzes and exercises at the bottom are surprisingly effective. Five questions, five minutes, one smug little feeling.
Colour pickers, tables and snippets are all just a click away. A very good tool for a quick lookup.
The site is a good way to start. A habit of reading the real spec comes later, around the third big bug.
If you only need a reminder of the syntax, this is faster than reading a long article.
Copying an example and changing one thing at a time is how most of us learned. Still works.
Close the tutorial and write the thing. The tutorial will wait. You have things to build.

## site docs devdocs
> devdocs
@ read
DevDocs. Many documentation sets in one fast, offline-capable page: JavaScript, Python, CSS, PHP and more.
Pick the docs you use in the settings and they download to your browser. Next time on a plane, you have a library.
The search is instant and keyboard-friendly. Type, arrow down, press Enter. A good way to look up a function in under five seconds.
Dark mode is built in. A little joy for late-night reference reading.
A page that loads in under a second is a page that people read. A page that takes forever is a page people copy from a blog.
You can bookmark a specific doc set URL, say for the version your project uses.
It is open source, so you can run your own copy. A very nerdy afternoon, and very satisfying.
Look it up, close the tab, use it. The loop is the point.

## site docs mslearn

@ search
Microsoft Learn. Documentation and free training paths for Microsoft products, Azure and developer tools. A big library with long URLs.
The "Learn" modules are short and often come with a sandbox. A fast way to try something without breaking your own machine.
If a page is out of date, scroll to the bottom and send feedback. They read it more often than you would think.
Use the filter at the top-left to choose the right version of the docs. Mixing versions makes a good bug.

Certifications and learning paths are long, but the first module of any path is a comfortable warm-up.
The Q&A section at the bottom of some pages collects answers from the community. Check it before posting.
Take a break between modules. Reading Azure docs is a marathon, not a sprint.

## site docs nodejs
> node.js v
@ think
The Node.js docs. One page per module, one long scroll per page, and an API version selector on the top right.
The stability index shows whether an API is stable, experimental or deprecated. Experimental means "try it, then be ready to change it".
Many things you used to install from npm are now built in: fetch, test runner, watch mode. Check the docs before adding a dependency.
Press Ctrl+F on this page a lot. The pages are long, and the browser's find is the best index.
The LTS version is the one most servers run. The current version is the one with the new toys.
Look at the "Added in" note under a function. It tells you whether your Node can run it.
A callback hell is escapable with promises and async/await. The docs show both styles side by side.
Before adding another npm package, ask whether the standard library already does it.
"{title}": check the "Added in" notes. A function that exists in the docs may not exist in the Node you have installed.

## site docs react
> – react | react.dev
@ search
The React docs. They teach hooks and thinking in components, with live examples in the page that you can edit.
"useEffect" is the hook that causes the most confusion. The docs have a page called "You Might Not Need an Effect". It is worth reading.
Keys in lists must be stable and unique. An index as a key works right up until you reorder the list.
State is a snapshot. Setting it does not change the variable on the current line, only the next render.
Lift state up when two components need to share it. It is the oldest trick and still the best one.
Re-renders are not always a problem. Measure before optimising, or you will spend a day speeding up the fast part.
The "Learn" section has a tic-tac-toe tutorial and a "thinking in React" guide. A quick tour to the right mindset.
Read the error message in the console. React's warnings are often right and surprisingly polite.
"{title}" on react.dev. Edit the live example in the page. Breaking it on purpose is the fastest way to learn what it does.

## site docs tailwind
> - tailwind css
@ cool
Tailwind CSS docs. Search for any utility class and the page shows the CSS behind it. The docs are the real manual and the best cheat sheet.
Press Ctrl+K to search the docs. It finds a class by what it does, not only by what it is called.
A long list of class names on one element looks messy, but it keeps styles next to the markup. A trade-off many people end up liking.
Use responsive prefixes like "md:" and "lg:" to change a style at a certain width. A mobile-first habit that pays off.
Dark mode is a "dark:" prefix away. Add it to the colours that need changing and no more.
If you repeat the same set of classes ten times, make it a component. Not a custom CSS file.
Config goes into tailwind.config.js. A few custom colours there will make the whole design feel yours.
Unused classes are removed in the build. The final CSS file is tiny. That is rather nice.

## site docs cppreference
> cppreference
@ fix
cppreference. The reference for C and C++, where every function has a signature, a notes section and an "Example" that you can run in your head.
Look at the "Since C++20" note in the page header. Whether your compiler can use a feature depends on that line.
Pages show "Defect reports" and "See also" sections. These are a good place to learn about subtle surprises.
Try the example in Compiler Explorer. A button on the right opens it, ready to run.
Undefined behaviour is not "it crashes". It is "anything may happen, including working fine until Tuesday".
Smart pointers and the standard library are your friends. Raw new and delete are a hobby for the brave.
The reference is dry but accurate. For learning, a book or a course is gentler. For lookup, this is the one.
Use the search box at the top right. It finds a std:: name faster than guessing.
"{title}": check the "since C++" note at the top of the entry. It decides whether your compiler may use it.

## site docs gopackages
> go packages | pkg.go.dev
@ read
Go Packages. The documentation site for Go modules, generated straight from the source code comments. Simple and readable.
Every exported function has its comment shown on the page. Writing a good comment is writing good docs.
The "Imports" and "Imported by" tabs show a package's neighbourhood. A small package with 40,000 importers is a quiet cornerstone.
Check the licence and the last commit. A package that has not changed in four years may be finished or abandoned.
Go has a standard library that does a lot. Check it before importing anything fancy.
Examples in the docs are tested, so they compile and do what they say. A pleasing honesty.
The error handling in Go is "if err != nil" a lot of times. The docs do not apologise for this.
Format with gofmt and never argue about style. The tool already decided.

## site docs kubernetes
> kubernetes
@ think
The Kubernetes docs. A very large manual for a very large orchestrator. The concepts are long and the YAML is longer.
"kubectl explain" shows the fields of any resource in the terminal. Use it before copying a random manifest from a blog.
A Pod is the smallest unit and a Deployment manages Pods for you. Start with those two before a dozen new words.
"CrashLoopBackOff" means a container starts, fails, and restarts with growing pauses. The log tells you why.
Namespaces keep things apart. Use them, or all your experiments end up in "default", like socks in a drawer.
kubectl get pods -w watches the state change live. A little cluster aquarium in your terminal.
Before running the cluster at home, ask whether a single Docker Compose file would do. It often does.
Read the docs on the version you run. The cluster changes quickly and old tutorials grow stale like bread.
"{title}" is one concept out of about a hundred. Learn it, ignore the other ninety-nine, and come back when needed.

## site docs dockerdocs
> docker docs | docker hub
@ fix
Docker docs and Docker Hub. Official images, tags and a lot of "latest". Pinning a version is a quiet kindness to your future self.
"docker compose up" is the single command that starts a whole local stack. If you only learn one, learn that one.
Official images have a blue badge. Many unofficial ones are fine, some are not. Check how recently they were updated.
A container that runs as root is a container with too much trust. Many images let you pick a non-root user.
"docker system prune" frees disk space. Read what it will delete before pressing y.
Layers are cached. Put the stuff that changes rarely, like dependencies, near the top of the Dockerfile.
Docs for Dockerfile instructions are short and clear. A good reference when you wonder what ENTRYPOINT does.
Volumes keep data when a container disappears. If you forget them, the database goes with the container.

## site code pypi
> pypi
@ read
PyPI. Before you "pip install" something, check the exact spelling of the package. Look-alike names exist, and they are not charming.
The "Release history" tab shows how long the project has been alive and how often it ships. A package that last updated in 2017 is on a long holiday.
Use a virtual environment: python -m venv .venv. Installing everything into the system Python is how a weekend disappears.
A "yanked" release is one the author withdrew. pip will skip it unless you ask for it by exact version.
Pin your versions in a requirements file. "It worked last month" is not a deployment strategy.
The project page's "Download files" section is useful when pip fails. Sometimes you just need the wheel.
Check the number of maintainers. A hugely popular package with one tired person behind it is a charity case. Say thanks.
Read the README before installing. Three lines of usage can save an hour of trial and error.

## site code cratesio
> crates.io
@ search
crates.io. Run "cargo add name" and the dependency is in Cargo.toml. Check the licence and the last update before you do.
The "Dependencies" tab shows what a crate pulls in. A little crate that brings 90 others deserves a glance.
Features are optional parts of a crate. Turning off the ones you do not need shortens compile times.
Look at the download counts and the repository link. A popular crate with active issues is a healthy crate.
"cargo update" bumps your dependencies within what Cargo.toml allows. Read the changes before you trust it blindly.
The docs link goes straight to docs.rs. If the docs are bare, the examples folder in the repo is the next best thing.
"unsafe" in a crate is not a crime, but it is a place to read twice. Ask what it is guarding.
Say thanks to the maintainers. A star, an issue that begins with "thanks", or a coffee. All three are welcome.

## site code npm
> - npm
@ fix
npm. "npm audit" lists known problems in your dependencies. It is a long list, and most of it is noise, and some of it is not.
A "node_modules" folder is larger than most operating systems from the nineties. This is not a joke, it is a measurement.
In 2016 a tiny package of eleven lines was removed and half the internet's builds failed. The lesson is to pin versions and use a lock file.
Before adding a dependency for something small, check whether a few lines of your own code would do. Every package is a stranger with a key.
"npx" runs a package without installing it permanently. Great for tools you need once. Check the name twice.
Weekly downloads look impressive until you realise most of them are other packages installing it.
A package with one maintainer and a million users is one long weekend away from trouble. Support small projects when you can.
"npm ci" installs exactly what the lock file says. Use it in CI. "npm install" is for experiments.

## site code flathub
> flathub
@ search
Flathub. The app store for Flatpak apps on Linux. Install with a click or with flatpak install flathub org.name.App.
Apps run in a sandbox with limited access. Look at the permissions on an app page before installing.
A "Verified" badge means the developer has proven they own the app. A humble kindness against fakes.
Flatpak apps update with "flatpak update". Do it now and then, the way you water a plant.
Flatseal is a tiny app that lets you manage the permissions of other Flatpak apps. A nice little control panel.
Disk space adds up because each app brings its own runtimes. "flatpak uninstall --unused" cleans up the leftovers.
Some apps are community builds and some are official. The app page says which. It matters if you want a bug fixed.
Look for the screenshots first. A beautiful app with no screenshots is a little suspicious.

## site code aur
> aur (en)
@ search
The AUR. User-made build scripts for Arch and its relatives. Always read the PKGBUILD before building. It is short and it is your safety net.
A helper like yay or paru makes AUR installs a one-liner. It does not make reading the PKGBUILD optional.
A package with "-git" at the end builds the latest commit, not a release. It is newer and a bit less predictable.
Check the votes, the popularity and the "last updated" date. A package with 600 votes and a fresh update is usually fine.
"Out of date" flags exist for packages that lag behind upstream. Flagging is helpful, and polite when you add a note.
Orphaned packages with no maintainer are up for adoption. If you use one, consider taking it. It is a good way to learn packaging.
Build in a clean chroot if you can. A package that builds only on your messy machine has not really been packaged.
Not every AUR package is a bargain. If the official repos or Flathub have it, prefer those. Fewer surprises.

## site docs archwiki
> - archwiki
@ think
ArchWiki. Widely seen as the best Linux documentation anywhere, and it helps even if you run another distribution. Often better than your own distro's docs.
The Installation guide and the General recommendations page are the first stop for anyone who has just set up an Arch system or a relative of it.
Search the wiki before a forum. The answer is probably on a page with a long, accurate title.
The pages are community-edited and fixed constantly. If you spot a mistake, you can correct it. The wiki appreciates that.

Commands shown in the wiki are usually exact. Read the "Warning" and "Note" boxes before copying anything.
Read the page about your hardware before asking why Wi-Fi, suspend or graphics misbehave. It is often written by someone with exactly your laptop.
The wiki also has pages for non-Linux topics like Vim, Firefox and Bash. Worth a bookmark.

## site news distrowatch
> distrowatch
@ think
DistroWatch. News, releases and a famous page-hit ranking of Linux distributions. A nerdy way to feel connected to the whole penguin ecosystem.
The ranking measures clicks on the site, not users. Do not choose an operating system by it. Choose by what you like using.

Distro-hopping is a hobby, not a lifestyle. Pick one, learn it well, and hop only on purpose.

## site code codepen
> codepen
@ search
CodePen. HTML, CSS and JavaScript side by side with a live preview. A great playground for a quick idea, and a wonderful place to lose an afternoon.
Ctrl+S saves the pen. Auto-save is a setting, so check it before you close the tab.

## site code jsfiddle
> jsfiddle
@ read
JSFiddle. A little online playground for HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Ctrl+Enter runs the code and "TidyUp" reformats it.
People often post a link to a fiddle in a question. A good bug report is a fiddle that shows the bug.

External resources are added in the left sidebar. Paste a CDN link and your library is loaded.

A minimal example is a shrine to clarity. Strip everything that does not cause the bug.

## site code replit
> replit
@ cool
Replit. A full coding environment in the browser, no install needed: pick a language, press Run, and it works. Handy for a quick test or a class.
Multiplayer editing lets two people code in the same file. A very modern way to say "let me show you".

Secrets go in the Secrets tool, not in the code. Never commit an API key, not even a quiet one.

## site code stackblitz
> stackblitz
@ cool
StackBlitz. A web IDE that runs Node.js inside your browser. No server, no wait, just a project that starts in a few seconds.
Great for reproducing a bug: a link to a StackBlitz project with the problem in it is worth ten paragraphs.
Projects start from templates for React, Vue, Angular and more. A quick way to try a new library.
The file tree on the left and the preview on the right make it feel like a real editor. It is a real editor, in a tab.

If the preview does not update, check the terminal at the bottom for an error. It is usually a missing import.
It is a very good teaching tool. A teacher can share a link and every student has the same environment.

## site code codesandbox
> codesandbox
@ think
CodeSandbox. Online sandboxes for front-end and full-stack projects. Fork one to try a change without touching the original.
Sharing a sandbox link lets another person edit alongside you, live. Good for a code review in a hurry.
Dependencies are added from a sidebar. If a package does not resolve, check the version and the spelling.
Devboxes give you a full development environment in the cloud. Handy when a laptop cannot cope with a monorepo.
Sandboxes can be embedded into docs and blog posts. A live example is better than a screenshot of one.

A quick trial in a sandbox is a good way to learn. Put the result into the real project and move on.
