## site code regex101
> regex101
@ read
regex101. Paste a pattern and some text, and it explains each piece in plain English and highlights the matches. Best invention since the undo key.
Pick the flavour on the left: PCRE, JavaScript, Python, Go. A pattern that works in one may not work in another.
The debugger shows each step the engine takes. A good way to see why a pattern is slow or matches too much.
Greedy matching takes as much as it can. Adding a question mark after a quantifier makes it lazy. Remember that and half your bugs go away.
The test strings should include the cases that should NOT match. A regex that only passes happy cases is a nice dream.
Save and share your regex with a permalink. Others can see exactly what you tested.
If a regex needs five lines of comments, consider writing a small parser. Some patterns belong in code.
When it matches, leave a comment explaining why. Future you will not recall what "(?<=^|,)" means.

## site code regexr
> regexr
@ search
RegExr. A friendly regex tester with a reference panel next to the editor. Hover over any part of your pattern and it tells you what it does.
The community tab has patterns for emails, dates and URLs. They are a great starting point and a terrible finishing point.
Switch between JavaScript and PHP flavours with a dropdown. The syntax is mostly the same until it is not.
Use the "Replace" tab to test a substitution. "$1" is the first group, which is often exactly what you need.
A tool that colours the matches makes it obvious when the pattern is too greedy. The wrong parts light up like a fairground.
Take your time. Regular expressions are a language that rewards patience and punishes confidence.
Test the empty string, the very long string and the string with weird characters. They are the usual troublemakers.
Add a comment to the final pattern in your code. The comment is the part you will read in six months.

## site code godbolt
> compiler explorer
@ think
Compiler Explorer. Type C, C++, Rust or Go on the left and watch the assembly appear on the right, colour-matched line by line. A microscope for code.
Add -O2 or -O3 in the compiler options and see how the optimiser rewrites your loop into something shorter and cleverer.
A function that returns a constant is often compiled to a single instruction. The compiler already did the maths.
You can compare different compilers or versions side by side. A fine way to see why a bug appears only with one of them.
Look at the short link button to share your example. A fiddle for assembly, in a way.
Reading assembly is a skill. A few lines at a time, and a cup of tea, and suddenly "mov" and "xor" are familiar.
Do not optimise anything without measuring. A shorter assembly does not always mean a faster program.
When you have seen enough, close the tab. The CPU will keep doing its thing without your supervision.

## site code cyberchef
> cyberchef
@ fix
CyberChef. The "Cyber Swiss Army Knife": a web tool to encode, decode, hash and transform data. Drag operations into a recipe and watch the output change.
The "Magic" operation tries to guess how a string was encoded and decodes it for you. Surprisingly often it works.
It runs entirely in your browser, so the data stays on your computer. Check that before pasting anything sensitive, as with any tool.
Chain steps like "From Base64", "Gunzip" and "To Hex". Complex conversions become a short recipe you can save as a link.
Developed by a UK intelligence agency and released openly. The internet being what it is, you can read the source.
It is great for quick conversions you would otherwise google: URL decode, timestamps, JSON formatting, CRC checks.
Save the recipe link for conversions you do often. A saved recipe is a little script with a nice face.
Remember that Base64 is not encryption. It is just a different costume for the same data.

## site code crontabguru
> crontab.guru
@ read
crontab.guru. Type a cron expression and it tells you in plain English when it will run. The five fields finally make sense.
The five fields are minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week. A star means "every". It is the only syntax lesson you need.
"*/5 * * * *" runs every five minutes. "0 9 * * 1-5" runs at nine on weekdays. Both are very useful and very easy to mistype.
The page shows the next few run times. Check them to make sure "at midnight" is really tonight and not in two weeks.
Cron uses the system's time zone, not yours. A job that runs at 3 a.m. server time can mean something else entirely.
Always redirect the output to a log or you will get a mysterious mail from "root". Add ">> /var/log/job.log 2>&1".
systemd timers are the newer way, but cron still runs happily on millions of servers. A very small, very reliable ghost.
Test your job by running the command manually first. Then schedule it.

## site code vercel
> vercel
@ cool
Vercel. Push to git and your site is live. Every pull request gets its own preview link, which is lovely for showing a colleague a change.
The build log is the first place to look when a deployment fails. Scroll to the first red line, not the last one.
Environment variables belong in the project settings, not in your code. Remember to add them for preview and production separately.
A free hobby plan is generous, but commercial use has its own terms. Read the fair use policy before launching a business.
Functions run on demand and cost fractions of a cent. Fractions of a cent add up if one of them loops forever.
A custom domain needs a DNS record pointing to Vercel. If it says "invalid configuration", check the record twice and wait for DNS.
A preview link is also a handy backup. If production breaks, you can look at the last working preview.
When deployment says "Ready", open the site in a private window. Cached pages lie.

## site code netlify
> netlify
@ think
Netlify. Drag a folder into the deploy box and your static site is online. It is still a bit magical.
Deploy previews give every pull request its own link. Reviewing a design change on a real URL beats screenshots.
Netlify Forms catches submissions from a plain HTML form without any backend code. A very pleasant shortcut.
Redirects go in a _redirects file or netlify.toml. A wrong redirect can make a loop. If the browser says "too many redirects", that is it.
Build settings tell it which command and folder to use. If the deploy fails, check that the publish directory is right.
Free tier is generous for hobby sites. Keep an eye on bandwidth if something goes viral. Not that it is likely. It is a fun thought.
Rollbacks are a click. Previous deploys are saved and can be published again. A kind safety net.
Always check the live site on a phone. The site on a big monitor is a flattering liar.

## site code cloudflare
> cloudflare
@ think
Cloudflare. DNS, a CDN and DDoS protection with a generous free tier. The orange cloud proxies traffic and the grey cloud only does DNS.
If a site stops loading after you add a record, check whether the proxy is on. Some services, like mail and SSH, will not work through it.
Cache problems can be solved with "Purge cache" in the dashboard. It is the big red button for stale pages.
SSL mode "Flexible" is a footgun. "Full (strict)" is the one to choose, if your origin has a valid certificate.
Workers run small pieces of JavaScript at the edge, close to the user. A neat trick for redirects, headers and APIs.
Always keep an extra copy of your DNS records somewhere. If an account gets locked, you will want the list.
Two-factor on this account is not optional. It controls the front door of your sites.
A "Verify you are human" page on other sites comes from here too. I am not allowed to help with that. Sorry.

## site code awsconsole
> management console
@ think
AWS Management Console. The region selector in the top right is the usual reason a resource "has vanished". It is in another region.
Set up a billing alert on day one. A budget with an email warning is cheap. A surprise bill is not.
Use IAM roles with the least access that works. A single "AdministratorAccess" user for every purpose is a hostage situation.
Never leave an S3 bucket public by mistake. Check the "Block public access" settings before uploading anything.
Free tier ends after 12 months for many services. A little calendar entry saves a nasty surprise.
Turn off what you are not using. A forgotten test instance is a quiet drain of money and attention.
The console search bar at the top finds services fast. Press the slash key and start typing.
Write infrastructure as code once you outgrow clicking. A console click is a memory. A template is a record.

## site code azureportal
> microsoft azure
@ read
Azure Portal. Resources live in resource groups. Delete the group and everything inside goes with it. Handy for cleanup and terrible for accidents.
Cost Management shows what you are spending. Look at it on Monday, not at the end of the month.
Cloud Shell opens a terminal inside the portal, with the Azure CLI ready. A lifesaver when your own machine is not set up.
Tags on resources help you find out who made what. "owner" and "purpose" are two good tags to start with.
The portal has "blades" that open to the right as you click deeper. The path back is the breadcrumb at the top.
Role-based access control assigns roles to people, not to your own account for everything. Use "Reader" for most colleagues.
Resource names often cannot be changed later. Think about a name before you press Create.
If a deployment fails with a quota error, the region may simply be full of VMs. Try another region.

## site code googlecloud
> google cloud
@ read
Google Cloud Console. Always check which project is selected in the top bar. Most "I cannot see my resource" problems are a wrong project.
Billing accounts are separate from projects. Set a budget alert at the billing level and you will sleep better.
Cloud Shell gives you a terminal and an editor in the browser, with gcloud already installed. Nice for a quick check.
Enable only the APIs you need. Unused APIs are an open door you forgot about.
Service accounts are for programs, users are for people. Mixing them up makes for strange log entries.
Delete the test project when you are done. It deletes all its resources too, after a grace period.
A free trial with credits is a fine way to learn. Set the limits first, then explore.
The documentation has a "Quickstart" for almost every service. Start there, not at the reference.

## site code digitalocean
> digitalocean
@ fix
DigitalOcean. Cloud servers called "Droplets" and some of the friendliest tutorials on the internet. Setting up a little server? You have probably read one.
A Droplet starts at a humble monthly price. Delete it when you are done, because a forgotten Droplet still bills.
Set up SSH keys instead of passwords and disable root login. The tutorial has the exact steps, and it is a good habit forever.
A firewall in the control panel is easy to add. Allow SSH, HTTP and HTTPS. Close the rest.
Snapshots let you save the state of a Droplet before a risky change. A tiny undo button for a whole machine.
Managed databases cost more than a DIY one but save you the 3 a.m. restores.
Backups can be switched on for a small fee. It is cheap insurance for a server that matters.
Read the tutorial in full before running commands. The footnotes often contain the warning.

## site code hetzner
> hetzner
@ search
Hetzner. German hosting with affordable servers, a cloud console and a "Server Auction" where used dedicated machines sell cheap. A nerd's candy shop.
Cloud servers are quick to create and delete. Dedicated servers live in the "Robot" panel and are more serious.
Firewalls and private networks are available in the console. Set one up before you put anything important on the server.
Traffic is generous, but check the included amounts. A forgotten test server that sends terabytes is a rude surprise.
Snapshots and backups are separate features. A snapshot is a manual picture, a backup is a daily routine.
An old dedicated server may be running an old operating system. Update it, or reinstall from the rescue console.
Good for self-hosting a humble stack: a website, a mail relay, a cloud storage. Respect the sysadmin job that comes with it.
Do not mine anything on it. They check.

## site database firebase
> firebase
@ fix
Firebase. A backend in a console: authentication, a database, hosting and storage. Great for a prototype, dangerous for a tired mind.
"Test mode" rules open the database to everyone for 30 days. Set real security rules before the date arrives, not after.
Firestore charges per read and write. A loop that reads a thousand documents on every page view is a hidden bill.
Authentication supports email, Google and phone sign-in. Setting it up is easy. Handling it properly is the interesting part.
The emulator suite lets you test locally without touching real data. A great habit for anyone with production credentials.
Hosting deploys with one command. "firebase deploy" and the site is live. Very satisfying, very risky when typed in the wrong project.
Keep the API keys for the client public and the service account keys private. The difference matters.
A backup of the data is the one feature you will not use until the day you really need it.

## site database supabase
> supabase
@ fix
Supabase. The open source Firebase alternative, built on Postgres. A real database with a friendly dashboard, authentication and storage.
Row Level Security decides which user can see which rows. Turn it on, write policies, and test them. A table without policies is a table without doors.
The Table Editor looks like a spreadsheet and speaks SQL underneath. A good bridge for people who are new to databases.
The SQL Editor is where you do the real work. Save your queries, and use migrations so the database setup lives in git.
The anon key is public and the service role key is not. Putting the second one in a browser is how data leaks.
The free tier pauses projects after inactivity. A paused project is not deleted. It just needs a click to wake up.
Edge functions run server code close to users. Good for webhooks and small APIs.
Check the logs when a query is slow. Often a missing index is the whole story.

## site database phpmyadmin
> phpmyadmin
@ think
phpMyAdmin. A web interface for MySQL and MariaDB. Tables, queries, exports, and the familiar tabs of Structure, SQL and Search.
"Export" gives you a SQL dump of a database. Do this before any big change, and store it somewhere other than the same server.
Never leave phpMyAdmin open to the public internet at a predictable address. Protect it with a password, an IP allow list or just a VPN.
A "DROP TABLE" in the SQL tab is instant and final. Read the statement twice before pressing Go.
The "Search" tab can find a value across all tables. Useful when you do not remember where the email address lives.
Large imports can hit PHP upload limits. If it fails, split the file or use the command-line mysql client.
Check the character set of the database. Strange question marks in names usually mean someone forgot utf8mb4.
Once the fix works, close the tab and log out. A forgotten admin session is a lovely open door.

## site database pgadmin
> pgadmin
@ fix
pgAdmin. The management tool for PostgreSQL, with an elephant for a logo and a query tool where F5 runs the statement. A gentle giant.
Right-click a table and choose "View/Edit Data" to look at rows. Right-click again for "Scripts" to generate SQL for it.
The ERD tool can draw a diagram of your tables and their foreign keys. A map of the database in a few clicks.
"EXPLAIN ANALYZE" shows how Postgres actually runs a query and how long each step took. Look for sequential scans on big tables.
Backup and Restore are in the right-click menu on the database. Test a restore on a scratch server before you need it.
Do not give your application the superuser account. Create a role with only the rights it needs.
A transaction begins with BEGIN and ends with COMMIT or ROLLBACK. Test your risky update inside one first.
Close the connection when done. An idle session is a quiet drain on a busy server.

## site database mongodb
> mongodb atlas | atlas - mongodb
@ think
MongoDB Atlas. A document database in the cloud with a free starter cluster. "Cannot connect" is usually the IP access list, not the code.
Documents are JSON-like, which is lovely until two of them have the same field with different types. The flexibility is a freedom and a trap.
The free tier is fine for learning and small projects. Do not store anything you cannot afford to lose without a backup plan.
Indexes make queries fast. Without one, the database reads every document. Use "explain" to see what it does.
Do not put the connection string with the password in git. Use an environment variable.
Atlas Search and Charts are built in. Handy features if you do not mind being a little tied to the platform.
"0.0.0.0/0" in the IP access list means everyone. It is the quick fix and the slow regret.
Backups on the free tier are limited. Export important collections now and then with mongodump.

## site code huggingface
> hugging face
@ think
Hugging Face. A hub for machine learning models, datasets and demo apps called Spaces. A very large library of other people's very clever weights.
Check the model card before using a model. It tells you what it was trained on, what it is for and what it should not be used for.
Licences vary a lot from model to model. "Open weights" does not always mean you can do whatever you like with it.
A small model that runs on your laptop is often enough for a specific task. A big model for everything is a big bill for nothing.
Downloading a model of 20 GB takes time and disk space. Check your free space first.
Spaces let you try a model in the browser. Some are free to use, others queue for hours. Patience, little traveller.
Be careful with datasets that contain personal data. A model that remembers a stranger's address is a poor souvenir.
Interesting is not the same as useful. Pick one model, apply it to one problem, and stop browsing.

## site code colab
> google colab | - colab
@ search
Google Colab. Jupyter notebooks in the browser with a free GPU, within limits. Shift+Enter runs a cell and Ctrl+M B adds one below.
The runtime disconnects after a while, and the files in /content vanish. Save to Drive or download anything you care about.
GPU time is limited and shared. If you cannot get one, try again later or switch to a CPU runtime for the small steps.
"Runtime → Restart and run all" is the best test of whether a notebook really works from top to bottom.
Pip installs in a cell are lost on reconnect. Put them at the top so a restart brings everything back.
Mount Google Drive with the little folder icon on the left to read and write your own files. It asks for permission.
Notebook outputs can include private data. Clear the outputs before sharing the file.
A neat notebook has headings and short cells. A messy one is a diary of panic.

## site code jupyter
> jupyterlab | jupyter notebook
@ fix
Jupyter. Esc for command mode, Enter for edit mode, Shift+Enter to run a cell, A and B to add cells above and below, DD to delete one.
Cells can be run out of order, so a notebook can show results that no longer match the code. "Restart kernel and run all" settles it.
Keep the notebook for exploration and move the stable code into a plain .py file. Your future self will thank you at the next import.
Use a virtual environment and register it as a kernel. "Which Python is this?" is the most common question in the world.
Large outputs make notebooks slow and git diffs unreadable. Clear outputs before committing.
Markdown cells are for explaining what the code does and why. Write one per section, and the notebook becomes a report.
The kernel can die when memory runs out. If it does, check how big your DataFrame really is.
Time to save the notebook and close it. Let the results sit for a day. Insight needs a night.

## site settings grafana
> grafana
@ cool
Grafana. Dashboards of graphs, with a time range selector at the top right. "No data" usually means the time range or the data source, not the universe.
Alerts can ping you when a graph crosses a line. Set one for the thing that would actually wake you up.
A dashboard with 40 panels is a wall of decoration. Pick the four that answer a real question.
Variables at the top let you switch between hosts or services without making a copy of the dashboard.
Export dashboards as JSON and keep them in git. A dashboard that exists only in a UI is one accident away from vanishing.
Annotations mark events on the graph: a deployment, an outage, a reboot. They answer "what changed?" at a glance.
Percentiles tell more than averages. A p99 of five seconds hides behind an average of 200 milliseconds.
If you only look at the graphs when something is wrong, you will not know what "normal" looks like. Glance at them on a calm day.

## site settings portainer
> portainer
@ think
Portainer. A web interface for Docker: containers, images, volumes and stacks in one place. A friendly face on a very command-line world.
Stacks are Compose files you paste and deploy. A good way to run a small home server without memorising commands.
Look at a container's logs before you restart it. Restarting without reading is how a mystery returns.
Volumes hold the data. Before removing a container, check which volumes it uses, or the database goes with it.
Keep the Portainer port off the public internet. A control panel for your containers is a very attractive target.
The "Update available" icon on a container means a newer image exists. Updating is easy. Reading the release notes first is wiser.
Tags matter: "latest" can mean something different next week. Pin versions for things you care about.
Prune unused images now and then. A dozen old versions of the same app is not a collection.

## site chatbot chatgpt
> chatgpt
@ think
ChatGPT. Ctrl+Shift+O starts a new chat and Ctrl+/ shows the other shortcuts. A new chat is the cure for a conversation that has gone sideways.
It writes with total confidence, whether it is right or not. Ask for sources and then check that they exist.
Paste an error message with a bit of context and it is a fast debugging partner. Paste a password, and you are a bit of a hero in the wrong way.
Be specific. "Make it better" gets mush. "Shorten to three sentences, friendly, no jargon" gets something usable.
Long chats drift. When it starts repeating itself or forgetting a rule, start a new chat and paste the summary.
It is excellent for a first draft, a summary or a nudge. It is not a replacement for knowing what you actually think.
Check numbers, dates and quotes yourself. "Sounds right" is the machine's favourite sound.
Close the tab and go and do the thing it described. The chat was never the work.

## site chatbot claude
> - claude | claude.ai
@ sly
Claude. Long documents and careful writing are its strong points. Paste in the text and say what you want done with it.
Give it a clear role, a short example and the format you want. A good prompt is half the answer.
A long conversation can be summarised and carried into a fresh one. Fresh context usually beats a heavy one.
If the answer sounds too sure, ask it how confident it is and what could be wrong. The second answer is often more honest.
Be careful with private and confidential material. A chat is not a vault.
Projects and files let you keep context between chats. A crisp folder helps the machine and you.
Use it to explain something three times in three ways, until one of them lands. Patience is free.
When you have what you need, close it and do something with your hands for ten minutes.

## site chatbot gemini
> google gemini
@ shock
Gemini. Google's chatbot, tied into Search, Docs and Gmail if you let it. Convenient and a little like giving the keys to a very efficient neighbour.
Check what it can see before you ask it anything personal. Settings, Extensions, and a quick read of the permissions.
It is good for quick explanations and drafts. For facts, ask it for links and open them.
Pasting a screenshot works. It will describe what it sees, and sometimes invent a button that does not exist.

## site chatbot copilot
> microsoft copilot
@ talk
Microsoft Copilot. A chatbot built into Edge, Windows, Word and Excel. If you did not press the button, someone did it for you.
In Excel it can write a formula from a sentence. Check the result. A confidently wrong formula is a lovely way to lose an afternoon.
In Word it can summarise or rewrite. Great for a first pass. The final voice should still be yours.
Work and personal accounts behave differently. If you are on a work account, assume your IT department can see more than you think.
The Copilot key on some keyboards opens it directly. The number of people who wanted that key is a surprising mystery.
Ask it to cite the file or page it used. Unclear sources make unclear decisions.

## site chatbot perplexity
> perplexity
@ sly
Perplexity. A chatbot that answers with numbered sources, which makes it a search engine that talks. Click the sources. They are the whole point.
A source on the list is not proof that the sentence is right. Open the link and check that the page really says it.
Follow-up questions are the strength of the format. Ask three narrower questions rather than one giant one.
Focus modes let you search academic papers or only certain sources. Use them for homework and for settling an argument.
Free daily limits for advanced features are a polite nudge toward a subscription. You decide.
Collections keep related searches together. A tidy way to research a trip or a purchase.
Not a replacement for reading the actual article. A summary of a summary is a long game of telephone.

## site chatbot lechat
> mistral ai | chat.mistral.ai
@ talk
Le Chat. The chatbot from the French company Mistral. Fast, multilingual and happy to answer in French if you start in French.
Many people like it because it is a European alternative with fast answers and a free tier. A fair choice if you care where your chats are processed.

## site chatbot deepseek
> deepseek
@ think
DeepSeek. A chatbot that shows its "thinking" before the answer. Watching a machine reason out loud is oddly relaxing and sometimes unsettling.
Seeing the reasoning helps you spot where it went wrong. A bad step in the middle is easy to notice when it is written down.
Free and capable, which has made it popular. Free tools still deserve a glance at where your data goes.
Good with code and maths. Check the final answer against a calculator or a test.
Long reasoning means longer waits. It is "thinking", which is a nice word for "slow".
Keep personal and confidential information out of any chat tool you did not set up yourself.
When it contradicts itself, ask it to check its own answer. The second pass often catches the first.
Ask the same question twice in different words. If the answers disagree, you have found the interesting part.

## site chatbot notebooklm
> notebooklm
@ shock
NotebookLM. Upload your own documents, PDFs and notes, and it answers questions only from those sources. Handy for studying a long report.
Answers come with citations that jump to the passage in your source. Click them. That is the whole trick.
The "Audio Overview" turns your sources into a chatty two-voice podcast. A strange and strangely effective way to review notes.
It cannot know what is not in your sources. If a question is outside the documents, it will say so, or guess. Notice which.
Good for exam prep: upload lecture notes and ask for a quiz. Quizzing yourself beats rereading.
Sources are stored in a notebook. Avoid uploading things you would not want in a cloud.
Combining ten PDFs into one question is a lovely use. Reading all ten is a lovely use too.

## site search google
> google search
@ search
Google. Quotes search for the exact phrase, a minus sign removes a word, and "site:" restricts to one website. Three tricks, ten minutes saved per day.
"filetype:pdf" finds documents, "before:2020" and "after:2020" narrow by date. Good for a manual that is not on the first page.
The first few results are ads. They look like results. They are not results. Scroll a bit.
The AI summary at the top is a confident paragraph that may or may not be correct. Check the links beneath it.
Ctrl+K or Ctrl+L focuses the address bar and lets you search from there. Fewer clicks, faster questions.
If the first page fails, rephrase with different words. A search engine is a very literal friend.
Be wary of results that begin with "Top 10 best". They are a list written to be found, not to help.
Got your answer? Close the tab. Twenty more tabs of "related searches" are a trap.

## site search duckduckgo
> duckduckgo
@ search
DuckDuckGo. A search engine that does not track you across the web. The "bangs" are the secret weapon: "!w" searches Wikipedia, "!yt" YouTube, "!g" Google.
Results come from several sources, mostly Bing. Privacy lives in how it treats you, not in a separate index.
Region and safe search settings are in the corner. Setting the region saves a surprising number of irrelevant local ads.
Searching in quotes works here too. So does "site:" for a single website.
The "Maps", "Images" and "News" tabs under the search box are easy to overlook. They do real work.
If you are logged out of everything, results will be the same for you and for everyone else. That is surprisingly pleasant.
Add it as your default search engine in the browser settings. A small act of digital housekeeping.
Close the tab when found. The duck will not take it personally.

## site search bing
> - bing | bing.com
@ search
Bing. Microsoft's search engine, and the traditional place to type "Chrome" to download Chrome. It has a pretty picture of the day on the front page.
Microsoft Rewards gives points for searching. A few pennies of gift cards, earned slowly by looking things up.
The daily wallpaper is genuinely pretty. Hover over it for a quiz or a fact.
Chat features sit right next to the search box. A single page for both a normal search and a chat with a bot.
Image search is a good one. Filters for size, colour and licence help you find the one that fits the slide.
The same search tricks work here: quotes, minus, "site:". An old search engine learns the old tricks.
Check whether you are signed in. The search is different when Microsoft knows who you are.
Close the tab when you have what you need. A search bar is not a hobby.

## site search ecosia
> ecosia
@ think
Ecosia. A search engine from Berlin that uses its profits to plant trees. Every few dozen searches, a tree. Your clicking has a quiet green side.
The counter in the corner shows how many trees you have helped plant. It rises slowly and is very satisfying.
Results are provided by partner search engines, and the ads are what pay for the trees. You do not have to click on them, but it helps.
It is a good everyday search engine for most things. For very exotic searches, you may switch to another.
Switching your browser's default search to Ecosia takes a minute. A small, easy act.
A search engine cannot plant a tree for a bad day. A walk outside might.
Fun fact: a tree does not mind if you misspell your search term.
Ecosia's tree counter is public, and the site explains how it plants trees in surprising detail. For a search engine, that is rare.

## site search startpage
> startpage
@ think
Startpage. A Dutch search engine that delivers Google results without the tracking. It is like sending a polite intern to ask on your behalf.
"Anonymous View" lets you open a result through Startpage's proxy. Handy for a quick look at a website that is nosy.
Results look like the big engine's and that is the point. You get the quality without the profile.
The settings page lets you save your preferences in a URL, not in a cookie. A clever bit of old-school privacy.
Ads still appear, but they are not based on a profile of you. Mildly more polite advertising.
If you travel, the region setting helps. Search for "bakery" and you get the right bakery.
Not every search engine needs to be everything. This one wants to be quiet.
Close the tab and let the intern rest.

## site search bravesearch
> brave search
@ wink
Brave Search. A search engine with its own independent index, so it does not rely on the big ones. A rare thing in 2024.
Goggles let you re-rank results with custom rules, such as "prefer small blogs" or "hide content farms".
Summaries appear above the results. They may be helpful, and may also be wrong. The links underneath are still the best part.
Privacy is a selling point. The search does not build a profile of you.
Its results can be thin for niche or non-English queries. Try another engine when a search comes up empty.
Searching with "site:" and quotes works. Old tricks for old friends.
Not everyone needs a different search engine. But it is good that someone is building one.
If a niche query returns thin results, try a different phrasing rather than more words. A new angle beats a longer question.

## site search qwant
> qwant
@ wink
Qwant. A French search engine that promises not to track you. A quiet, European option, with a clean page and a gentle voice.
Tabs for Web, Images, News and Shopping are neatly laid out. No clutter.
Results come partly from partners and partly from its own index. If something is missing, try another engine.
Qwant has a children's version called Qwant Junior, in which filters take care of the nasties.
A European search engine is a nice option for people who care about where the company lives.
Set it as your default and see how long it takes before you miss the old one. You may be surprised.
Short, clean, quiet. That is the style.
Close the tab. Un petit moment de silence.

## site search kagi
> kagi
@ search
Kagi. A paid search engine with no ads and no tracking, which makes it unusual. You pay with money, not attention.
You can raise or lower the rank of sites or block them entirely. Content farms vanish from your results with one click.
"Lenses" focus a search on forums, small web or academic papers. A quick way to change the flavour.
Paying for search is a strange idea until you notice there are no ads in the results. Peace has a monthly fee.
The summariser can digest a page or a video in a few seconds. Handy when the page is long and the author is chatty.
Not for everyone. A free engine is good enough for most things, and that is perfectly fine.
Whatever you search with, your own judgement is the best filter.
Use a Lens to focus on forums or small sites. Content farms vanish, and recipes suddenly come from people who cook.

## site learning googlescholar
> google scholar
@ read
Google Scholar. A search engine for academic papers, with a "Cited by" count under each result. That number tells you which papers shaped the field.
The "Cite" button gives you a ready-made reference in APA, MLA and others. A kind gift to everyone who has to write a bibliography.
Look at the "[PDF]" link on the right. Many papers have a free version hiding there, even if the main link wants money.
"Related articles" and "Cited by" are the quickest way to find more papers on the same topic.
Set up an alert and Scholar emails you when a new paper matches your search. A very nerdy newsletter.
A paper being cited a lot does not make it right. Look at the year and read the abstract.
Use your library's login to get past paywalls. Many universities have a proxy that works at home.
Save the papers you will actually read. A hundred PDFs in a folder is a hobby.

## site search wayback
> wayback machine
@ think
The Wayback Machine. The Internet Archive's collection of old web pages. Paste a URL and see what it looked like in 2004. Mostly blue links and optimism.
"Save Page Now" lets you archive a page yourself. Useful for an article you want to cite before it vanishes.
A broken link is not always the end. Paste it into the Wayback Machine and the page may still be there.
Not every image or script was saved, so old pages can look odd. That is part of the charm.
The calendar view shows the dates when a page was captured. The more dots, the more important the site was to someone.
The archive is a non-profit library. A donation or a thank-you helps keep the lights on.
Looking at an old version of a site you once loved is a very particular kind of nostalgia.
Do not spend the whole afternoon there. It is a time machine, not a time home.

## site search wolframalpha
> wolframalpha | wolfram alpha
@ search
Wolfram Alpha. A computational engine that answers maths, units and data questions directly. Type "integrate x^2" or "distance to the moon" and it replies.
It gives step-by-step solutions for many maths problems, which makes it a handy homework helper, and a handy way of checking your own work.
Unit conversions, dates, nutritional values and population figures are all here. A very nerdy almanac.
It works best with a clear, short query. "Population of Switzerland 1950 vs 2020" is a good one.
Pro features exist for step-by-step details and more, but the basic version already does a lot.
A neat trick: ask it to plot a function. The graph appears instantly.
Check units and assumptions. It tells you what it assumed. Read that line.

Wikipedia. The "Random article" link in the sidebar is a lovely, harmless way to lose eight minutes and gain one fact about a lighthouse.

## site translate wiktionary
> wiktionary
@ read
Wiktionary. A dictionary of every word in every language, with etymology, pronunciation and a table of translations. A very big small town.
The Etymology section tells you where a word came from. It is often more entertaining than the definition.
Click the speaker icon next to the IPA for an audio pronunciation, where one exists. It is very useful for unfamiliar words.
The Translations table shows the word in dozens of languages. Handy when you need a word that is not in your usual dictionary.

Rare words, slang and old spellings are all covered, with example sentences. A fine rabbit hole for lovers of language.

"{title}": check the etymology, which is the most interesting part, and the pronunciation, which is the most useful.

## site howto wikihow
> wikihow
@ read
wikiHow. Illustrated step-by-step guides for everything from tying a tie to cleaning a toaster. The illustrations are a genre of their own.
The "Tips" and "Warnings" boxes at the end are the best part. A small thing that stops you from making the common mistake.
Many guides are written by a community, so quality varies. A guide with photos and recent edits is usually good.
"How to" pages often have a "Things you'll need" box. Check it before you begin. Nothing ruins a Sunday like a missing screwdriver.
If the guide has twelve steps and step four says "the rest is easy", step four is the part that takes three hours.
Reading the whole guide before starting is the single best DIY habit.
Videos are embedded in many guides, often with the sound off. A little subtitled tutorial is enough.
If the job involves electricity, gas or a ladder, ask someone who does it for a living. This is a guide, not a dare.
"{title}": read the whole guide first. The step where it says "carefully" is the step where it goes wrong.

## site wikipedia britannica
> britannica
@ think
Britannica. The encyclopedia that started in Edinburgh in the 1700s, stopped printing in 2010, and now lives online with articles written by named experts.
Articles are signed and edited, which makes a nice contrast to the crowd-written ones. Good for a second opinion.
Many articles are partly behind a subscription, but the first few paragraphs are free. Often enough for what you need.

Reading an encyclopedia is a lovely way to waste an hour. Make it a good one.
"{title}" in Britannica: signed, edited and fact-checked. A slower, tidier kind of knowledge. Pour a tea.

## site wikipedia imdb
> - imdb | imdb.com
@ read
IMDb. The film and TV database. "Trivia" and "Goofs" are where the fun is: continuity errors, hidden cameos, a wristwatch in a Roman epic.
"Where have I seen that actor?" is the most common reason to open this site. The cast list and the filmography answer it in seconds.

## site wikipedia rottentomatoes
> rotten tomatoes
@ think
Rotten Tomatoes. Two scores: critics and audience. When they disagree wildly, the film is usually interesting.
The Tomatometer is the percentage of critics who liked it, not how much they liked it. A 90% film can be a gentle "pretty good" from nearly everyone.
"Certified Fresh" is a badge for films with good scores from enough critics. A decent shortcut, not a verdict.
Read the critic quotes, not just the number. A pan can sound like a rave and a rave can sound like a pan.
The audience score can be skewed by a lot of votes in the first week. Check again in a month.
Films with a split score are a good evening. Watch one and decide who is right.
Do not trust a number for a film you will love. Trust your own taste.
Pick something and press play. The tomatoes will wait.

## site wikipedia letterboxd

Letterboxd. A social diary for films: log what you watched, rate it in stars and write a review in three lines. A very pleasant corner for film people.

Your watchlist grows faster than you watch. That is normal. It is a wish list with a pulse.

"Diary" entries show the date you watched something. At the end of the year, you will see your habits laid out. It is mildly humbling.

"{title}" will get a rating from you eventually. Half a star is allowed. Writing the three-line review is optional.

## site chat discord

Discord. Ctrl+K opens the quick switcher, so you can jump to any server or channel by typing a few letters. A good way to escape a busy channel.
Alt+Up and Alt+Down move between channels. Handy when you have forty and only one is talking.

## site chat whatsapp

@ cool
WhatsApp Web. Link a computer by scanning the QR code in your phone. It is a handy way to type long replies on a real keyboard.
Blue ticks mean read. Turning that off in the privacy settings is allowed. Nobody has to know you saw it.
Voice messages can be played at 1.5x or 2x. A three-minute story becomes ninety seconds.
The family group chat has 40 unread messages. Thirty-six are pictures of food, two are a birthday and two are a fight about the barbecue.

## site chat telegram

@ wink
Telegram Web. "Saved Messages" is a chat with yourself, and a very good notebook. Send links, photos and files there.

## site chat slack

@ wink
Slack. Ctrl+K jumps to any channel or person and "/remind me to call Anna at 3pm" sets a reminder from the message box. Two features worth the app.
Esc marks the current channel as read and Shift+Esc marks everything. A quiet relief for a very large unread count.
Threads keep conversations tidy. A reply in the thread, not in the channel, saves everybody's attention.
A thumbs-up reaction is a whole sentence: "seen it, agree, no need to reply". It is one of Slack's best inventions.

The #random channel is where the best content lives: photos of pets, articles about snacks and a dispute about pineapple on pizza.
A message that says "quick question" with no question is a classic. The answer is "go ahead".
Huddles are quick audio chats built into Slack. A reason to hold a five-minute talk and not a 30-minute meeting.

## site chat mattermost

@ wink
Mattermost. An open source, self-hostable chat for teams, a bit like Slack but under your own roof. Channels, threads and a lot of integrations.

@ think
Eventbrite. Workshops, concerts, meetups and one very ambitious quiz night, with tickets and reminders. A fine place to find out what is on this weekend.
Check the venue, the time and the language of the event. A "workshop" can be a talk, a class or a very long sales pitch.
Tickets are sent as a QR code to your email. Save it where you can find it from a phone on the day. A screenshot is not a bad idea.
Read the cancellation and refund policy before buying. Fees and rules vary by organiser.
"Going" and "Interested" are different. One is a plan and one is a wish.
Put the event in your calendar with the travel time. A good idea that is also a rare one.
Going alone to a meetup is a fine experience. Everyone is there because they wanted to meet someone.
Pick something and book it. A calendar full of "maybe" is a calendar full of Tuesdays.

## site translate deepl
> deepl
@ think
DeepL. Click any word in the translation and a list of alternatives opens. It is the quickest way to rescue a sentence that sounds slightly off.
The formal and informal switch picks between "Sie" and "du" or their cousins in other languages. Choose before sending the email to your landlord.
The free version has a limit of 5,000 characters per text. A long document needs the document upload or a break between chunks.
Document translation keeps the layout of Word, PowerPoint and PDF files. A modest gift for anyone with a 40-page contract.
DeepL Write polishes text in the same language. Handy when your English email sounds like a translated German one. Which it is.
Read the result once more. A translation can sound perfect and say something slightly different. Pay attention to numbers and names.
Words with several meanings are its weak spot. The alternatives list shows you which one it picked.
Paste, translate, check, send. Four steps, no panic.

## site translate googletranslate
> google translate
@ search
Google Translate. Good for the gist of a text in over a hundred languages. The "Documents" and "Websites" tabs are easy to overlook and very handy.
Translate the result back into the original language. If it sounds odd, the first translation probably is too.
Idioms are translated word for word, which is how a polite phrase turns into "I understand only train station". Use plain sentences instead.
The detect language option is surprisingly good. Paste a text you cannot read and it will tell you what it is.
Short sentences translate better than long ones. A sentence of 60 words is a recipe for confusion.
For anything official, such as contracts or letters to an authority, use a human translator or ask a native speaker.
The speaker icon reads the text aloud. A helpful way to check how a word is pronounced.
It is a tool, not an interpreter. Treat it like a map, not like a tour guide.

## site translate linguee
> linguee
@ search
Linguee. A dictionary that shows how a word has been translated in real texts from the web and EU documents. Context is the whole point.
It belongs to the same company as DeepL. One writes the sentence for you, the other shows how humans did it.
Examples have a quality grade. Green dots are from official sources, red ones are less reliable. Read the little dots.
Use it when you need to know whether a word fits a particular context, like "appointment" versus "meeting".
Searching with a phrase works better than a single word. "Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren" gives good formal examples.
A good habit for emails in a foreign language: look up the key phrases here and copy the natural ones.
Not for long texts. For those, use a translator and use this one to double-check.
If the example sounds odd, search another. The first result is not always the best.

## site translate leo
> leo.org | dict.leo
@ search
LEO. A German online dictionary for English, French, Spanish and more, with a very good forum for the finer points. A dictionary, not a translator.
Entries show several translations with a short note on usage. Look at the little tags like "formal" or "coll." before picking one.
The vocabulary trainer lets you build your own list from lookups. A spotless way to learn the words you actually met.
The forum is where the strange cases go. "How do you say 'Feierabendbier' in English?" The answers are many and good.
Pronunciation audio is available for many entries. A very good habit for words that look easy and are not.
The site shows false friends: words that look the same and mean something different. "Gift" is the classic.
A dictionary is best used to confirm a guess. If you only look up the first word, you will mistranslate everything.
The tags after an entry, like "coll." and "fig.", tell you the register. "Coll." means you would say it, not write it to the tax office.

## site translate dictcc
> dict.cc
@ read
dict.cc. A very quick online dictionary with a clean list of translations, user-added audio and a vocabulary trainer. Pure muscle memory for many.
The entries are added by users, so very new words appear quickly. And very odd ones occasionally. Check the vote count next to the entry.
Audio pronunciation is recorded by real people. Often it is a person in a kitchen, which is perfectly fine.
The vocabulary trainer lets you tick words as you look them up. Over a few weeks it builds a personal list.
Switch the language pair with the little arrows. Looking up a German word in English and back is a good test.
Phrases and idioms are listed under the main word. A line like "to be on the ball" helps more than a single translation.
No ads in the middle of the entry, just on the side. A decently polite dictionary.
The little speaker icon plays a recording. Say the word back out loud once and it moves from your eyes to your mouth.

## site translate reverso
> reverso
@ search
Reverso. A translator and dictionary with plenty of real examples in context, plus a verb conjugator. Good when a word has no neat match.
The "Context" section shows how a phrase is used in real texts. Compare three examples, pick the one that sounds like your sentence.
The conjugator lists every form of a verb. French and Spanish verbs are a long journey. The table is a map.
Grammar and spell checks are included. A bit like a polite teacher who is not allowed to sigh.
Free searches are generous and some features need an account. The usual trade.
Phrases from film subtitles appear as examples. Learning a language from film dialogue is a joy and a trap.
Add words to favourites and you can revise them later. Do it for the ten you keep forgetting.
The synonyms tab helps when you have used the same word three times in a paragraph and the paragraph knows it.

## site translate wordreference
> wordreference
@ think
WordReference. A dictionary with an excellent forum: when the entry does not help, someone in the forum has already discussed your exact phrase at length.
Look at the forum threads at the bottom of an entry. Search first, because your question has probably been asked, with polite, long answers.
Entries are sorted by meaning with example sentences. Skim down to the one that matches your sentence.
The conjugator and the "Spanish-English" and "French-English" sections are very popular. Good, quick references.
The English dictionary also explains idioms and regional differences. "Pants" means different things on different sides of the Atlantic.
Anyone can ask in the forum, but read the rules first. Posting the full sentence and what you think it means is polite.
The audio files are recorded by native speakers from different regions. A fine way to hear accents.
Look up, read, move on. A dictionary is a service, not a home.

## site translate duden
> duden
@ think
Duden. The German dictionary people mean by "look it up in the Duden". Spelling, grammar, synonyms and the smug explanation of "das" versus "dass".
Each entry gives the spelling, the grammatical forms and often a note on usage. Perfect for a word that looks wrong on the page.
The "Rechtschreibung" section settles arguments about commas, hyphens and compound words. German compounds are a sport.
Synonym suggestions help when you have used "wichtig" five times in one paragraph.
The "Wort des Tages" is a nice small habit. One new German word a day, from the serious to the strange.
Free access shows the core of an entry. Some details are for subscribers. It is enough for most questions.
Language changes. If a word is not listed, it may be too new, or too spoken. Not everything belongs in the Duden.
"Das" or "dass": if you can swap in "dieses" or "welches", it is "das". A very quiet trick with a very large reputation.

## site translate merriamwebster
> merriam-webster
@ read
Merriam-Webster. An American dictionary with a Word of the Day, a thesaurus and a very good tendency to explain things in plain English.
The "Word of the Day" is a little habit: one fresh word, one example, one chance to use it in a meeting without anyone noticing.
Entries show the first known use and the etymology. A very short history of a very common word.
The thesaurus lists synonyms by shade of meaning. "Big" has many cousins and each has its own manners.
"Words at Play" explains slang and new words that are about to enter the dictionary. A very nerdy newspaper.
The pronunciation button reads the word aloud. A kind way to avoid saying "epitome" wrong.
There is a quiz and word game section. A decent five-minute break with some vocabulary in it.
The audio button next to a word saves you from saying "epitome" wrong in a meeting. You will only get it wrong once.

## site learning duolingo
> duolingo
@ happy
+ Pomodoro = pomodoro
Duolingo. Five minutes a day beats an hour on Sunday. The owl will remind you in an increasingly disappointed tone.
A streak is a number that grows each day you practise. It is a motivating number until you break it on holiday.
Leagues and XP make it a small competition. Being in the "Emerald" league is a quiet honour you cannot explain to anyone.
It is good for vocabulary and basic phrases. For real conversation, find a human to talk to now and then.
Some sentences are strange: "The bear drinks beer." Treat them as a mild improvement on a phrasebook that only knows "where is the station".
Listening exercises can be done with headphones in the office. Mutter quietly and nobody will notice.
Pick a time of day and stick to it. A habit with a fixed time beats a habit with a good intention.
Do your five minutes, then close the tab. The streak is safe.

## site learning coursera
> coursera
@ think
Coursera. University courses online, many of which can be "audited" for free if you do not need the certificate. Watch the lectures and skip the paperwork.
Peer-graded assignments mean other learners review your work. Be kind, because you will be on the other end next week.
Deadlines are usually flexible. The progress bar is the real teacher, and it is usually at 11%.
Playback speed at 1.25x works for most lectures. Switch back to 1x for the hard bits.
Take notes by hand. It slows you down just enough to remember.
A specialisation is several courses in a row. A lovely idea, and a longer road than the brochure says.
A course with a "Cancel anytime" button is a course with a subscription. Check before you begin.
Pick one course, schedule two evenings, and keep them. The rest is a library.
You are on "{title}". Watch the video at 1.25x, pause to take notes by hand, and do the quiz before the weekend ends.

## site learning khanacademy
> khan academy
@ search
Khan Academy. Free lessons in maths, science and more, from a non-profit that believes everyone deserves a decent explanation. And practice with no ads.
The exercises give you hints without giving the answer away. A very patient tutor who never gets tired of "why is it that?"
Mastery points reward you for coming back. Level up the topic instead of racing through it.
If a topic stumps you, go back one level. The block is usually two lessons earlier.
Videos are short and hand-drawn on a dark background. Very calming, a little hypnotic.
It is also a good place to refresh high-school maths you have forgotten. No shame, only fractions.
A short session every day beats a big one once a week. Make it a ten-minute habit.
Do one lesson, then try one exercise. Learning by doing, politely.
"{title}": do the exercise before you watch the video. If you get it right, you have saved ten minutes.

## site learning udemy
> udemy
@ read
Udemy. Thousands of video courses, all permanently "on sale". A course that costs 89 or 14.99 depending on the day has an odd relationship with arithmetic.
A new course bought at midnight is the traditional first step to not taking it. Finish what you have started before buying another.
Read the reviews for the instructor's style and whether the content is up to date. A course from 2017 on a fast-changing tool may be a museum.
Preview videos are free. Watch one before you buy. If the instructor makes you tired, so will the other twenty hours.
Playback speed and subtitles are in the player. At 1.5x most courses get a lot more efficient.
The refund window exists. If a course does not match the description, use it within the allowed time.
Do the projects. Watching someone build a thing is not building a thing.
Look for courses that end with a project you build. Watching someone else code is not learning to code.
"{title}": watch the first lecture and do the first exercise tonight. A course started is a course ten percent finished.

## site learning babbel
> babbel
@ read
Babbel. A language app from Berlin with short lessons, dialogues and a gentle push to speak out loud. Better for grammar than a game of streaks.
Each lesson takes ten to fifteen minutes. A coffee break is the perfect slot.
The speech recognition checks your pronunciation. It is harsh to the shy and gracious to the confident. Speak with conviction.
Dialogues are set in real-life situations: ordering a coffee, asking for the way, complaining about the room.
The review section brings back words you are about to forget. A friendly flashcard system with a hat.
Learning a language takes months. Plan a short session a day and give it a fixed time.
Try talking to a real person as soon as you can. The app is the gym, the world is the match.
Switch the review mode to listening once a week. Hearing a language at speed is a different skill from reading it.

## site learning busuu
> busuu
@ read
Busuu. A language learning app where native speakers correct your written and spoken exercises. A very human touch, and a little nerve-racking.
Writing a short text and waiting for a correction is one of the best language habits there is. It is also very humbling.
Correct the exercises of others in return. It is a quick way to learn how your own language works.
Study plans set a goal like "A2 in three months". It is a good way to stay honest.
Offline mode lets you study on a train. A tunnel is no excuse.
Vocabulary is more fun when linked to pictures. The app does that nicely.
A short talk with a real person in the language, even a minute, beats an hour of listening to a recording.
Write about your real day, not a made-up one. "I had a sandwich" is easier to remember than an invented cat, and the corrections stick.

## site learning quizlet
> quizlet
@ read
Quizlet. Flashcards for exams, languages and anything else you want to memorise. "Learn" mode and the "Match" game make revision feel like a puzzle.
Making your own set is a better way to learn than using someone else's. The act of writing the card is half of the learning.
Spaced repetition, even in a basic form, beats cramming. A few minutes on five different days beats an hour the night before.
The "Match" game against the clock is oddly addictive. Beat your own time. Beat the clock. Beat the tab.
Check the set you borrowed before trusting it. Someone may have mistyped a date, or a formula.
Add images and audio to cards. A word with a picture is a word that lingers.
Share the set with the class and they will thank you. Or they will ask for the answers. Either way, you are popular.
Study the cards you got wrong first. The ones you already know feel nice and teach you nothing.

## site learning kahoot
> kahoot
@ happy
Kahoot. A quiz game for classrooms and parties: everyone joins with a game PIN and answers on their own device. The countdown music stays in your head.
Faster answers earn more points, so the loudest keyboard wins. Take your time with a hard question, then answer quickly on the easy ones.
Teachers use it to wake up a sleepy class. Hosts use it for pub quizzes. Both are respectable uses.
Pick a good nickname. "Cat", "Rocket" and "Anonymous" are taken.
The podium at the end gives a smug feeling to the top three and a mild shrug to the rest.
Creating a kahoot takes about 15 minutes. Add images and short questions and a very bad pun in the answers.
It is a good icebreaker. A weird question about pineapple on pizza gets a room talking.
Hosting? Keep questions short and answer options to four at most. Nobody reads a long question while a countdown runs.

## site learning moodle
> moodle
@ search
Moodle. The learning platform of countless schools and universities: courses, assignments, forums and a gradebook with a very crisp menu on the left.
Assignments are due at 23:59, which is the traditional time for pressing "Submit" with six seconds left.
Check that your file actually uploaded. A grey status "No attempt" is the sound of a missed deadline.
Course pages are a long list of PDFs. Names like "Lecture_07_final_v2.pdf" are a work of art.
Forums are where the questions are asked and answered. Search first, because your question was asked last semester.
Notifications can be tuned in your profile. A weekly digest beats forty emails.
Calendar shows all deadlines in one view. Look at it on Sunday evening, not Monday morning.
Do the thing that is due soonest first. Then everything else.

## site learning ilias
> ilias
@ search
ILIAS. An open source learning platform used by many universities in Switzerland and Germany. Courses, files and navigation that rewards patient clicking.
The "Magazine" and "Repository" are different things. The repository holds the courses, the magazine shows what is new. It takes a week to learn.
Bookmarks and the "Favourites" list save you from clicking through five levels of folders every day.
Tests and exercises can have strict time limits. Read the instructions twice before pressing Start.
Upload your files in the format the course asks for. "I sent a pages file" is not an argument.
Forums and wikis in ILIAS are used by students more than teachers expect. A decent place to ask a question quietly.
The system times out if you are idle. Save long answers elsewhere before submitting them.
Download the course files at the start of term, not the night before an exam. Servers get shy at 23:00 on deadline day.

## site learning codecademy
> codecademy
@ search
Codecademy. Interactive coding lessons in the browser: read, write the code, press Run, see the output. A very gentle first step into programming.
The early lessons are easy so that you feel good. The middle lessons are where you have to sit and think. That is the point.
Do not copy the solution. Type it out and change one thing. Then see what breaks.
Projects at the end of a path matter more than the lessons. Build one small thing that does not come with instructions.
A daily streak of ten minutes beats a Sunday marathon. The brain likes repetition.
The community forum is a good place to ask if you get stuck. Show your code and your error and people will help.
After finishing a course, make something real: a small script, a page for a friend. That is how it sticks.
Type the code instead of pasting the solution. Fingers learn syntax that eyes politely skip.
"{title}": type the code yourself, then change one thing and watch what breaks. That is the lesson inside the lesson.

## site learning freecodecamp
> freecodecamp
@ think
freeCodeCamp. Free coding courses, projects and certifications from a non-profit. You build real projects for each certificate, which teaches well.
The curriculum is long and you can pick your own pace. Start with the basics, but build something ugly early on.
The forum has a beginner-friendly culture. Post the problem, the code and what you have tried.
Each project asks you to meet user stories. It is a humble taste of real work: a list of requirements and a deadline you set yourself.
The project also publishes long, free video courses. A great way to spend a weekend, and a lot cheaper than a bootcamp.
Do not binge. Four hours of video, then build something for an hour.
Tests that turn green are the best reward. They are also the first thing you stop noticing.
Use the "Reset this lesson" button without shame. Starting over is faster than debugging a mess you made at 1 a.m.

## site learning leetcode
> leetcode
@ happy
LeetCode. Coding puzzles that are used to prepare for job interviews. Problem 1 is "Two Sum", and it is the world's most famous warm-up.
"Easy", "Medium" and "Hard" are labels, not promises. Some "Easy" problems are cruel and some "Hard" ones are a nice stroll.
Reading the discussion tab after solving is the best learning. You see five other solutions, and one of them is a one-liner that makes you sigh.
Time complexity matters more than elegance here. If your solution is O(n²) and the input is a million, the page shows a "Time Limit Exceeded".
Do a few problems a week, and do the same type several times in a row. Patterns appear when you repeat them.
The skill transfers to the job only partly. It is a puzzle sport. Enjoy it as one, and prepare for the interview as one.
Write the solution in your own words afterwards. If you cannot explain it, you do not own it.
Stuck for thirty minutes? Read the hint, then close it and try again. Reading the full solution too early steals the lesson.
"{title}": write down your approach in plain words before touching the keyboard. It is half the solution.

## site learning hackerrank
> hackerrank
@ read
HackerRank. Coding challenges and timed assessments that some companies send to applicants. Practise the format before the real one lands in your inbox.
Read the sample input and output carefully. Many wrong answers are only a missing newline or an off-by-one.
Choose the language you know best, not the one you think looks impressive. The clock does not care.
Run the sample tests before submitting. Then add a couple of your own: empty input, one element, the biggest case.
Domain tracks for SQL, Python, 30 Days of Code and more let you pick a topic. A friendly path through the forest.
If you get stuck in a timed test, leave a comment on your approach and move on. A partial solution beats a blank page.
Do a practice run in a calm hour, with a drink and a quiet room. The real test will feel tamer.
Read the problem statement twice before typing. Half of all wrong submissions answer a question nobody asked.

## site learning adventofcode
> advent of code
@ happy
Advent of Code. Small programming puzzles, one per day in December, with a silly story about elves. Many start keenly and drop out around day 14.
Each puzzle has two parts and a very long input file. Part two is always a twist you did not see coming. That is the fun.
Stars are the reward for solving a part. A fine small hoard of gold in a very nerdy treasury.
The community posts solutions and memes. Do not look at them before you have tried yourself.
Use whatever language you want. Many people use it to learn a new one, and the first three days are very hopeful.
Puzzles unlock at midnight US Eastern. If you are in Europe, that is 6 a.m. Sleeping in is allowed.
You do not have to finish all 25 days. Stopping at day 12 and having a good time is a legitimate result.
Work on it in the evening, not in your meeting. The elves can wait.

## site learning kaggle
> kaggle
@ read
Kaggle. Data science competitions, datasets and notebooks. The "Titanic" competition is the classic first one: predict who survived from a table.
Notebooks run in the browser with free GPU hours. You do not need a powerful computer to learn.
Read the top public notebooks of a competition. They are a free masterclass in how people approach a problem.
A leaderboard rank is not the same as a useful model. Watch out for overfitting: a perfect score on training data is not a promise.
Clean the data first. Half the work of any data project is looking at the table and finding the strange row.
Datasets are free and varied: football, flights, films, food. Pick one you actually care about.
Fork a top public notebook and change one thing. Watching the score move because of your edit is wonderfully addictive.
Finish a notebook before starting another. A pile of half-done notebooks is a cairn of ambition.

## site learning arxiv
> arxiv
@ happy
arXiv. A free archive of preprints in physics, maths and computer science. Papers appear before peer review. Some are brilliant, some are drafts.
The number like 2310.12345 is the year and month plus a running count. Fresh papers appear daily, so check the date.
Preprints have not been peer reviewed. If a paper makes a big claim, look for a published version or a discussion.
The abstract and the conclusion tell you in two minutes whether the paper is worth an hour.
"Download PDF" saves a copy. Keep a folder of the ones you read, with a short note on each.
Many mathematicians and physicists read the daily listings as a morning ritual. A very nerdy newspaper.
Every paper has a BibTeX link for citing. A humble gift to your bibliography.
Pick one paper, read it, and write a three-line summary. That is a better use of the afternoon than collecting twenty.

## site learning researchgate
> researchgate
@ happy
ResearchGate. A social network for researchers where you can find papers or ask the authors for a copy. The "Request full text" button is very polite.
Many papers have a full text and others are only an abstract. If it is missing, check the author's profile or the journal's site.
The emails about "your paper was read by 3 people" are a surprisingly sweet form of encouragement.
Q&A is where researchers ask each other for help with methods. A friendly corner of the academic world.
Check copyright before uploading a paper. Publishers have opinions about who can host what.
A good way to see who has cited a paper and how it is used. A paper with many citations has a little fan club.
The feed and the notifications are a distraction for some. Use the site when you need a paper, not as a place to browse for an afternoon.
If the full text is not here, search the paper's title plus "pdf" or check the author's university page. Many post a free copy.

## site jobhunt indeed
> indeed.com
@ sly
Indeed. A giant list of job ads from everywhere. Set up an alert for your search so the new ones come to you, not the other way round.
A job ad that asks for "10 years of experience in a 5-year-old technology" tells you something about the employer. Possibly the whole story.
Read the requirements as a wish list, not a checklist. If you tick 60 percent, apply anyway.
Salary ranges, where listed, are worth a glance. If an ad hides the range, ask in the first call.
Tailor the first three lines of your application to the job. A copy-and-paste cover letter is easy to spot from across the room.
Keep a note of where you applied, when and to whom. A simple list saves you from the awkward "which company is this?" call.
A rejection is a sorting decision, not a verdict on you. Apply to the next one.
Do one application, then a break. Doing ten in a row turns them all into the same one.

## site jobhunt glassdoor
> glassdoor
@ sly
Glassdoor. Reviews and salary reports for employers, written by people who work or have worked there. Read the middle reviews, not just the extremes.
A review from three years ago may describe a different manager and a different company. Look at the dates.
Salary data is a starting point, not a promise. A big range means a big difference between roles and cities.
Interview reviews give you a feel for the process and sometimes the questions. Read a few, then relax.
Company ratings are an average of whoever felt like writing. That is a particular sort of person.
Use it alongside other sources: ask a former employee, read the company blog, look at how they write job ads.
If you write a review yourself, be fair and specific. "The coffee machine was bad" is a review. "Everything was bad" is a mood.
Sort reviews by "most recent" and look for one detail: how long people wait for an answer after an interview. It is a surprisingly good signal.

## site jobhunt stepstone
> stepstone
@ search
StepStone. A big German-speaking job portal with ads from all sorts of industries and a "Gehaltsplaner" that estimates salaries. Handy for a rough idea.
A search by title and place is a good start. Add the radius, and remember that a 50 km radius is a long commute twice a day.
Many ads use "w/m/d" to say that the role is for anyone. If you see "(m/w/d)", that is the German way of saying "everyone welcome".
Save a search and get alerts. A daily email of three relevant jobs beats a daily hour of scrolling.
A short CV and a sentence about why you want the role beats a long motivational paragraph. Be clear and brief.
Look at the company name behind recruiting agencies. The ad may be for a real firm, or for a pool of CVs.
Update your profile once and let the site do the work. Then spend your energy on the real conversations.
Keep one master CV and a short list of three bullet points you tweak per ad. Rewriting everything each time is how people burn out.

## site jobhunt xing
> xing.com
@ think
XING. The German-speaking professional network: a bit more formal than the international one and a good deal more local. Many DACH recruiters start here.
A profile with a clear headline, a current role and a decent photo goes a long way. The rest is polite filler.
Messages from recruiters range from "perfect match" to "do you know anyone who...?" Reply to the ones that name the role and the salary range.
"Gruppen" are a bit like old-fashioned forums. Some are lively, most are lonely. Find one in your field and say hello.
Events listed here are good for meeting people in a calmer way than a mass conference. A small afternoon talk is often better.
Check what your profile shows to strangers. If you are looking quietly, switch on the right visibility.

Connect with people you actually know. A list of 3,000 strangers is not a network, it is a crowd.

## site jobhunt jobsch
> jobs.ch
@ think
jobs.ch. The big Swiss job portal, with ads from Basel to Lugano and a search that handles German, French and Italian. A good one for local roles.
Many ads list the percentage of the role, like 80-100%. That is Swiss for "ask me about part-time". A very practical custom.
The salary is often not listed. The Swiss are fond of discussing it politely in the second interview.
Check the language requirement. "Deutsch verhandlungssicher" means fluent enough to negotiate, not "knows the word Bahnhof".
Set up a job alert for your region, then check it once a day. Not every hour.
A cover letter in Switzerland is usually short, factual and polite. Skip the poetry. Add the date you could start.
Keep your CV in a clear format with a recent date. A very Swiss thing to be tidy.
Apply, note it down, and take a walk by the lake, river or whichever body of water is nearest.

## site jobhunt kununu
> kununu
@ think
kununu. Employer reviews from the German-speaking world, rating salary, management and work-life balance. A good second opinion on a company.
Look at the sub-scores, not only the average. A company with good colleagues and a poor boss reads very differently from one with the opposite.
Read the most recent reviews first. A new manager or a big reorganisation can change everything.
Companies respond to reviews. The tone of the reply tells you almost as much as the review itself.
Interview reviews describe the process: how many rounds, how long it took, what was asked. A handy preview of the road.
A few angry reviews do not make a bad company, and a few glowing ones do not make a great one. Look for patterns.
Write your own honest review after you leave a job. It helps the next person, and it is oddly satisfying.
Look for reviews that mention onboarding and the first month. A good first month is a good sign. A bad one is a long year.

## site jobhunt arbeitsagentur
> arbeitsagentur
@ write
The Bundesagentur für Arbeit. Germany's employment agency: a big job board, advice pages and forms for everything. Very official wording.
The job board is a solid, free place to look for work. It also lists apprenticeships, which are well worth a look.
Forms and applications usually need a login with the eID or a user account. Allow time for the setup, and have your documents at hand.
The "Kurzinfo" pages explain things in short, plain language. They are much easier to read than the full letter.
Advice appointments can often be booked online. Prepare three questions before you go.
Keep copies of everything you submit. A saved PDF of each form is a very quiet safeguard with a very large value.
Deadlines matter. A date in a letter is a date. Put it in your calendar the day the letter arrives.
Take one task, finish it, and rest. Bureaucracy is a marathon with paperwork at every kilometre.

## site taxes elster
> elster
@ shock
ELSTER. The German tax portal. The login wants a certificate file, and the activation code arrives by post a week later. Start early.

## site taxes estv
> estv
@ shock
The Federal Tax Administration of Switzerland. Calculators, forms, rates and explanations in several languages. The tax itself is mostly handled by the cantons.
Cantons and municipalities handle most of what you pay and how. The details change with where you live. Look up your own canton for the real numbers.
The tax calculator gives you a rough estimate. It is a rough estimate, not a bill, not a promise.
Withholding tax, wealth tax, the third pillar: the words pile up fast. A glossary on the site explains most of them.
Gather your documents early: salary statement, bank statements, insurance letters, receipts. The earlier it is in a folder, the lighter your March.
Deadlines can be extended by request, often in your canton's online portal. Ask before the date, not after.
The official site is the one to trust. If a message says you owe money and sends a link, go to the site yourself.
Copy last year's return as a template if your canton lets you. Most of it does not change, and the changes are easier to spot.

EasyTax. Tax software used by several Swiss cantons for filing the annual return. It guides you through the sections and does the maths at the end.

Return and warranty are easy and clearly explained. A short trip to a pick-up point does it.
Do not buy the most expensive model because it is the best. Buy the one that has the features you will use.
Check the energy label. A fridge is on for 20 years.
The delivery slot can usually be changed from the confirmation email. Do it early if you will not be home.

## site shopping mydealz

@ wink
mydealz. A German deals community: users post offers and vote them "hot" or "cold". A deal at 500 degrees is popular. One at minus 20 is a lesson.

A deal that is a bargain only if you buy three of something is not a bargain. Check the unit price.

## site shopping check24

@ carry
CHECK24. A German comparison site for energy, insurance, flights, phones and more. The ranking is a starting point. Check what the top result actually includes.

## site shopping swisspost

Swiss Post. Track a parcel, send one, check branch hours. An "Abholungseinladung" (pickup notice) means the parcel waits at a branch, not that it is lost.

## site travel bahn

Deutsche Bahn. Check "Sparpreis" tickets for a fixed train and the "Zugbindung" that comes with them. The delay display is a kind of national sport.
