Opening hours are often right and sometimes hopeful. Call before driving to the shop in the next village.
Reviews are mostly from locals and tend to be fair. A plumber with 4.7 stars and 300 reviews is probably good.
You can add your own business or update your details. A correct phone number in the directory is a quiet public service.
The print phone book once sat in every hallway. The web version is lighter and does not hold a door open.
Flag a nuisance number if the page lets you. A short note helps the next person who looks it up.
Add the number to your contacts so you will not need this again.

## site maps googleearth
> google earth
@ spin
Google Earth. Fly from your desk to any place on Earth. The "Timelapse" feature shows how a place has changed over decades. It is both lovely and sobering.

@ think
Bergfex. Austrian site for ski resorts, snow reports, hiking routes and webcams. If you want to know whether there is snow on a slope, this is the page.

## site sports komoot

komoot. A route planner for hiking and cycling, with surface type, elevation and highlights. Paved road and gravel look alike until you see the surface bar.

## site weather meteoswiss

MeteoSwiss. The official Swiss weather service. The rain radar and the thunderstorm warnings are the ones to check before an Alpine hike or an outdoor party.

## site weather windy

@ search
Windy. An animated map of wind, rain, clouds and waves, with different forecast models to compare. It is hypnotic and also actually useful.
Switch between forecast models like ECMWF, ICON and GFS. When they agree, the forecast is likely right. When they disagree, take an umbrella.
The layers include wind, rain, thunderstorms, clouds, waves and air quality. Choose the one you need and ignore the rest.

A rolling-release distribution like yours gets new kernels quickly. A new kernel may bring a bug, a feature or both.

## site design figma
> figma
@ fix
Figma. Press Shift+A to add auto layout and Ctrl+/ for quick actions. On Linux it runs in the browser only, so the browser is your desktop app.
Alt+drag duplicates a layer and Ctrl+Alt+K turns a selection into a component. Two moves that make a messy file tidy.
Layers named "Frame 1204" and "Rectangle 87" are a sign of a file in a hurry. Name them while it is fresh.

## site game lichess

@ spin
Lichess. A free, open source chess site with no ads and no premium tier. Puzzles, analysis with an engine and games at every speed. A rare internet success.

The comments are often better than the article. Click the "comments" link first and read the top few.

A comment thread can be collapsed with the little [–] next to the name. A tidy way to hide a very long argument.
The monthly "Who is hiring?" thread is a long list of job ads from real people. It can be a good place to start a search.
Many comments begin with "Actually". It means a correction is coming. Brace for a detail.
Do not read the whole thread. Read the top three branches and the funniest reply.
Upvotes on a comment mean "useful or witty", not "true". The two overlap less than people hope.

## site forums lemmy
> lemmy
@ read
Lemmy. A link aggregator like Reddit, spread across many servers that talk to each other. Pick an instance and still subscribe to communities on the others.
A community is written like "!linux@lemmy.ml". The part after the @ is the server where it lives. You can reach it from any other instance.
The instance you join sets the rules and the culture. If it feels wrong, you can move your subscriptions and your account.
Servers are run by volunteers. If a server vanishes, the communities on it may vanish too. Donations help. Gratitude helps more.
It is quieter than the big sites, and that is the appeal. A day with twelve posts is a feed you can finish.
The Linux and open source communities are lively. If you run a rolling release on a laptop, you will feel at home.
Treat the people as people. A quiet corner of the web depends on the quiet manners of its members.
Block a community or instance you dislike instead of arguing with it. Your feed is yours.

## site forums fandom

@ think
Fandom. A host for thousands of wikis about games, series and films. Very useful for checking a boss's weakness. Also very full of ads.
Spoiler warning: the page you opened to check one detail may contain the ending. Read the first paragraph only.

The "Characters" and "Locations" pages are where the lore lives. A very good rabbit hole for a rainy Sunday.
A wiki is written by fans, so it is detailed and sometimes opinionated. Cross-check anything you will build a strategy on.
Table of contents on the left, an infobox on the right. Learn those two and you can read any page quickly.
Contribute if you spot a mistake. Wikis improve when someone cares for a minute.
Look up the one thing, then close the tab and go and play.

## site forums cachyos

The CachyOS forum. Your own distribution's corner: Arch-based, performance-tuned. Post your kernel version and hardware when you ask for help.

## site podcasts applepodcasts

Apple Podcasts. Every podcast is an RSS feed, so the shows you find here can also be added to any other podcast app. The big directory is open.
A show with 400 episodes is not a commitment, it is a buffet. Start at episode one, or at a "best of" list if one exists.
Speed 1.25x is the sweet spot. Silence trimming can save more time, though it makes everyone sound slightly breathless.
Download the next few episodes over Wi-Fi before leaving the house. A tunnel is a bad place to start buffering.

## site podcasts audible

@ happy
Audible. Audiobooks, with a monthly credit that gets one book of your choice. The narrator makes or breaks it. Listen to the sample first.
Speed 1.25x suits most audiobooks. A very dramatic narrator at 1.5x sounds like an excited auctioneer.

kicker. The German football magazine with a live ticker, tables and player ratings from 1 to 6, where 1 is the best and a 6 is a little catastrophe.
The live ticker is a text commentary of the match. It is a fine way to follow a game in the office without anyone noticing.

Fantasy leagues are a lot of fun and a lot of time. Set aside a fixed hour per week for managing your team.

## site housing homegate
> homegate
@ search
homegate. The big Swiss property portal for renting and buying. Save a search for notifications, because good flats disappear within hours.
Reply within an hour if you like a listing. A flat in a good area may get a hundred replies in a day. A short, polite message with your details is a good start.
Switzerland has its own paperwork: a debt enforcement extract, proof of income, an ID and maybe a reference. Get them ready before any viewing.
Look at the "Nebenkosten", the additional costs. A low rent with high extra costs is a middling rent.

## site housing immoscout24

ImmoScout24. The big property portal in Germany and Switzerland. "Kaltmiete" is rent without extras, "Warmmiete" is rent with them. Look at the second number.

Flatfox. A Swiss flat portal where you create a profile once and use it to apply for each flat. Fewer forms and a nicer experience than the old ways.

## site housing rightmove
> rightmove
@ think
Rightmove. The main UK property portal. Check the council tax band, the EPC energy rating and whether the property is "chain free", which means a quicker sale.
A "chain" is the line of buyers and sellers that depend on each other. If one falls through, the whole line shuffles. "Chain free" is a lovely phrase.
The EPC rating shows how efficient the home is. A G rating is a cold house with a cold bill.
Use the map view and look at the street view. A beautiful house on a very busy road is a beautiful noise.
"Needs modernisation" is estate-agent language for "bring a builder". It may be a bargain or a long project.
A viewing is a short visit. Look at the corners, the ceilings and the water pressure. Flush a toilet. It is a classic.

## site passwords bitwarden
> bitwarden
@ think
Bitwarden. An open source password manager with a web vault. The browser extension fills logins with Ctrl+Shift+L. Remember the master password.
Make the master password a long phrase of several words, and do not use it anywhere else. A phrase is easier to remember than "P@ssw0rd!".
Turn on two-step login for the vault itself. An authenticator app is the sensible choice.
The generator makes random passwords of any length. Use long ones for everything. You will never type them.
You can host your own compatible server, with an unofficial project called Vaultwarden. A fun weekend for the self-hosting crowd.
Check the vault for old, weak or reused logins once a year. A fresh start is possible.
Emergency access lets a trusted person open your vault if you cannot. A small, human safeguard.
The Send feature shares a secret with an expiry date and a view limit. Better than pasting it into a chat that lives forever.

## site passwords onepassword
> 1password
@ cool
1Password. A password manager with a Secret Key as well as a master password. Print the Emergency Kit and put it somewhere safe, with the Secret Key on it.
The Secret Key is a long string made for your account. Together with the master password, it opens the vault. Neither is enough alone.
Watchtower flags weak, reused and exposed logins. It is not nagging, it is a very patient to-do list.
Login items can hold one-time codes too. A single place for the password and the code is handy and less secure than a separate app, so decide knowingly.
Share items with family in a shared vault. A shared Wi-Fi password is the classic first use.
Update the weak ones first, starting with email and banking. A strong email password protects all the rest.
A subscription is how this company makes money. Check what you actually use once a year.
Treat the Watchtower list as a Sunday task: fix three entries a week and in a few months it is empty.

## site settings googleaccount
> google account
@ fix
Google Account. Run the Security Checkup and the Privacy Checkup now and then. It lists your devices, your apps with access and the sign-in methods you set up.
"My Activity" shows what has been recorded: searches, places, videos. You can turn the logging off, or set it to delete itself after a few months.

FRITZ!Box. The router many German and Swiss homes have, with its own page at fritz.box. The password on the sticker underneath is the one to use at first.

## window projects
> kanban | backlog | sprint planning | roadmap | project board | issue tracker
@ write
+ Take a note = notes
A project board. Anything in the "In progress" column for more than a week is not in progress, it is hiding.
A card with "TBD" in the description is a card nobody has thought about yet. That is fine, until it is Thursday.
The "Blocked" column is the most honest column on any board. It is also where good tickets go to wait.
Three cards in progress is a plan. Eleven is a mood.

Meetings about the board are not the board. Close the meeting, open the card.
Move one card to Done before lunch. A small start is a large help.
Tickets are a record of intention. Intentions only count when somebody acts on them.

## tips projects
Tip: On Trello, press Q to show only your own cards and hover over a card and press Space to assign it to yourself.

Tip: Limit the number of cards in progress. A work-in-progress limit of three keeps a Kanban board honest.

## window translate
> translator | translation | dictionary | wörterbuch | übersetzer | übersetzung | vocabulary
@ read
A translator is open. Paste in short pieces. In long paragraphs the meaning gets lost, and the translation with it.
Idioms translate word for word, and you end up in a sentence about a cow on the ice. Use plain words.
Short sentences translate much better than long ones. If a sentence has three commas, cut it in two.
Formal or informal? In many languages the choice is "Sie" or "du", and getting it wrong is memorable.
A dictionary shows several meanings. Skim down to the example that looks like your sentence.
Numbers, dates and names are where a translation is most likely to slip. Check those twice.
A translated email is fine. A translated contract is a job for a human.
Learning a few phrases in the other person's language is worth more than a perfect translation. A "thank you" goes a long way.
False friends are words that look alike and mean something different. "Gift" and "gift" are very different things.
Read the result aloud once. If it sounds wrong aloud, it is wrong on the page.
A quick look is fine. If you translate for an hour, you may be about to learn the language instead.
Save the new word you just learned somewhere. It will not stay by itself.
When it sounds right and you are still unsure, ask a native speaker. They like to be asked.

## tips translate
Tip: In DeepL, click a word in the translation to get alternatives. It is the quickest way to rescue an almost-right sentence.
Tip: For anything important, ask a native speaker to read the translation. The machine gets the words right and the tone slightly wrong.
Tip: Google Translate has "Documents" and "Websites" tabs. Paste a link or upload a file and it translates the whole page.
Tip: Linguee and Reverso show real sentences from real texts. Use them when you need to know how a phrase is actually used.
Tip: Firefox can translate whole pages on your own computer, without sending the text anywhere. Look for the translate icon in the address bar.
Tip: Many dictionaries have forums. If an entry does not help, search the forum for your phrase. Someone has already argued about it.
Tip: Choose formal or informal on purpose. "Sie" or "du" and similar pairs change how a message feels.

## window docs
> documentation | api reference | developer docs | man page | readthedocs | cheatsheet | cheat sheet
@ read
Documentation. Ctrl+F is the index. The page is long because it is complete, and you only need the third paragraph.
Check the version selector. The docs for 3.2 are not the docs for 5.0, and your project is on 4.1.
The example is the part everyone reads. Copy it, read it and understand it before you paste it into anything important.
"Since version 3.4" on a feature means older versions cannot do it. Check that before spending an hour on it.
If the docs say "see also", follow one link. If you follow six, you have left the original question far behind.
Deprecated means "still works, will not for long". Move away from it before it becomes a surprise.
Reading the tutorial first and the reference second is a fine order. Reading neither is a very bold one.
A bad doc page can often be fixed with a one-line pull request. A kind thing to do for the next person.
When the docs and the behaviour disagree, trust the behaviour and file an issue.
Bookmark the one page you always need. Everyone has one.
Once you find the answer, close the other four tabs. They have served you.
A short break after a long page is a wise move. The next page is just as long.

## tips docs
Tip: Ctrl+F is the best index on a long documentation page. Search for the function name or the error text.
Tip: Check the version selector before reading. Docs for the wrong version describe a different library.
Tip: On docs.rs and other rustdoc pages, press S to jump to the search box and ? to see the other shortcuts.
Tip: In a Python shell, help(name) shows the docstring of anything. No browser needed.
Tip: Add a browser search keyword for the docs you use most, such as "mdn array.map". It is faster than any site search.
Tip: DevDocs works offline after you pick your doc sets. Great for a train or a plane.
Tip: Look for "Added in" or "Since" notes next to a function. They tell you whether your version can use it.
Tip: On Linux, "man" and "tldr" give you a command's manual and a short example without leaving the terminal.

## window cloud
> cloud storage | file sharing | shared with me | my drive | sync folder
@ carry
Cloud storage. A reminder that "sync" and "backup" are different words. If you delete a file here, it vanishes everywhere.
Check who can see your shared links once a year. "Anyone with the link" is a quiet, open door.
Folders called "New folder (3)" and "Misc" are folders that need a name. Give them one.
Version history is the quiet hero. If you saved over the wrong one, look there before you panic.
Large files fill the free space quickly. Sort by size once and delete the video you forgot.
A file sent as a link, not an attachment, saves everybody's inbox. It also lets you remove access later.
Offline access needs a switch. Mark the files you need on the train before you leave Wi-Fi.
Name files with a date in the form 2026-11-08. They sort themselves, and future you is delighted.
A shared folder with 40 people in it has a tiny problem: 40 people.
Back up what you cannot replace somewhere you own. Photos and documents first.
Empty the trash, because the trash counts toward your quota in some services.
Close the tab. The file is where it was.
Tidy one folder a week. In a year you will have a clean drive.

## tips cloud
Tip: Sync is not backup. If you delete or overwrite a file in one place, the cloud passes that on to every device.
Tip: In Google Drive, Shift+Z adds a shortcut to a file in another folder, so it can live in two places without being copied.
Tip: Most services keep older versions of a file. Right-click and look for "Version history" or "Manage versions" if you saved over the wrong one.
Tip: Add a password and an expiry date to a public link when the service allows it. Two small guards, one open gate.
Tip: Google Drive's search understands things like "type:pdf" and "owner:me". Quicker than clicking through folders.
Tip: Put a folder in a ZIP before sending it. Everything arrives in one piece and in the right order.
Tip: For end-to-end encrypted services, write down the recovery key on paper. If you lose it, nobody can help you.

## window news
> breaking news | headlines | nachrichten | newspaper | live ticker | live blog | zeitung
@ read
The news. Twenty minutes is plenty. The world will carry on happening at its own speed, with or without you.
A headline is a promise. The first paragraph is the contract. Check that they match.
Check the date on the story. An article from last year looks very fresh in a search result.
A "live blog" is a list of updates with the newest at the top. Skim the top, and you are caught up.
Notifications from news apps are loud and rarely urgent. Turn most of them off.
A second source is a habit worth having for the big stories. It takes ninety seconds.
Opinion and news are different things. A label near the headline says which one you are reading.
The comment section is optional. It is rarely the best part, and almost never the reason to stay.
A break from the news is a perfectly fine thing. It will be waiting for you, a little older.
If a story is making your shoulders go up, close the tab and drop them.
A newspaper in the morning is a calmer thing than a feed all day. Pick a time and stick to it.
Read one article properly rather than skimming ten.
Close the tab, and then do something with a real beginning and end.

## tips news
Tip: In Firefox, press F9 (or Ctrl+Alt+R) to switch a news article to Reader View: no ads, no popups, just the text.
Tip: Ctrl+Shift+T reopens the tab you closed by accident. It remembers more than one.
Tip: Ctrl+D bookmarks a page. Ctrl+Shift+D bookmarks every open tab at once, which is the cleanest way to end a reading spree.
Tip: Many news sites offer an RSS feed. Add it to a reader and you see the headlines without the front page.
Tip: Turn off push notifications from news apps. If something truly big happens, someone will tell you.
Tip: Look at the date near the headline before you share an article. A year-old story often travels as if it were new.
Tip: On cookie banners, "Reject all" is usually next to "Accept all", sometimes in a smaller font. It is worth the extra second.

## window banking
> e-banking | ebanking | online banking | account overview | kontoübersicht | kontoauszug
@ read
Banking tab open. Read the payee and the amount once more before you confirm. The bank will not unsend it for you.
The address of this page should be one you typed or bookmarked. A link from a message is a stranger's invitation.
Log out of the bank when you are done instead of just closing the tab. One click, and the session really ends.
Banking is better done in a calm moment. A rushed payment is a wrong payment.

A coffee after the paperwork is permitted.

## tips banking
Tip: Type the bank's address yourself or use a bookmark you made. A search result or a link in a message is somebody else's choice.
Tip: Log out when you finish, instead of just closing the tab. It takes a single click.

Tip: A bank does not ask for your login or PIN by email or message. If one does, go to the real site yourself.

## window forums
> forum | discussion board | message board | community forum
@ talk
A forum. Search before you ask. Your question was probably asked in 2014 and answered at length by someone with the patience of a saint.
Say which system and version you use and paste the error text. "It does not work" has never solved anything.
Put logs in a code block. A wall of unformatted text is a very rude thing to hand someone.
Read the pinned posts and the rules. They are short and they will save you a polite telling-off.
The best answer is often the third reply, after the first two people argue about the question.
If you solve it yourself, post the solution. The next person with the same problem will think you are a hero.
Thank the people who helped, and mark the answer as solved. It is a humble courtesy with a large effect.
Keep a thread polite even when the other person is not. Silence is allowed.
Long threads can be skimmed with Ctrl+F. Search for the word "solved" or the name of your error.
A forum is not a chat. Wait a day before you bump the thread.
Read for ten minutes, answer one question you know. A forum is a community, not a vending machine.
When the thread turns into an argument, close the tab. The argument will survive.
Pick a good username. You will wear it for ten years.

## tips forums
Tip: Search the forum and the web before you post. Add the exact error message in quotes and your question is probably already answered.
Tip: A good post says what you want, what you tried, your system and version, and the exact error. Those four things get you answers.
Tip: Paste logs and code in a code block, or on a paste site. Unformatted text is hard to read and impossible to copy cleanly.
Tip: Use "site:forum.example.com your words" in a search engine to search one forum much better than its own search box.
Tip: Press Ctrl+F in a long thread and search for "solved", your error, or the name of a command.
Tip: Ctrl+click or middle-click a link to open it in a new tab without losing your place in the thread.
Tip: Come back and post what fixed it. A thread that ends in "never mind" helps nobody.

## window podcasts

@ music
A podcast. Speed 1.25x is the sweet spot for talk. Any faster and everyone sounds like they have an important appointment.
A sleep timer saves you from waking up in the middle of a different episode at 3 a.m.
Podcasts are the best use of a washing-up session. The dishes do not mind the audience.
A show with 400 episodes is a buffet, not an obligation. Start at the "best of" list or at episode one, not at 387.
If you have not played a subscribed show in three months, unsubscribe. It will not mind.
Every podcast is an RSS feed, so you can listen in any app you like. You are not locked into one.
Download episodes over Wi-Fi before you leave. A tunnel is not the place to buffer.
Skipping the ads is a joy. Skipping the whole show because the ads were long is a tragedy.
A good audiobook narrator is half the book. Listen to the sample before you commit twelve hours.
Audio is for walking, cooking and long drives. It is less good for writing emails.
Radio plays are the secret treasure. A good one has footsteps and a creaking door.
Put one on and go for a walk. The episode will wait.

## tips podcasts
Tip: Every podcast is an RSS feed. If your app does not list a show, you can add its feed address by hand.
Tip: Listening at 1.25x gives you back about a fifth of the time. Few people notice the difference after a day.
Tip: Use the sleep timer, so the episode stops when you do and not three hours later.
Tip: Download the next few episodes over Wi-Fi and delete them once heard. The phone stays light and the journey stays quiet.
Tip: Many apps have "trim silence" or "skip silence". It shortens an episode by minutes without changing the pitch.
Tip: Chapters let you jump to the part you want. If a show offers them, the little list icon in the player shows them.
Tip: Unsubscribe from shows you have not played in three months. A short list is a list you actually use.

Sports on the screen. A quick look at the score is fine. A second quick look, then a third, becomes the second half.

## tips sports
Tip: If a live page freezes, Ctrl+Shift+R (or Ctrl+F5) reloads it from scratch. It often fixes a stuck score.

@ coffee
Food delivery. Look at the total with the delivery and service fees. Two pizzas and a fee is a very little-print kind of lunch.

## tips food

Tip: Use a group order for a team lunch so everyone shares one delivery fee.

## window housing

@ carry
Flat hunting. Reply to a good listing within the hour. A short, friendly message with a few facts beats a long one sent tomorrow.
Look at the total cost: rent plus extra costs, and the deposit. A flat that looks cheap may be a flat with large extras.
Keep a folder with your documents ready: ID, proof of income and any references. When a good flat appears, you are first.
Check the street on the map and look around it. The photos do not show the tram line or the bar downstairs.
Before a viewing, write down three questions: heating, noise, neighbours. People who ask are the ones the landlord remembers.
Be careful if someone asks for a deposit before you have seen the flat. A real landlord lets you look first.
A fresh coat of paint can hide a lot. Look at the corners and the ceiling and the window frames.
Check the notice period and the move-in date. A flat that is free in two months is not free now.
Do not hurry into a decision because of a "five other people are interested" message. There is always a flat.
Flat hunting is a marathon with surprise sprints. Eat something and rest between sessions.
Keep a simple spreadsheet of flats seen: rent, extras, pros, cons. After the fifth, they blur.
A good flat feels right and has a decent landlord. The rest can be fixed.
Close the tab. Take a deep breath. Tomorrow there will be new listings.

## tips housing
Tip: Save your search and switch on notifications. Good flats are gone within hours, and the first replies get the viewings.
Tip: Keep a folder with ID, proof of income, references and any extracts a landlord may ask for. When the right flat appears, you are ready.
Tip: Add up rent, extra costs and deposit before you fall in love. The total is the real number.
Tip: Look at the address on a map and in street view. The photos will not show the busy road or the noisy bar.
Tip: Ask about heating, noise and the neighbours at the viewing. A short list of good questions makes you memorable.
Tip: Never pay a deposit or fee before you have seen the flat and met the landlord. Genuine landlords show first.
Tip: Check the move-in date, the notice period and the contract length. A bargain that ends in six months is a short story.

## window markets
> stock price | share price | stock market | candlestick | exchange rate | aktienkurs | börse
@ think
A price chart. A price on a screen is a snapshot, and often a delayed one. Looking at it every five minutes does not move it.
Zoom out. A five-year chart is calmer than a one-day chart, and neither is advice.
Check the currency of the quote. Dollars, francs and euros are different numbers for the same thing.
Markets pause at night and on weekends. The number you see on Saturday is Friday's last word, repeated.
A price alert is a healthier habit than refreshing the page every thirty seconds.
Headlines move prices for about an hour and then everyone looks at something else.

A tab is information, not advice. I am a paperclip. I have a spreadsheet and no portfolio.

A ticker symbol with a suffix like ".SW" or ".DE" tells you which exchange the quote comes from. Check it.
Do something with your hands afterwards. A tidy desk is a good investment. In the loose sense.
Close the tab and drink some water.

## tips markets
Tip: Many free quotes are delayed by about 15 minutes. Check for a "real-time" label before you trust a number to the minute.
Tip: The ticker suffix tells you the exchange: ".SW" is Switzerland, ".DE" is Germany. The wrong one means the wrong company or the wrong currency.
Tip: Always check the currency of a quote. A price in dollars and one in francs are different numbers for the same thing.
Tip: Markets are closed at night and on weekends. The price you see on a Saturday is Friday's last one.
Tip: Zoom the chart range from days to years. A longer view makes a day's wobble look like what it is.
Tip: Set a price alert instead of refreshing the page. The alert does the watching and you do the work.
Tip: Read the fees and the quiet print. A little number every year adds up to a large one.
