## program 1password
Quick Access in 1Password (Ctrl+Shift+Space on Windows and Linux) fills things without opening the whole vault.
Password manager up. Every unique password in there is one fewer you have to remember. Wonderful trade.
A reminder: turn on two-factor for the vault itself. The vault guards the keys to everything.
Most managers flag reused passwords. Listen to them. They are right and they are tired.

## program VirtualBox
The default host key in VirtualBox is Right Ctrl. Press it to get your mouse back from the guest.
Shared folders move files between host and guest without USB sticks. Or sorcery.
Giving the VM half your RAM? Your host needs the other half. Arithmetic still applies.

## program VirtualBoxVM
Close the VM window carelessly and VirtualBox asks what to do. Save the machine state is the polite answer.
A slow guest? Check that hardware virtualisation is switched on in the BIOS. Common cause, rare joy.
Host key plus F toggles full screen for the guest. Right Ctrl is the host key by default.

## program abiword
AbiWord saves .abw by default but opens and saves .docx as well. Use Save As when someone else needs the file.
It starts in about the time it takes to type the first word. This is by design and a rarity.
A word processor with no ribbon. A menu bar, a toolbar, words. The way nature intended.

## program aisleriot
Undo is Ctrl+Z in Aisleriot, and there is no shame in using it.
There are dozens of game variants in here. Klondike is only the one everybody knows.
Stuck? The hint option exists. Using it is not cheating. It is research.

## program alacritty
Alacritty has no tabs and no splits on purpose. That is what a multiplexer like tmux is for.
The config file is TOML now. Old guides that show YAML are out of date.
Ctrl+Shift+C and Ctrl+Shift+V copy and paste on Linux. Plain Ctrl+C stays an interrupt.

## program anki
Ten minutes a day beats two hours on Sunday. Do the reviews first, then the new cards.
Space shows the answer, then 1 to 4 rates it. Hands stay on the keyboard.
One fact per card. A card with a paragraph on it is a chore with a front and a back.

## program apt
apt update refreshes the list. apt upgrade installs the new versions. Two steps, not synonyms.
apt autoremove clears out packages nobody needs any more. It asks before it does.
At the [Y/n] prompt the capital Y is the default, so Enter means yes. Read the list first.

## program ardour
Spacebar starts and stops playback in Ardour. Press it before Record, not after.
A smaller buffer means less delay while recording. A larger one stops the crackle. Pick your poison.
Ardour has been around since the early 2000s. It is older than most of your plugins.

## program ark
Right-click an archive in your file manager and pick Extract here. Faster than opening Ark at all.
Extract into a fresh folder. An archive with 500 loose files is a rude guest.
Password-protected archives are supported. Forgetting the password is not.

## program audacious
Z, X, C, V, B: previous, play, pause, stop, next. Winamp muscle memory works here.
MP3, FLAC, Ogg, all welcome. No codec drama.
A playlist of 4,000 songs, mostly never played. Audacious will cope. Your decision-making is the bottleneck.

## program battle.net
Check the install location before a big download starts. Moving 90 gigabytes later is no fun.
Launch on startup is a setting. Turn it off if your PC takes its time waking up.
Read the patch notes, if only to know what they changed this time.

## program bitwarden
Bitwarden can generate passwords. Ask for twenty characters. Your pet's name cannot do that.
In the Bitwarden browser extension, Ctrl+Shift+L fills the login on the current page.
Set the vault to lock after a timeout. Five minutes is a fair start.

## program blueman-manager
Tinny Bluetooth audio usually means the headset profile. Switch to A2DP in the sound settings.
A device that will not pair: remove it, power-cycle it, pair again. The Bluetooth version of a deep breath.
Bluetooth keeps nibbling at the battery in the background. Turn it off when nothing needs it.

## program brave
The shield icon in the address bar controls blocking per site. If a page breaks, switch it off for that site only.
Brave is built on Chromium, so Chrome extensions install there too.
Ctrl+Shift+N opens a private window. Private is not invisible, but it is tidy.

## program btop
Press f in btop and type a name to filter the process list. Quick, once you know which suspect you want.
Esc opens the menu with options and help. q quits. Everything else is graphs.
The disk panel shows what is left. Check it before blaming the slow Wi-Fi for everything.

## program calc
Copy the result with Ctrl+C and paste it. Retyping is where digits get swapped.
Round at the end, not at every step. Totals behave better that way.
Need units or currencies? Qalculate handles those and saves a trip to a search engine.

## program calibre
Calibre converts between e-book formats. EPUB to AZW3 and back takes a couple of clicks.
It can fetch covers and metadata online. A library with no covers is a library with no faces.
Send to device: plug in the e-reader, pick the books, click. It sorts the folders for you.

## program calligrawords
Calligra uses the OpenDocument format by default, and LibreOffice opens those files too.
Words works in frames, closer to a layout tool than a plain word processor.
Sheets is the spreadsheet: formulas, charts, no ribbon, no judgement about your formatting.
Not seen it in years? It is still here. Quiet suites usually are.

## program cargo
cargo check compiles without building a binary. It is quicker and it shouts the same errors.
cargo build --release makes the fast version and the slow wait. Choose your moments.

## program celluloid
Celluloid plays whatever mpv plays, which is nearly everything.
Space pauses, F goes full screen, the arrow keys seek. Cinema basics.
Drop a video file on the window and it plays. No library, no import, no fuss.
Subtitles with the same file name as the video get picked up automatically. Name them alike.

## program chromium
Shift+Esc opens Chromium's own task manager. It names the tab eating your memory.
Ctrl+Shift+T reopens the tab you just closed. Chromium forgives.
On Linux, updates usually arrive through your package manager rather than the browser itself.

## program clion
CLion builds with CMake. If something breaks, reload the CMake project first. The usual suspect.
Double Shift searches everywhere in CLion: files, symbols, actions.
Try a sanitizer before you blame the compiler. Address sanitizer finds a lot.

## program cmd
Tab completes file names and the up arrow brings back old commands. Two thirds of the skill.
cd /d changes drive and folder at once. Handy when D: is not C:.
Ctrl+C stops a running command. Closing the window works too, but less politely.

## program codium
Ctrl+Shift+P opens the command palette in VSCodium. Everything is in there, including things you forgot you wanted.
Extensions come from Open VSX, so a few well-known ones may be missing.
Ctrl+K then Ctrl+S opens the keyboard shortcuts. A chord to list the chords.

## program cupsd
A stuck print job? Cancel it in the queue, then restart the printer. The queue is almost always the culprit.
localhost:631 opens the CUPS web page, where printers and jobs can be managed.
Pages not coming out? Check that the right printer is set as the default.

## program cursor
Read what the AI writes before accepting it. It is confident either way.
Cursor is a fork of VS Code, so most of your old shortcuts and extensions still work.

## program dbeaver
Ctrl+Enter runs the current statement in DBeaver. Alt+X runs the whole script.
Switch to manual commit mode before touching production. A rollback beats an apology.
Double-click a table and the Data tab shows the rows. Look before you write the query.

## program deezer
Flow learns from what you like and what you skip. Be honest with it.
Offline mode needs a subscription and some disk space. Check how much the downloads take.
Many tracks show lyrics in the player. Singing along is optional but encouraged.

## program digikam
digiKam keeps its database apart from the photos. Back up both, or the tags are lost with the library.
It can write tags into the image files themselves. Turn that on and the work travels with the photo.
Face recognition runs on your own machine. The faces stay home.

## program dnf
dnf history lists past transactions, and dnf history undo can roll one back.
dnf check-update lists what is available without installing anything.
dnf remove lists the dependencies it will take with it. Read that list.
dnf5 is the newer and faster rewrite. Recent Fedora releases use it.

## program docker
docker system prune clears stopped containers and unused images. It asks first. Run it now and then.
docker ps shows what is running. docker ps -a includes the ones that stopped.

## program dolphin-emu
Dolphin runs GameCube and Wii games from your own disc dumps. Bring your own games.
Save states freeze the game so you can come back to the exact moment.
Pick the graphics backend that suits your card, such as Vulkan. If something looks wrong, switch.
Map the controller before the game starts. Keyboards were not designed for this.

## program dropbox
Share a link instead of an attachment. The recipient gets the latest version, not the one from last week.
Selective sync keeps big folders off the local disk. Use it when the laptop starts complaining.
Deleted files can be restored from the website for a while. Do not rely on it, but it is there.

## program eadesktop
Choose the install folder yourself. The default drive is always the full one.
It can start with the computer and sit in the tray. Turn that off if boot feels slow.
Many games sync saves to the cloud. Check before you uninstall one.

## program elisa
Elisa scans your music folder and builds the library itself. Tag your files properly and it looks great.
The Now Playing view shows the cover art large. A fine screen to leave open.
Drag a folder in and it plays. No import wizard.
Playlists can be saved and reloaded. Build one for work, one for chores.

## program emacs
Ctrl-g cancels whatever you started by accident. Learn that one first.
M-x runs any command by name. Type a few letters and Tab finishes the thought.

## program epiphany
Reader mode strips a page down to its text. Good for long articles and bad for adverts.
It can install a website as an app with its own window. Good for sites you keep open all day.
It follows the GNOME look so closely that it hardly looks like a browser.

## program evince
Ctrl+F searches inside the document. Faster than scrolling for the page with that one clause.
Evince remembers where you stopped. Reopen the file and you are back on the same page.
F5 starts presentation mode. Handy when the PDF is a slide deck.

## program evolution
Ctrl+Shift+M opens a new message in Evolution. A blank page is only scary for a few seconds.
Search folders gather mail by rule into one virtual list. A filing system that files itself.
Calendar invitations can be accepted straight from the message. One click.

## program excel
F4 toggles absolute references like $A$1 while you edit a formula. It saves many broken sheets.
Ctrl+T turns a range into a table that grows with your data. Formulas stop breaking.
Newer versions have XLOOKUP, which replaces VLOOKUP and looks in any direction.

## program explorer
Ctrl+Shift+N makes a new folder. Win+E opens a new Explorer window.
F2 renames the selected file. Quick, cheap and nobody looks.
Alt+Up goes up a folder. Alt+Left and Alt+Right go back and forward.

## program falkon
Falkon is built on Qt WebEngine, the same engine family as Chromium.
The speed dial start page shows tiles of your favourite sites.
It has a built-in ad blocker that uses the usual filter lists.

## program file-roller
Select files, right-click, Compress. Archive Manager makes the zip for you.
A zip made on one system opens on any other. That is the entire point of zip.
Choose Extract Here only if you know what is inside. Otherwise pick a fresh folder.
Password-protected zips open here too. Ask the sender for the password, not the internet.

## program epicgameslaunch
The free games rotate weekly. Claim them in the Store tab, and decide later whether you will ever play them.
Pick the install drive before the 100 GB download, not after.
Game crashing at launch? Three dots, Manage, Verify. It re-checks the files.

## program flameshot
In Flameshot, Ctrl+C copies the capture to the clipboard and Ctrl+S saves it. Esc backs out when you lose your nerve.
The pixelate tool is right there. Use it on the names, the emails and anything that looks like a token.
A screenshot of a whole screen for one small error. Select just the error. Your colleagues will thank you.

## program flatpak
Tidy-up tip: flatpak uninstall --unused removes runtimes nothing needs any more. Free disk space for one command.
flatpak update brings every installed app up to date in one go. A rare case of one command doing what it says.
Flatpak apps live in sandboxes with permissions. If one can't see your files, that's why, not malice.

## program foot
foot --server keeps one process alive, and footclient opens new windows from it almost instantly. Small, fast, smug.
Foot is configured in a plain text file, foot.ini. No settings dialog, no menus. Very on brand.
Another minimal terminal. Somewhere a settings window is crying that nobody visits it.

## program freecad
In a sketch, the constraint count matters. When the sketch is fully constrained, it turns green. Green is good.
Save before you rearrange the feature tree. Dragging an old feature around can break everything after it.
Parametric means the numbers are the boss. Name your spreadsheet cells, or you'll hate the future you.

## program galaxyclient
GOG sells offline installers too. Keep one on a drive and your game outlives any launcher.
GOG Galaxy can pull your other libraries into one list. One shelf for every game you meant to play.
Cloud saves are on by default for supported games. A save file is only safe when it exists twice.

## program gamemoded
In Steam, put gamemoderun %command% in a game's launch options to switch Game Mode on for that game. One line, done.
Game Mode asks the system for performance while the game runs and lets go when it ends. A tidy lodger.
If the fans spin up, that's the point. Check the temperatures, not the vibes.

## program gamescope
gamescope -f -- game launches a game fullscreen in its own tiny compositor. Flags go before the double dash.
Gamescope can render a game at one resolution and scale it to another. Useful for old hardware, and for bragging.
Gamescope can cap the frame rate too. Fewer frames, cooler laptop. A fine trade.
A game in Gamescope gets its own display. Alt-tabbing out may feel odd. That's the room's rules.

## program gcc
Compile with -Wall -Wextra. Warnings are free advice, and ignoring them is how bugs get tenure.
Add -g and your debugger will show real line numbers instead of hexadecimal poetry.
-O2 for speed, -O0 when debugging. An optimised build can make the debugger lie to you, politely.

## program geary
Geary groups mail into conversations. Your twenty replies become one thread. Enjoy the quiet.
Several accounts can live in one Geary window. Work and private, side by side. Do check the From line.
A mail client that stays out of the way. The inbox is still full; Geary just won't make a show of it.

## program ghb
HandBrake's quality slider is constant quality: a lower RF number gives a better picture and a bigger file. It feels backwards.
The Fast 1080p30 preset is a sensible start. Pick a preset before you start fiddling with settings.
Add several videos to the queue and let it run overnight. It's the only time HandBrake is not the loudest thing in the room.

## program ghostty
Ghostty is configured in a plain text file. No settings dialog, only a config and your convictions.
New terminal, same shell. The shell will still say command not found, only faster.
A GPU-accelerated terminal. Your ls output is rendered at a frame rate it never asked for.

## program git
git status before anything else. It's free, it's fast and it tells you what you forgot.
git stash parks your half-done work so you can switch branches. Do remember what you stashed.
git log --oneline gives the history in one line per commit. The shame is compact and readable.

## program github-desktop
A commit has a short summary and a longer description box. Use both. Your future self reads the log like a detective.
Committed too soon? The Undo button right after a commit takes it back. Only until you push.
Fetch before you start, not after you're done. It's the difference between a pull and a surprise.

## program gnome-boxes
Take a snapshot of the virtual machine before you experiment. Boxes can, and a snapshot costs less than a reinstall.
Ctrl+Alt gets your mouse back from the guest when it won't let go. Clingy, but it passes.
Give the guest enough RAM and the host enough left over. Two computers, one memory. Negotiate.

## program gnome-calculato
Type a whole expression instead of clicking digits. Typing is faster than clicking, even for a paperclip.
Programming mode shows a number in decimal, hex and binary at once. Handy, and also unsettling.
Unit conversions work in the entry line, like 10 km in miles. Hands up who still uses a search engine for this.

## program gnome-calendar
Add your online accounts in Settings and their events show up here. One calendar, no shuffling between three.
Week view tells the truth a month view hides. Check it before you say yes to anything.
Click a day and type a title. Quick add is quicker than most excuses to not add it.

## program gnome-chess
You can play against the computer if a chess engine is installed. If not, this is just a very quiet game with yourself.
Undo a move with Ctrl+Z. A takeback is a mercy and also a lie. Nobody will know.
Games can be saved as PGN, the standard chess notation. The blunders will be stored for later study.

## program gnome-clocks
The World tab shows several time zones. Handy for scheduling calls with people who are already at lunch.
Clocks keeps alarms and timers running in the background. Close the window and the timer still rings.
A timer for five minutes is the cheapest productivity trick there is. Use it. Chess clock not included.

## program gnome-control-c
Press Ctrl+F in Settings and type what you want. Searching is faster than guessing the right panel.
Night Light in Displays warms the screen in the evening. Your eyes will mind less. Your tabs won't.
Sound settings let you pick the output device. If there's silence, check this before you panic.
Default Applications is the place to fix which program opens which file. Fix it once and be done.

## program gnome-disks
Disks shows a drive's SMART health data. A fine way to learn about a dying drive before the drive tells you.
You can create a disk image of a drive here. Image first, then experiment. Always the same advice.
Disk Usage Analyzer draws your storage as rings. The big ring is the one to question.
The Disks benchmark gives read and write speeds. Run it once, then stop comparing with the shop's promises.

## program gnome-mines
A number on a square is how many of the eight neighbours are mines. Everything else follows from this.
If a 1 touches only one unopened square, that square is a mine. Start there and breathe.
When a number already has all its flags, the other neighbours are safe. Logic works. Luck is optional.

## program gnome-screensho
Take a screenshot after a delay. That's how you capture a menu before it closes itself.
Window and area options spare you from cropping. A cropped screenshot with your bookmarks bar visible is a classic.
Check what's behind the window before you share the picture. Tabs, names, the lot.
Captures land in Pictures. Rename the useful one now, or find it in six months as Screenshot 4081.

## program gnome-software
Check the source before you install. The same app from different sources can update on a different schedule.
The Updates tab shows what's waiting. Do it before shutdown, not during the meeting.
Installed apps can be removed here too. Nobody does. Do some spring cleaning.

## program gnome-sudoku
A valid sudoku puzzle has exactly one solution. If your answer is different, it's the puzzle that's right.
Hints exist. Using one is not cheating, it's research. Use it and tell no one.
You can print puzzles from here. Paper, pencil and a coffee: a time machine with a grid.

## program gnome-system-mo
Click the Memory column header to sort by who's eating RAM. The answer will be a browser. It's a formality.
End asks a process politely to stop. Kill doesn't ask. Try End first; manners cost nothing.
The Resources tab shows the last minute of CPU and memory. A spike that finished before you looked is a ghost.

## program gnome-terminal-
Ctrl+Shift+C and Ctrl+Shift+V copy and paste in the terminal. Plain Ctrl+C means stop. Mix them up once, learn forever.
Ctrl+R searches your command history. You typed that long command once. Let the shell remember it.

## program gnome-text-edit
Text Editor keeps unsaved documents as drafts, so a crash won't eat them. A rare mercy in the text editor world.
Ctrl+F finds and Ctrl+H replaces. Replace is quick. Replace All is how typos become policy.
A plain file, no formatting. If it needs bold, it was never a text file.

## program gnucash
Every transaction in GnuCash has two sides that must balance. Annoying for a week, then oddly comforting.
Reconcile an account against the statement once a month. It's the least glamorous good habit there is.
Scheduled transactions handle the rent and other regular things. Set them once, stop typing the same line.

## program gnumeric
Gnumeric shows an import dialog for CSV files, so you choose the separator. A comma is not always a comma.
Dollar signs lock a cell reference. $A$1 stays put when you copy the formula. This saves entire afternoons.
Gnumeric is known for its careful statistics functions. If a number matters, check the sample size, not the app.

## program godot
F5 runs the project and F6 runs just the current scene. Test the small piece, not the whole game, every time.
Godot is a small download and starts fast. Your game will take years, but the engine will be on time.
Signals let nodes talk without hard wiring. Use them and the game stays a game, not a plate of spaghetti.

## program gparted
GParted queues its operations and applies them only when you press Apply. Nothing happens until then. Read the queue twice.
A partition has to be unmounted before most operations. If it refuses, it's mounted. It's usually that.
Resizing takes longer than you think, and power cuts mid-resize are the worst. Plug in the laptop.

## program gthumb
Photos can carry the location they were taken at. Strip it before sharing. Your address isn't a caption.
Cull on the first pass: delete the blurry, the duplicates and the thumbs. A smaller album gets looked at.
Rating the keepers with stars makes the second pass quick. Nobody does it. Be nobody.

## program haruna
Haruna is built on mpv, so it plays nearly anything you throw at it. Even that file with no extension.
Films often hold several audio tracks. If the language is wrong, switch tracks before blaming the file.
Speed it up to 1.5x for lectures. Slow it down for tutorials you pretend to follow. Both are valid.
A subtitle file with the same name as the video loads by itself in most players. Name them alike.

## program heroic
Heroic can run Epic, GOG and Amazon Prime Gaming libraries. One launcher to hold the other launchers.
Each game has its own Wine or Proton setting. If a game crashes, try another version before you rage.
Game saves can sync to the cloud where the store supports it. Check, before you reinstall.

## program hx
Helix has a built-in tutor. Run hx --tutor and learn the keys in an afternoon. Vim users may look away.
In Helix you pick the selection first and then the action. x selects the line; d deletes it. Honest grammar.
Space opens a menu of commands, including the file picker. A modal editor that explains itself. How rude.

## program idea
Double Shift opens Search Everywhere: files, classes, settings, actions. The only shortcut you need to remember.
Alt+Enter shows suggested fixes for the problem under the cursor. The red squiggle always has an exit.

## program insomnia
Use environment variables for the base URL and tokens. Switching staging to production should be one dropdown, not a find and replace.
Ctrl+Enter sends the request. Faster than reaching for the mouse and nowhere near as dramatic.
Don't sync collections containing real tokens to a shared workspace. Passwords in a request are still passwords.

## program itch
Plenty of games on itch are free or pay what you want. Pay something, if you like it. A coffee's worth keeps a dev going.
Game jam entries are often rough and often brilliant. Check the page for what the author says it needs.
You can download from the website without the app. The app just keeps the updates tidy.

## program java
java -version tells you which Java you are really running. Often it's not the one you installed on purpose.
-Xmx sets the maximum heap size. If a Java program gobbles memory, a ceiling can be a kindness.
Minecraft launchers need the right Java version for the game version. If it crashes at start, check that first.

## program jellyfin
Give everyone in the house their own account. Watched marks and progress stay per person. Peace in the living room.
Jellyfin fetches posters and descriptions from online sources. Name files neatly, like Film Name (2010), and it guesses right.
Phone and TV apps connect to the same server. Cast a film from the sofa to the bathroom if you must.

## program joplin
Joplin syncs through services like Nextcloud, Dropbox or OneDrive. Switch on end-to-end encryption if the notes are private.
Notes live in Markdown. Plain text under the hood means your notes outlive the app.
The web clipper saves a page as a note. Use it instead of sixty open tabs. The tabs know why.

## program jupyter-lab
Shift+Enter runs the cell and moves on. Press Esc and then B to add a cell below. That's most of the app.
Restart the kernel and Run All before you share a notebook. If it fails, it was never really working.
Notebooks store output inside the file. Clear secrets and big outputs before committing.

## program kate
F7 toggles the built-in terminal at the bottom of Kate. An editor and a shell in one window. Convenient and slightly dangerous.
Ctrl+Shift+F searches across all files in the project. Use it before you rename something you swore was used once.
Kate saves sessions: the set of files you had open. Close the day, reopen the mess exactly as you left it.

## program kcolorchooser
Use the screen picker to grab a colour from anywhere on screen. Great for matching a logo. Less great for matching your socks.
The HTML field holds the hex code. Copy it and paste it into the stylesheet without squinting.
Add favourites to the custom colours and you have a tiny palette. A palette of one is a nice start.
Check contrast before falling in love with a colour pair. Pretty text you can't read is a poster, not a document.

## program kdeconnectd
Pairing needs approval on both devices. If one device doesn't ask, check they're on the same Wi-Fi.
KDE Connect can share your clipboard and send files to the phone. It's a cable that never gets tangled.
Find my phone makes it ring, even on silent. The revenge you have wanted since Tuesday.
Notifications from the phone can show on the desktop. Mute the group chats first. You know the ones.

## program keepassxc
Ctrl+B copies the username and Ctrl+C copies the password. The clipboard clears itself after a few seconds. Faster than you.
A key file or hardware key adds a second lock to the vault. A good master password plus a second thing is the way.
Back up the database file. A password vault with no backup is a very secure way to lose everything.

## program kicad
Run the ERC on the schematic before you start the board. The electrical rules check finds what you forgot to connect.
Run the DRC before you order boards. Fixing a copper clearance in software costs nothing. In a factory it costs a week.
The 3D viewer, Alt+3, shows the board as it will look. A fine way to find the connector facing the wrong way.

## program kitty
kitty +kitten icat picture.png shows an image in the terminal. A feature you needed, urgently, never.
Ctrl+Shift+Enter opens a new window inside kitty and Ctrl+Shift+T opens a new tab. Splits without a multiplexer.
Everything is set in kitty.conf, a plain text file. Edit, reload, repeat until it's lovely.

## program kmail
KMail has filters for incoming mail. Set one rule that moves the newsletters out of your sight. Peace costs one rule.
Kontact's first start can be slow while Akonadi indexes your mail. It's thinking. Leave it be.
KMail supports encrypting and signing mail with OpenPGP. If you use it, you've already been told to back up the key.

## program kodi
Kodi runs on a TV with a remote, but a phone app can control it too. The sofa can have remote control, finally.
Name films neatly, like Film Name (2010), and the library scraper finds the posters. Chaos in, chaos out.
Add-ons come from the official repository. Download the ones you need and ignore the rest. The menu is long.

## program kolourpaint
The text tool is in there somewhere. So are selections, which can be made see-through. Plenty of power for a "simple" paint app.
Quick edit? Crop with a selection, save, done. Nobody needs layers to trim a screenshot.
Fill tool warning: a gap of one pixel and the colour floods the whole canvas. It happens to everyone.

## program konsole
Tabs and split views live in here. One window, five shells, zero idea which one is the server.
Ctrl+Shift+T opens a new tab. Long-running command in one, thinking in the other.

## program kwrite
KWrite and Kate share the same editing engine. The syntax highlighting is real; only the ambitions are modest.
A fast editor for config files. Make a backup first. You know the one.
Opening KWrite to avoid opening an IDE. A wise and lazy instinct. I approve.

## program libreoffice-dra
Scanning tip: 300 dpi is plenty for text. Higher makes the file huge and the scan no better.
Scan to PDF, then check the page order. The scanner never gets it right when you feed it upside down.
Draw is surprisingly good at editing PDFs. Surprisingly. Not wonderfully. Surprisingly.
Single page or twenty? Combine the scans into one PDF before you email them. Your recipient will thank you.

## program librewolf
It clears cookies when you close it, by default. Your logins will vanish. That is the privacy working, not a bug.
Ad blocker included. The web looks different without ads. Emptier. Calmer. Slightly suspicious.
If a site breaks, the settings have an exception list. Use it sparingly, like salt.

## program lmms
The Beat+Bassline editor is the quick way in. Four kicks, a snare, done. Go from there.
Piano roll: draw notes with the mouse, then fix the timing. Everybody fixes the timing.
Save projects often. A crash takes the whole song and never says sorry.

## program logseq
Everything is stored as plain Markdown files on your disk. If Logseq vanishes, your notes do not. Rare and good.
Typing [[ links to another page, creating it if it does not exist. It will exist a lot.
The journal page opens fresh each day. It is a small, daily invitation to write something. Accept it.

## program mailspring
Send later is hiding in the menu. Use it for the 2 a.m. emails you will want to unsend.
Unified inbox on, and all accounts land in one list. Convenient. Slightly overwhelming.
Reminders in mail: tell it to bring a thread back if nobody replies. Chasing people, automated.

## program make
Tabs. A Makefile wants tabs. "Missing separator" means your editor put in spaces.
make -j8 uses eight jobs at once. Match it to your cores, or enjoy a slow, noisy compile.
make clean first if the build behaves oddly. Half of all mysteries live in stale object files.

## program megasync
Selective sync: you do not have to mirror the whole cloud onto the laptop. Choose the folders you need.
Mind the file count in your sync folder. Hundreds of thousands of tiny files slow any sync client. Zip the old stuff.
Encryption happens before upload. Lose the password and the files are gone. Write it down somewhere safe.

## program minecraft
F3 shows your coordinates. Write down where home is before you wander off. Future you will be lost.
Sleeping in a bed skips the night. A good policy for any day, really.
Zombies burn in sunlight. Sadly, so do the rest of us if we sit near that window.
Monsters spawn in the dark. Torches are cheap. Light up the cave and the cave behaves.

## program minecraft-launc
Memory settings live in the launch options. More RAM is not always faster. It is sometimes just more RAM.
The version dropdown lets you run old releases. A good way to revisit a world exactly as you left it.
Back up the saves folder before updating. Worlds are not forgiving about version changes.

## program mpv
Press I to see playback stats, and S to take a screenshot of the current frame. Both are quiet and useful.
Brackets speed up and slow down playback. Great for lectures. Terrible for music.
Drag a file onto the window and it plays. That is the whole interface. It is beautiful.

## program msedge
Ctrl+Shift+U reads the page aloud. F9 opens Immersive Reader, which strips a page down to the text. Both beat squinting at ads.
Edge is built on the same engine as Chrome, so extensions mostly carry over. The sidebar, however, is its own adventure.
Sleeping tabs free up memory for tabs you are not using. Which is most of them. All sixty-two.

## program mspaint
Paint has shipped with Windows since the very first version in 1985. It has outlasted several operating systems and one paperclip.
Newer Paint has layers and transparency. The mustache I mentioned earlier can now sit on its own layer.
Resize and Skew sits under Ctrl+W. Useful for shrinking a screenshot before you email it.

## program musescore
In note input mode, N starts it, the letters A to G place notes, and the number keys pick durations. Fast once it is in your fingers.
Space plays your score back. Listen to it before you print it. The ear catches what the eye forgives.
Mixxx is for mixing, Hydrogen is for drums. Different job from MuseScore, same love of a steady beat.

## program mutt
Press ? and mutt lists every key it knows. Press it early and often. There are many keys.
The l key limits the index to messages matching a pattern. Search, but with confidence.
The config lives in a muttrc file. The first one takes an evening. The tenth is a hobby.

## program mysql-workbench
Safe Updates mode refuses UPDATE or DELETE without a key in the WHERE clause. It is annoying. It is also the reason you still have customers.
Run EXPLAIN in front of a slow query. It tells you whether an index is being used. It rarely flatters you.
The server may be MariaDB under the hood. Same family, same habits, mostly the same typos.

## program nautilus
Ctrl+H shows hidden files. Ctrl+L gives you a typeable path bar. Ctrl+Shift+N makes a new folder. Three shortcuts, much less mouse.
F2 renames the selected file. Select a batch first and it will offer bulk rename.
Files, once open, wants to search before it browses. Start typing and it will look. Handy, and slightly eager.

## program nemo
F3 opens a second pane. Drag a file across and you have a poor man's two-column manager. Efficient and rather satisfying.
Nemo grew out of Nautilus and went its own way. A fork with excellent manners.
Ctrl+L turns the breadcrumbs into a path you can type. Paste a path and press Enter. It is the fastest way anywhere.
Right-click offers "Open as Root" if it is installed. Use it like a loaded stapler. Sparingly, and carefully.

## program nextcloud
Nextcloud began as a fork of ownCloud in 2016. It has been growing apps like a tree grows leaves ever since.
Selective sync saves disk space. You do not need every holiday photo on the work laptop.
A server dies quietly when nobody updates it. Check for updates on your instance, not just in the client.

## program nm-applet
In a terminal, nmcli device wifi list shows the networks around you. Boring, fast and does not require a menu.
nmtui is a text menu for the network. It works when the desktop does not. A handy parachute.
Forgot the Wi-Fi password? It is stored in the connection settings. Check the router sticker before you panic.
Connected but nothing loads? Toggle the connection off and on again. The oldest fix in the book.

## program node
node on its own starts a REPL. Press Ctrl+C twice to leave. A tiny scratchpad for trying a function.
npm ci installs exactly what the lockfile says. Use it in CI, and keep package-lock.json in version control.

## program notepad
F5 inserts the current time and date. Add a .LOG line at the very top and the file stamps itself every time you open it. A classic trick.
Newer Notepad has tabs and restores your unsaved text. A mild miracle for the "Untitled" generation.
Ctrl+H finds and replaces. One of the few features, and a good one.

## program notion
Type / and you get a menu of blocks. Type [[ and you link a page. The mouse is optional here.
Ctrl+P opens quick search. A workspace this deep needs a way to find things in it.
Markdown works while you type: # makes a heading, - starts a list, [] makes a checkbox. Faster than any toolbar.

## program nvtop
It shows NVIDIA, AMD and Intel cards in one view. A bit like a family reunion, but for graphics hardware.
If the GPU sits at zero while a game stutters, the game is the bottleneck. If it sits at a hundred, you have found the bottleneck.
Memory climbing steadily means something is leaking. Close the app before the card closes it for you.

## program obsidian
Ctrl+O is the quick switcher, Ctrl+P the command palette, Ctrl+G the graph. Learn those three and the vault gets small.
Your notes are plain Markdown files in a folder. Back up the folder and the vault is safe.

## program okular
Okular opens more than PDFs: EPUB, DjVu, comic book archives. A reader with open-minded taste.
Ctrl+F searches the whole document. Faster than scrolling, and you will not pretend you read it.
Annotations get saved separately unless you export. Check before you send the file. Your margin notes may be unfit for others.

## program ollama
By default it listens on port 11434, on your machine only. Other tools find it there. It does not phone anyone.
ollama list shows what you have downloaded. The models are big. Your disk has noticed.

## program onlyoffice
It works on docx, xlsx and pptx natively, rather than converting them. Fewer surprises when a colleague sends a file.
The tabs keep your document, sheet and slides in one window. A tidy way to lose track of which file is which.
Co-editing works when you connect it to a server. On its own, you will be co-editing with yourself. Productive, but lonely.

## program openscad
F5 previews fast. F6 renders properly, and takes its time. Preview often, render once.
A higher $fn makes curves smoother and rendering slower. A trade as old as geometry.
Variables at the top of the file make the design adjustable. Future you will be pleased. Present you will skip it.

## program opera
There is a free built-in VPN, which is really a proxy for the browser only. Know what it covers before you rely on it.
The sidebar holds messengers and music. Your browser has become a small desktop. Convenient, and a little crowded.
Opera is a Norwegian browser built on the same engine as Chrome. Extensions from that store mostly work.

## program outlook
Ctrl+R replies, Ctrl+Shift+R replies to all, Ctrl+Enter sends. The reply-all key is the one to keep a respectful distance from.
Ctrl+1 is mail, Ctrl+2 the calendar. Switch quickly, and pretend the inbox did not see you leave.
Rules can file newsletters away for you. A tidy inbox is a minute of setup and a year of quiet.

## program pacman
pacman -Qdt lists orphaned packages. pacman -Rns removes one with its configs and unused dependencies. Read the list before you press Y.
Uncomment Color in pacman.conf for readable output. Add ILoveCandy and the progress bar becomes Pac-Man. Entirely pointless. Entirely good.

## program pavucontrol
Configuration tab: pick the right profile for the device. HDMI instead of analogue is a common reason for silence.
Playback shows each app with its own slider. One tab for the music, one for the meeting that should be louder. Peace.
Recording and Input Devices decide which mic is live. Check them before the call, not during it.

## program pcmanfm
It also draws the desktop icons, in some setups. Light, and quietly working in two places at once.
Tabs, a sidebar, and bookmarks. Everything a file manager needs, and nothing that needs patching.
It is the default in LXDE. If it feels fast, it is because it does less. A rare design philosophy.
Archive support is through other tools. Install a plugin if the right-click menu looks bare.

## program pcsx2
You need a BIOS dump from your own console. The emulator does not come with one, and that is the right way round.
F1 saves a state, F3 loads one. A rewind for the part you keep failing.
Per-game settings matter more than the global ones. Some games want a gentler renderer. Check the compatibility notes.
Controller mapping first. Playing a platformer on a keyboard is a test of friendship.

## program peek
Peek makes short GIFs of a window or an area. Keep it under ten seconds. Longer is called a video.
Click the area you want, press record, press stop. Three steps and a shareable loop. A cleaner way to say "look at this bug".
GIFs get big fast. Lower the frame rate and the file shrinks. Nobody needs sixty frames of a button being pressed.

## program pgadmin4
In psql, \dt lists the tables, \d name describes one, and \q quits. The backslash is the shortcut to everything.
The query tool has EXPLAIN ANALYZE in a menu. It runs the query and shows where the time went. Mostly in the part you wrote last.
Test a destructive query inside a transaction. BEGIN, run it, look, then ROLLBACK or COMMIT. A parachute for your tables.

## program pinta
Pinta is modelled on Paint.NET. Familiar if you ever used that. Slightly unfamiliar if you came from anything else.
Adjustments and Effects menus hold the fun. Brightness, curves, blur. Nothing here will rescue a bad photo, but it will try.
Layers have blend modes. A drop shadow takes one layer, one blur, and a little restraint.
Save as PNG for screenshots, JPEG for photos. A small rule that saves many arguments.

## program plasma-systemmo
Ctrl+Esc opens this from anywhere in KDE. Faster than hunting for it when the fans take off.
Sort the process list by memory, not CPU, when the machine feels sluggish. It is usually memory.
The Applications view groups processes by app. One browser, forty-one processes. Now you know what "multi-process" meant.

## program plex
Name your files the way Plex expects, with the title and year. Then the posters appear on their own. Order, rewarded.
The server needs a fixed place for the library. Move the drive and the library goes with it, in confusion.
Plex listens on port 32400. If remote access fails, the router is usually why. The router is always why.

## program podman
Many people just alias docker to podman and carry on. It mostly works, which is the highest praise a tool can get.
Rootless containers cannot bind ports below 1024 by default. If a web server refuses to start, that is probably why.
podman ps -a shows the stopped ones too. They have been there for weeks. They will not leave on their own.

## program postman
Ctrl+Enter sends the request. Save it in a collection, or it is gone with the tab.
Put the base URL and token in environment variables. Switching between test and live becomes one click, and one less disaster.
A tests tab can check the status code after each call. Write one, and the collection starts to look professional.

## program powerpnt
F5 starts the show from the beginning, Shift+F5 from the current slide. B blanks the screen. Press B again to bring the room back.
Ctrl+M adds a new slide. Ctrl+D duplicates the one you are on. A deck is mostly duplicates anyway.
Slide Master sets the fonts and layout once. Change it there and every slide follows. The magic nobody tells you about.

## program powershell
Add -WhatIf to many cmdlets and it shows what would happen without doing it. A seatbelt for a script.
Get-Help and Get-Command are your map. Learn those two and the long names become a puzzle, not a wall.
pwsh is PowerShell 7, which also runs on Linux and macOS. The shell with the blue background is now everywhere.

## program prismlauncher
Each instance has its own mods, version and RAM setting. Make one per modpack, and no pack contaminates another.
Export an instance and a friend can import it. That is the polite way to share a modpack, and the only one that works.
Give it a sensible amount of RAM. Too little crashes it, too much makes the garbage collector sleepy.

## program proton
protondb.com tells you whether a game works, and which setting it needs. Read it before the download, not after.
Set PROTON_LOG=1 in the launch options and a log file appears. When a game crashes, the log knows why. It rarely says so kindly.
Different Proton versions fix different games. Switching one is a free experiment. Try the older one first.
Shader compiling happens on the first launch. The stutter is the sound of it learning. It gets better.

## program pycharm
Press Shift twice to search everywhere: files, symbols, actions, settings. The one shortcut worth memorising.
Alt+Enter offers a fix for whatever the editor is complaining about. Most of the time it is even right.
Make sure the project interpreter is the venv you created. It is often the system one. Pip would like a word.

## program python3
python -m venv .venv creates a virtual environment in one line. Do it per project and your system Python stays clean.
python -m http.server serves the current folder on port 8000. Share a file on the local network in five seconds.

## program qbittorrent
Set an upload limit that leaves room for the rest of the house. The video call will thank you.
Alternative speed limits can be turned on at the push of a button. A good one for working hours.
Sequential download is there, but it hurts the swarm. Use it for a single file you want to watch while it arrives.

## program qemu-system-x86
-enable-kvm uses hardware virtualisation. Without it, a virtual machine runs about as fast as thought in a queue.
qemu-img create makes the disk, and qcow2 gives you snapshots. Take one before the risky update.
-m 4G gives the guest four gigabytes. Mind how many guests you plan to run. The host needs some air.

## program qutebrowser
Qutebrowser is up. Press f to get letter hints on every link, then type the letters. The mouse can have the day off.
In qutebrowser, o opens a URL, d closes the tab and u brings it back. Undo exists even here.
J and K switch tabs, H and L go back and forward. Your fingers never leave the middle of the keyboard.

## program ranger
In ranger, yy copies, dd cuts and pp pastes, just like vim. If you know vim, you already know it.
Press zh in ranger to show hidden files. Press it again to stop looking at dotfiles you do not understand.
Type cw to rename a file, or :bulkrename to rename many in your editor. Useful before anyone sees them.

## program rawtherapee
RawTherapee saves your edits in a sidecar file next to the photo. The original raw stays untouched. Fearless sliders.
The batch queue lets you process a whole shoot overnight. Set the output and go to sleep. The fans will keep watch.
Check the histogram before you trust your eyes. Screens at night lie about brightness.

## program retroarch
RetroArch runs games through cores. If a console needs BIOS files, they must be in the system folder, or you get a black screen and doubt.
F2 saves a state, F4 loads it, F1 opens the menu. Save before the boss. Save before the second boss, too.
Turn on shaders for that scanline look. Your old TV has been gone for years, but its glow can return.

## program rhythmbox
Rhythmbox can play internet radio and podcasts, too. A small corner of the web, politely contained.
Automatic playlists in Rhythmbox pick songs by rule: rating, play count, last played. Set it once, enjoy for months.
Check the Rhythmbox queue before a meeting. The queue remembers what you added at 2 a.m.

## program rstudio
In RStudio, Ctrl+Enter runs the current line and Alt+Minus types the assignment arrow. Two shortcuts, half your wrist saved.
Restart R now and then, then run the script from the top. If it only works in your current session, it does not work.
Set the working directory with a project, not setwd(). Your future self and your colleagues will thank you.

## program rustc
Run rustc --explain E0382 (or any error code) for a full explanation with examples. The compiler even does tutoring.
cargo check skips code generation and finds most errors far faster than a full build. Use it while editing.
The borrow checker is not being mean. It is stopping two parts of your code from changing the same thing at once.

## program scribus
Run the preflight verifier before you export a PDF. It finds missing fonts and low-resolution images while it is still cheap.
Scribus keeps your layout in its own .sla file. Save one, export the PDF, and keep both. Print shops will ask.
Master pages hold what repeats on every page: page numbers, headers, a logo. Set them once, never place them by hand.

## program shotcut
In Shotcut, press S to split a clip at the playhead. It is the single most useful key in the program.
Enable proxy mode in Settings if the preview lags with big files. The edit runs smooth, the final render uses the originals.
Render takes a while, so close other heavy programs and leave the laptop plugged in. Do not watch the bar. It knows.

## program skypeforlinux
Test your camera and microphone before the call starts. Waving at a frozen screen is a very particular kind of silence.
A blue app opens and the ringtone lives in your memory. Please mute the speakers before you check anything.
Skype is a reminder that "can you hear me?" has been the first sentence of every call since the start of calls.

## program spectacle
Spectacle: Print takes a screenshot, Meta+Print grabs the active window, Meta+Shift+Print a region. Pick your level of fuss.
Spectacle has a delay option. Set a few seconds, open the menu you want captured, and wait for the click.
Spectacle can copy the shot to the clipboard instead of saving a file. Handy for chat. Check the frame for tabs you would rather hide.

## program ssh
Put your servers in ~/.ssh/config with short names. Then "ssh prod" replaces a long line you will typo anyway.
If an ssh session freezes, press Enter, then ~ then a full stop. It closes the connection without closing the terminal.

## program strawberry
Strawberry can fix tags in place and fetch cover art. A tidy library sounds better. Not scientifically, but emotionally.
Smart playlists in Strawberry build themselves from rules, like rating, genre or year. Make one called "Friday".
Last.fm scrobbling is built in, if you want your listening history kept. It will remember the song from 2 a.m. too.

## program stremio
Stremio keeps a Continue Watching row. It remembers where you stopped, which is more than the sofa does.
Decide in five minutes or put on something you have already seen. Browsing the catalogue is a film of its own, and it has no ending.
Subtitles are on the player's bottom bar. Check the language before the film starts, not ten minutes in.

## program studio.sh
In Android Studio, double-tap Shift to search everywhere and Ctrl+Shift+A to find any action by name. Menus are for tourists.
Give the IDE more memory in Help, Change Memory Settings if it stutters. And close the emulator you forgot about.
Logcat filters by app and by level. Choose your package first, or you will read the whole phone's diary.

## program sublime_text
Ctrl+P jumps to any file, Ctrl+R to any symbol, Ctrl+Shift+P opens the command palette. Learn those three and never browse a tree again.
Select a block, then Ctrl+Shift+L puts a cursor on every line. Typing once edits them all. Magic, but legal.
Shift+F11 is distraction-free mode. Just you, the text and a blinking cursor with a lot of free space.

## program supertuxkart
Try soccer or time trial when the Grand Prix feels too tense. Nitro bottles are worth the detour.
Bananas on the track are fair play, and so is putting one behind you. Use the rear-view button, because someone is behind you.
Plug in a gamepad if you can. Drifting with arrow keys is a lifestyle, but a gamepad is gentler on the fingers.

## program syncthing
Syncthing's web interface lives at 127.0.0.1:8384. Bookmark it, since this is where the devices, folders and mysteries are.
A .stignore file tells Syncthing what to skip: build folders, caches, anything huge you do not need on the laptop.
Both sides edited the same file? You will see a .sync-conflict copy next to it. Compare them, keep one, delete the other.

## program systemsettings
Use the search box at the top. Typing "mouse" or "sound" beats clicking through five categories you half remember.
Changes are only applied when you press Apply. If a setting looks odd afterwards, there is a Reset button on the page.
Check Startup and Shutdown from time to time. That is where programs quietly volunteer themselves to launch every morning.

## program taskmgr
Ctrl+Shift+Esc opens Task Manager directly. No need to go through the Ctrl+Alt+Del screen first.
The Startup tab shows how much each program slows boot. Disable what you do not need. You can always turn it back on.
Right-click a process and choose Open file location to see where it really lives. Handy for suspicious names.

## program teams-for-linux
Ctrl+Shift+M mutes you in Teams calls. Use it before you start talking to yourself, not afterwards.
Set your status to Do Not Disturb before focus time. People will see it and respect it. About a third of them.

## program terminator
Ctrl+Shift+O splits the terminal horizontally, Ctrl+Shift+E vertically. Split first, think later.
Ctrl+Shift+X zooms one terminal to full size and back. Handy when your log scrolls faster than your reading.
You can drag terminals around by their title bar to rearrange the layout. Tidy panes, tidy mind. Roughly.
Terminator can broadcast typing to several terminals at once. Do not do that on a production server. You know why.

## program thunar
Select several files and press F2 for bulk rename. It is quick, and it can number them.
Ctrl+L opens a typed path in Thunar, Alt+Up goes to the parent folder, Ctrl+H shows hidden files. A tidy trio.
Custom actions let you add your own right-click commands, like "open terminal here". It is a small feature worth ten minutes.

## program tidal
Check that your system sound output uses the right device and sample rate. Lossless music through the laptop speaker is just a gesture.
Tidal can download tracks for offline listening. Handy for flights and for the Wi-Fi in that one meeting room.
Volume normalisation can be switched on in the settings. It keeps loud tracks from startling you after a quiet one.

## program tilix
Ctrl+Alt+R splits the pane to the right, Ctrl+Alt+D splits it downward. Memorise those and you are a tiler.
Tilix has a Quake mode: a terminal that drops down from the top of the screen on a key. Fast, dramatic, mildly smug.
Drag a terminal by its title bar onto another one and they swap places. Tidy up your layout like a kitchen drawer.
Tilix can save a layout of sessions to a file. Reopen it tomorrow and your six shells are exactly where you left them.

## program timeshift
Timeshift by default does not back up your home folder. It protects system files, not your photos. Plan accordingly.
Set a schedule: monthly snapshots plus a few before each update. Then forget about it until the day you need it.
Keep a live USB around in case the system will not boot. Restoring from a snapshot works from there, too.

## program tmux
Ctrl+B then % splits the pane left and right, Ctrl+B then " splits it top and bottom. The prefix key does the rest.
Detach with Ctrl+B and d, and "tmux attach" brings the session back. Long jobs keep running when your laptop closes.
After the prefix, z zooms the current pane to full size and back, and [ lets you scroll. Everything else is optional.

## program top
Press 1 in top to see each CPU core on its own, and M to sort by memory. P goes back to CPU. q quits.
Three numbers for load average cover the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes. If the first is higher than the last, something is happening now.
Press k and type a process ID to send it a signal. Read the ID twice. Then once more.

## program tor-browser
Do not maximise the Tor Browser window. The default size is part of how it keeps many users looking alike.
Ctrl+Shift+U gives you a new identity, which closes your tabs and starts fresh. Ctrl+Shift+L gets a new circuit for one site.

## program totem
Drop a subtitle file with the same name beside the video and Videos picks it up. No hunting through menus.
Press F for full screen and Space to pause. A player that behaves is a rare and precious thing.
Check the audio track menu if the film is in the wrong language. It is almost always the second one.

## program transmission-gt
Set a ratio limit or a seeding time, and the client stops by itself. Fair play, with a finish line.
Use the turtle button for alternative speed limits. Slow downloads during video calls, full speed after.
Right-click a torrent and choose Verify Local Data if something looks broken. It rechecks the pieces without starting over.

## program typora
Ctrl+1 to Ctrl+6 sets heading levels, Ctrl+0 goes back to a normal paragraph. Faster than typing hash signs, if you like that.
Ctrl+/ switches to source mode and shows the raw Markdown. Handy when the formatting does something clever you did not ask for.
You can paste an image straight into the page. Check where it ends up. A path with "image (3)" will not age well.

## program unityhub
Unity Hub keeps each project tied to an editor version. Open the project with the same version, or expect a long upgrade and some sighing.
Changes made while the game is in Play Mode are lost when you stop. Set a tint for Play Mode so you notice which mode you are in.
The Library folder is regenerated on opening. If things get odd, close the editor, delete it and let it rebuild. Keep it out of version control.

## program vim
vimtutor teaches the basics in about half an hour. It is installed with Vim, and it is the best investment you will make today.
In Vim, ciw changes the word under the cursor and a full stop repeats the last change. Two small spells that save hours.

## program virt-manager
Take a snapshot before you install updates or experiment in a VM. Restoring takes seconds, regretting takes longer.
Install the VirtIO drivers for the guest. Disk and network become far quicker, and it feels like the machine is awake.
Ctrl+Alt releases the mouse from a virtual machine window. Remember that before you panic and think the cursor has died.

## program vivaldi-bin
Press F2 to open Quick Commands: a search box for settings, tabs, bookmarks and commands. The mouse can stay in its drawer.
Tab tiling puts two or more pages side by side in one tab. Useful for comparing, copying and quietly ignoring your inbox.
The side panel holds notes, bookmarks and a few web panels. A pocket of tools beside the page. Do not fill it with everything.

## program wezterm-gui
Edit ~/.config/wezterm/wezterm.lua and WezTerm reloads the configuration as soon as you save. A tight little feedback loop.
Ctrl+Shift+P opens the command palette, and Ctrl+Shift+Space starts quick select, which labels URLs and hashes you can copy with a key.
Search the scrollback with Ctrl+Shift+F. The error you want scrolled by forty lines ago. It is not lost.

## program whatsapp
Mute noisy groups for 8 hours, a week or always. The group will not notice, and neither will your family.
Use Starred Messages for the address, the code, the plan. Scrolling back through 300 chat bubbles is not a plan.
Linked devices stay connected only while your phone checks in now and then. If the desktop logs out, open the phone and wake it up.

## program wine
Give each program its own prefix with the WINEPREFIX variable. A broken installation then stays in its own small room.
winecfg is the settings window and winetricks installs fonts and runtime libraries. Many stubborn programs need one of the two.
Wine's AppDB lists how well programs run, with notes from other people who suffered first. Read it before you install.

## program winword
Ctrl+Shift+8 shows the hidden formatting marks. It reveals why that paragraph will not behave: three spaces and a tab.
Use Styles for headings and not manual bold and font size. A table of contents will build itself, and it will mean it.
F4 repeats the last action. Ctrl+Shift+C and Ctrl+Shift+V copy and paste formatting, and it saves your wrist a surprising amount.

## program wireshark
Use display filters like "tcp.port == 443" or "dns" to cut the noise. Without one, a capture is just a waterfall of packets.
Ctrl+E starts and stops a capture. Pick the right interface first, or you will record a very quiet loopback.
Capture only on networks you own or administer. Right-click a packet and choose Follow, TCP Stream to read a whole conversation.

## program xournalpp
Xournal++ can annotate a PDF: open it from the File menu and write straight on the pages. Exporting it afterwards is one click.
Press the pen, highlighter and eraser buttons, or hold the stylus button for the eraser. Pick one tool and settle.
Notes are saved as .xopp files. Export to PDF if you want to share them with someone who does not own the program.

## program xterm
In xterm, selecting text copies it to the primary selection and a middle click pastes it. Older than Ctrl+C, and still works.
Ctrl and a mouse button opens menus for font size and options. The settings live in ~/.Xresources.
Shift+Page Up scrolls back through the output, in case something important fell off the top.

## program yay
Run yay with no arguments and it updates the system and the AUR packages in one go. Short for "yay -Syu".
yay -Yc removes dependencies nobody needs anymore. A little spring cleaning for the packages, and your disk will thank you.

## program zathura
Press Tab to toggle the index and the table of contents, / to search, and a to fit the page. That is most of the manual.
Ctrl+R recolors the page to dark mode, which saves your eyes at night. The text is the same, only moodier.
J and K go to the next and previous page, and the lowercase ones scroll. Zathura expects you to learn them in an afternoon.
Zathura remembers where you stopped reading in each document. Close it without ceremony. It will wait.

## program zed
Ctrl+Shift+P opens the command palette and Ctrl+P finds a file. Zed wants you to keep your hands where they are.
Zed's vim mode is a setting away. If you miss modal editing, turn it on and enjoy the speed.
You can share a project with a teammate and edit in the same file at once. Agree on who types first.

## program zotero
The browser connector saves a paper, its metadata and its PDF in one click. Faster than copying the title into a notes file.
Add an item by its DOI or ISBN with the magic wand button. It fills in the author, the year and the journal for you.
Zotero has a Duplicate Items view. Merge the double entries now, or meet them again in your bibliography.

## window letter
A letter needs a date, a greeting, a point and a sign-off. Everything else is decoration.
Check the spelling of the name you are writing to. Getting it wrong costs more than any clever opening.
A complaint works best with the facts first and the adjectives last. Dates, amounts, what you want.
"To whom it may concern" is fine when you truly don't know. Five minutes of looking for a name is better.
Cover letter? Say what you can do for them. Your life story can wait for the interview.
Write the ugly first draft. A blank page can't be edited, only feared.
I keep templates for complaints, thank-yous and resignations. Say "letter" and I'll fetch one.
Save it now under a real name. "Document1" is where letters go to be lost.
Dear, Hello, Hi: three levels of formality. Pick the one the reader would pick.
Short letters get read. Long ones get skimmed, then answered with a question from paragraph two.
Printing it? Sign above the typed name, in real ink. It still impresses people.
Don't apologise in the first line. Make the request, and say sorry in the second if you must.
If the letter is angry, write it today and send it tomorrow. Paper is patient.
Yours sincerely goes with a name, Yours faithfully with "Dear Sir or Madam". That's the British rule, anyway.

## window writing
Use heading styles instead of bold-and-bigger. Then the table of contents builds itself.
In Google Docs, Ctrl+Shift+V pastes without formatting. It ends the mystery-font problem.
Read it aloud. Your ear catches what your eye has agreed to forgive.
The first paragraph is usually warm-up. Try deleting it. The second is often the real start.
One idea per paragraph. If it holds three, it holds two too many.
Search for "very", "really" and "just", then delete half. The text won't miss them.
Stuck? Write the next sentence badly and move on. Fixing is a different job from writing.
Ctrl+Enter makes a proper page break. Pressing Enter forty times is a trap.
Before someone else edits, switch on track changes or suggestion mode. Spot-the-difference is no fun.
Spellcheck knows words, not meaning. "Form" and "from" sail through every time.
Save a copy under a new name before a big rewrite. Undo has limits. Backups have fewer.
A sentence with three "and"s in it wants a full stop. Give the reader somewhere to stand.
Working on "{title}": a date in the file name makes the next version easy to find.
"{title}" is getting long. Headings and a table of contents would help you and any reader.

## window spreadsheet
F4 cycles a reference through the $A$1 forms. Learn it once and stop typing dollar signs by hand.
Ctrl+Arrow jumps to the edge of your data, Ctrl+Shift+Arrow selects all the way. The scroll wheel can rest.
A formula copied down went wrong? Check which references needed a dollar sign. It's usually that.
Freeze the top row so the headers stay put. Row 4,000 shouldn't be a guessing game.
Keep raw data on one sheet and the calculations on another. Future you will say thanks.
Colour-coding thirty columns is a rainbow, not formatting. Two colours do more.
The #DIV/0! error only means a division by an empty cell. The sheet isn't angry, just literal.
Dates are numbers in costume. If sorting goes odd, check whether one is secretly text.
A formula 400 characters long is a puzzle, not a formula. Split it over a few columns.
Save a copy before a big sort or delete. The sheet will not feel sorry.
In a lookup, mind the last argument: exact match or nearest. Nearest is a very polite way to be wrong.
Label the units. "Total" of what? Euros, kilos, hours? Next month you won't remember.
A chart shows the trend in a second. Nine hundred rows show it in a week.
Is "{title}" the real file or the copy? Check the name before you edit.
Saving "{title}" with a date in the name makes the next version easy to find.

## window slides
One idea per slide. If you need to say "as you can see", the audience can't.
A big photo beats a bullet list. People need somewhere to look that isn't text.
Rehearse once out loud. The slide you stumble on is the slide to cut.
High contrast, please. The people in the back row will love you.
Use the speaker notes. The slides are for the audience, the notes are for you.
Title a chart with its conclusion, not "Figure 3". Tell people what to see.
Fonts of 24 points or more. If it doesn't fit, say less.
Set fonts and colours on the master slide once, not on forty slides by hand.
Export a PDF as a backup. The projector doesn't know your fonts and never will.
The last slide shouldn't say "Questions?" and nothing else. Put the main point or next step there.
Open the deck on the laptop that will present, before the room fills. Cables betray everyone.
Don't read the slides out loud. The audience reads faster than you talk, and will.
Sixty slides in twenty minutes is a book. Aim for about a slide a minute, or fewer.
Does the first slide of "{title}" say what the talk is about in one line?
Presenting "{title}" soon? Run it once from start to finish first.

## window email
Put the ask in the first line. "Please approve by Thursday" beats three paragraphs of lead-in.
Cc is for people who only need to know. Bcc is for large groups who needn't see each other. Neither is for revenge.
Mentioned an attachment? Check that it's attached. I'll wait.
A subject line should say what you need: "Question about invoice 4417", not "Hi".
Read it once as the recipient. If it sounds sharp there, it is sharp.
Three questions in one email get one answer. Number them, or split them.
Most mail apps can delay sending. Use it for the 2 a.m. inspiration.
"Per my last email" is a sentence with an eyebrow. Use with care.
Tone is invisible in text. A "thanks" costs nothing and works as insurance.
Signature: name, one phone number, done. Quotes and logos are rarely appreciated.
Replying to a long thread? Quote only the part you answer. Nobody wants the trail twice.
A deadline should be a date, not "soon" or "ASAP". ASAP means a different day to everyone.
End with what happens next: who does what, by when. "Let me know" is a loop with no exit.
Is this one email or two? A second topic in the same mail usually gets forgotten.

## window inbox
Check the inbox at set times, not constantly. Mail is a visit, not a residence.
Two-minute rule: if the reply takes under two minutes, do it now. Otherwise schedule it.
Unsubscribe from a newsletter you never read. Three clicks that save a hundred.
Search is faster than folders. A good search beats a filing system you won't maintain.
Flag the three emails that matter today. The other forty can wait their turn.
Unsure about a link in a message? Type the address into the browser yourself.
Snooze exists in most mail apps. Send the email to a better version of Tuesday.
Answer everything from one person in one go. Switching context costs more than typing.
A reply you keep postponing gets heavier. Short and late beats perfect and never.
Filters can sort receipts and newsletters for you. Ten minutes of setup, months of calm.
Turn off the pop-up notifications. The mail will arrive anyway. It's reliable that way.
A tidy "waiting for" folder gets you most of the way to a calm Friday inbox.
Read the whole message before replying. The answer is often in the next line.
The unread count only ever goes up. It's weather, not a score.

## window code
Name things for what they do. "temp2" has never helped anyone.
Commit small and often. A tiny commit is easy to undo, a giant one is a lottery.
Read the whole error message once, slowly. The answer is often in the first line.
Explain the bug out loud to anything nearby. I'm available. I'm shiny.
When a test fails, believe the test first. Then check the test.
A comment should explain why, not what. The code already says what.
Delete dead code. Version control remembers it for you.
Run the tests before a big refactor. Otherwise it's a rewrite with extra steps.
Stared at a bug for half an hour? Change the view: another file, a short walk, a restart.
A TODO with no name and no date is a message in a bottle.
Use the editor's rename instead of find and replace. It knows which "id" you meant.
Keep secrets out of the repository. A key you committed lives in the history forever.
Change one thing at a time while debugging. Two changes and you won't know which one fixed it.
Working in "{title}": does the file name say what's inside? Future you reads names before code.
Still on "{title}"? Run the tests before you move on to the next file.

## window terminal
Tab completes names, double Tab lists the options. Typing a full path is a hobby, not a requirement.
In most Linux shells Ctrl+C stops the running command, Ctrl+D ends the input and Ctrl+L clears the screen.
In bash and zsh, "!!" repeats the previous command. "sudo !!" is the classic.
The up arrow brings back old commands. It's the shell's way of saying "again?".
Most commands answer to --help. It's shorter than a forum thread and nearly always correct.
Before rm -r, run ls on the same path. You'll see exactly what you are about to lose.
Quote paths that contain spaces. Everything breaks at the first unquoted one.
Ctrl+A jumps to the start of the line, Ctrl+E to the end, Ctrl+W deletes a word. Small spells that work.
A pipe sends one command's output to the next. grep, sort, head: three small tools, a lot of power.
Alias the long command you type daily. Two letters beat forty characters.
PowerShell commands are Verb-Noun. Get-ChildItem is ls with more syllables.
Before you rerun a command you don't understand on another machine, read it once.
Printed a binary file and got a screen of symbols? Type "reset", or close the tab.
Output scrolling past too fast? Pipe it into less. Press q to leave.

## window howto
Check the date on the guide. A tutorial from 2014 may describe buttons that no longer exist.
Compare two sources before running a command from either. The second often has the warning.
Write down the steps you actually took. When it works, you have your own guide.
If the guide says "just", expect trouble. "Just reinstall" is never just.
Read the comments below a tutorial. Someone has already found which step is wrong.
Skim the whole guide before step one. Learning at step six that you needed a tool is a classic.
A tutorial video can run at 1.5x, and chapters save half an hour.
Screenshots in old guides rarely match current menus. Look for the same words, not the same layout.
Make a backup before following a guide that edits system files. The system doesn't mind. You will.
Search the exact error text in quotes. It beats describing the problem in your own words.
A good how-to has the goal at the top and a check at the end. If yours has neither, find another.
Bookmark the guide that worked. You'll need it again, and it will have disappeared.
Official docs are boring and right. Blog posts are fun and often right. Start with the first.
Reading "{title}": a good guide lists what you need before step one. Does this one?
"{title}" worked for someone once. Check the date and the version before you trust it.

## window search
Quotes force an exact phrase. A minus sign removes a word. Two tricks that fix half of all searches.
"site:" followed by an address limits a search to one website. Google, DuckDuckGo and Bing all accept it.
Add the year or version number when you search for software help. Answers age badly.
Searching an error message? Paste it in whole, minus your own file paths.
If page one is ads and listicles, add "forum" or "docs". That's where the answer lives.
Search for what the answer would say, not for the question. Answers speak differently.
Ten tabs from one search? Read two, close eight. You'll miss one, at most.
Found a surprising number? Find three sources. One may be copying another.
Ctrl+L jumps to the address bar. Search from there and save a click.
Read the real address before you click. The URL is the most honest sentence on the page.
Searched the same thing three times? Write the answer down. "note" and I'll keep it.
A question nobody answers may have the wrong name. Look for the technical term.
An answer from five years ago is either right or exactly wrong. Check the date.
Changed the words and the results stayed the same? Change the language of the search instead.

## window video
Speed 1.25 saves a lot of time over an evening, and most voices cope. Not every film does.
"Are you still watching?" is the streaming service's version of last orders.
Subtitles make dialogue clearer and keep the person sleeping next to you asleep.
Chapter markers on long videos let you jump to the part you came for. Check the description.
A tutorial video isn't learning until you've done the thing. Pause and try.
Autoplay is a setting. Turn it off, and the next episode becomes your decision.
Bedtime check: after eleven, the next episode will still exist tomorrow.
Recommendations show what keeps you watching, not what you wanted. Search for the thing itself.
Watch Later lists are where videos go to retire. Clear yours on Sundays.
Full screen is for the film. A small window is for the tutorial you follow along with.
Headphones make an average video much better. Sound matters more than picture.
Long video, one answer needed? The description often has timestamps.
"{title}" has been playing for a while. Worth it? Carry on. Not worth it? Closing it is allowed.
Is "{title}" what you meant to watch when you sat down?

## window social
Muting a few words or accounts costs nothing and takes the edge off a whole feed.
Before replying in anger, ask whether you're angry at the post or at the day. Usually the day.
Close the app and reopen it. You didn't miss anything. The feed refills itself.
A feed's job is to keep you scrolling. Yours is to leave on purpose. "timer 5m" helps.
A post that makes you feel worse within a minute deserves an unfollow. It won't notice.
People post the good bits. You're comparing your whole week with their best photo.
Seen the same three stories twice? The feed has run out and started recycling.
Notifications on phone and desktop at once are a double doorbell. Pick one.
Writing a post? Wait ten minutes. Most hot takes cool to lukewarm.
Saved posts are a cemetery of good intentions. Read one, or clear the lot.

Logging out is a speed bump. Even a small one helps.
Five minutes with something funny, then back to work. Past that you're paying with time.
Comment threads are where long evenings go. Time check: it has been a while.

## window shopping
Read the three-star reviews. They're the most honest and the least angry.
Check the return policy before you check out, not after.
A crossed-out old price isn't proof of a discount. It's just a price that used to be there.
Look at the seller, not only the product. Same listing, different seller, different experience.
"Only 2 left!" is a sentence, not a measurement.
Shipping can eat the saving. Compare the total with shipping and tax, not the headline price.

Twenty minutes in, the tabs are a catalogue. Compare, close all but one, and decide tomorrow.

"{title}" is in your tabs. Do you need it, or do you need to have looked at it?
Is "{title}" on your list? If not, it's a want. Wants are allowed. They can wait a day.

## window music
Lyrics compete with writing. For text work, try instrumental.
One album on repeat is a legitimate focus technique. The familiar beats the new when you're concentrating.
If your colleague has to wave at you, the volume is a bit high.
Crossfade, equaliser, volume normalising: a minute in settings, years of nicer sound.
Your liked songs hide a few you've forgotten. Shuffle them for a reunion.
A song from your school days is a time machine with a built-in singalong.
Play one album from start to finish, the way it was made. It's a nice change.

A podcast and a playlist compete for the same ears. Pick one while you write.
Queue the next hour now and you won't need to touch this window again.
