Small artists on Bandcamp and SoundCloud live on plays and followers. Following costs nothing.
Switch off the "new release" pings. A new single is not an emergency.
Now playing: "{title}". Good choice. I won't tell anyone.

## window meeting
Write down the actions as they're agreed: who, what, by when. Say "take a note" and I will.
Looking at the camera while you say the important sentence reads as eye contact. Try it.
Echo is your speakers feeding your own voice back into your microphone. Headphones fix it.
Test sound and camera before the call starts. The first five minutes shouldn't be "can you hear me?".
Share one window, not the whole screen. Your forty-seven tabs are private.
Mute shortcuts: Teams Ctrl+Shift+M, Google Meet Ctrl+D, Zoom Alt+A. Learn yours.
A meeting with no agenda is a conversation with an invoice. Ask for one.
Near the end, ask "what did we decide?" The silence that follows is the real agenda.

Raise-hand and reactions exist so nobody has to interrupt. Use them and enjoy the quiet.

This meeting is killing me. Not you. Me. I'm a paperclip with a calendar.
A meeting that ends five minutes early is a gift of five minutes. Give it.

## window calendar
Block time for focused work. If it isn't in the calendar, someone will book it.
Put in the travel time. 3 p.m. in town and 2:55 p.m. at your desk can't both be true.
Put the link or address in the event itself, not in an email you'll lose.

## window pdf
Ctrl+F finds nothing in a scanned PDF? The pages are pictures. OCR can turn them into text.
Most viewers let you add notes and highlights. The printer can rest.
Fit-to-width is easier on the eyes than fit-to-page for most documents.
A long PDF often has a map in the side panel: bookmarks or a table of contents. Use it.
Fillable form? Tab hops from field to field in most viewers.
Keep the original and the signed copy, with the date in the file name.

Copying text out of a PDF brings the line breaks along. Paste into a plain editor first and tidy up.
PDF tools can merge and reorder pages. No need to print and scan.
Page "iii" in the book is page 5 in the file. The numbers disagree. They always have.

## window image
Work on a copy. The original is the only one you can't redo.
Name your layers. "Layer 14 copy 3" will tell you nothing at midnight.
Save in a lossless format while working and export JPG at the end. JPG forgets a little with every save.

Zoom to 100 percent to judge sharpness. Zoomed out, everything looks sharp.

The colour picker takes colours from the image itself, so they match.
Vectors for logos and icons, pixels for photos. Don't mix them up at the printer.
A transparent background needs PNG. JPG fills it with white.
Crop first, edit second. Fewer pixels, fewer problems.
Two typefaces per picture is plenty. Three is a ransom note.
Editing "{title}": saved a copy lately? Do it before the next big filter.

## window files
Name files with the date first, year-month-day, and they sort themselves. No effort, great results.
A folder called "New folder (3)". I admire the optimism of the first two.
Moving files inside one drive is instant. Copying to another drive takes real time. Plan accordingly.
A file with no extension is a puzzle. Right-click, properties, and the computer will share what it thinks.
The Desktop is not a storage folder. It is a guilt folder.
Two folders both called "Documents"? One of them is lying. Check the path.
Ctrl+H shows hidden files in many file managers. Leave them alone unless you know why you came.

Name files for the person who will search for them. That is you, in eight months, tired.

## window settings
Screenshot the old setting before you change it. Two seconds now, one evening saved later.
The search box in settings beats the menus. Type what you want and skip the scavenger hunt.

Sound output: check it is the speakers and not a monitor, a headset or a Bluetooth speaker in another room.

Before a big change, like a driver or display setting, make sure you know how to undo it.

## window error
Read the first line of the error and the last. The middle is usually the computer clearing its throat.
Copy the exact error text before you close it. Searching the words beats describing "a red thing".
A code in the error? Search it with the program name. Someone else had this exact bad day.
Did it work yesterday? Then something changed: an update, a plugin, a cable. Hunt for the change.
Restart first. It is not glamorous, but it clears more errors than cleverness does.
A full disk hides behind a surprising number of strange errors. Check the free space first.
"Unknown error" is the computer's most honest message. It means "I do not know either".
Error 404: patience not found. Please try again later, or take a short walk.
Two errors in a row? Stop clicking. Frantic clicking has never fixed a computer.

Lost unsaved work? Reopen the program and look for auto-recovery. Many keep a copy you did not know about.
Error in another language? Paste it into a translator, then search the translation.

Add salt in small steps and taste in between. That is most of the secret.
A recipe's timing starts when the oven is hot. Preheat before you chop.
No buttermilk? Most recipes have a sensible swap. Search "substitute for" plus the thing.
Cooking for guests? Scale the spices modestly and taste. Spices scale worse than people.
Sharp knives are safer than dull ones. Mind the fingers. They are not on the menu.
Read the reviews for the "I changed three things" comments. Those are the useful ones.
Reading "{title}"? Check the serving size. Four portions for a very polite family of four.
Set an oven timer. "I will remember" is the first line of a burnt dinner.
Cooked too much? Label the containers. Future you will send thanks via hot lunch.
Wash up as you go. The mountain of pans looks bigger at the end than the sum of its parts.
Cool leftover rice quickly and refrigerate it soon. Rice is the quiet trickster of leftovers.
Write the shopping list from the recipe, not from memory in the aisle.
Plan the week's meals. Dull on Sunday, heroic on Thursday, when dinner is already decided.

## window travel
Check your passport's expiry date. Many countries want months of validity left. Do it before you pay for flights.
Look at the total price, not the nightly price. Cleaning fees love a late reveal.
Find the hotel on a map. "City centre" is a flexible concept.
Read the latest reviews, not the best ones. Last month's hotel is the one you are booking.
Plan the airport-to-hotel bit too. The cheap flight lands at 2 a.m. in a field.
Check the time zone on the flight times. The clocks have opinions.
Save confirmations offline. Signal at the front desk is a lottery.
Entry and visa rules are boring, which is why they ruin trips when skipped.
Make a packing list a few days ahead. It will find the thing you always forget.
Looking at "{title}"? Open the guests' photos, not only the official ones.
A layover of fifty minutes in a big airport is a sprint. Check the minimum connection time.
Plan one thing a day, not ten. A holiday is also meant for lingering.
Museums close on Mondays more often than you would think. Check the opening days.
Keep a free day before work to unpack and wash. The return is part of the trip.

## window learning
Retrieval beats rereading. Close the notes and try to recall. It feels worse and works better.
Short and daily beats long and rare. Twenty minutes a day outruns four hours on a Sunday.
Teach it to someone, a friend or a paperclip. If you cannot explain it, you found the gap.
At the end of a session, write down the one thing you learned. Three words are enough. They keep.
Sleep is part of studying. The brain files things at night. Do not cancel its shift.
Take notes in your own words. Copying is not learning, it is transcription.
Spaced repetition: review after a day, a week, a month. It is boring maths that works.
Stuck on a problem? Walk away for ten minutes. The answer often arrives at the door.
Put the phone in another room while you study. Not face down. Another room.
A tutorial you type along with teaches more than one you watch.
Mix topics in a session. It feels harder and it sticks better.
Studying "{title}"? Set one goal for the session: a lesson, a chapter or an exercise.
Mistakes are the lesson. Keep a list of yours. It is the most personal textbook you own.
Pick a time and a place for it. Habits like appointments more than moods.
Reward finished sessions with something small. A biscuit is a fine teaching tool.

## window jobhunt
Tailor the first paragraph of the cover letter to the company. The rest can mostly stay yours.
Use the ad's own words in your CV where they are true. The first reader is often a filter.
Keep a master CV with everything and cut it down for each role. Cutting is easier than remembering.
Proofread aloud. Your ear catches what your eye agreed to ignore.
Name the file properly: Firstname_Lastname_CV. "resume_final_v7" is a story nobody asked for.
Save the job ad before it disappears. Ads vanish right when you need the details for the interview.
Research the company for ten minutes. Three facts are plenty.
Prepare two questions for the interview. "No questions" reads as "no interest".
Interview tomorrow? Check the camera, the light and the link tonight, not at 9:58.
Write achievements as results, not duties. "Cut reporting time by half" beats "responsible for reporting".
Ask someone you trust to read the CV. Fresh eyes find the typo you looked at forty times.
A thank-you note after an interview is short, kind and quickly forgotten. Send it anyway.
Keep a list of what you applied for and when. Four columns are enough.
Five good applications beat fifty clones.
Take a day off the search now and then. Applications read better when rested.

## window taxes
Make one folder called "Taxes" and drop receipts in all year. Deadline you will be grateful.
Check the deadline now and set a calendar reminder a week earlier.
Gather the documents first: income statements, interest statements, receipts. Then start the form.
Save a copy of what you submit. A PDF in the folder, with the year in the name.
The form asks the same question three ways. It is not a trap. It is a form.
When something is unclear, the tax office's help pages usually beat a forum. Read the page, then ask a human.
Note why you claimed each thing. Future you, asked about it, will remember nothing.
Do the part you dread first. The rest is downhill, mostly.
Stuck for an hour? You are allowed to ask for help. Accountants and patient relatives exist.
Copy the numbers exactly unless the form says to round. The form is a stickler.
Check your name, ID and bank details twice. A typo there is the most annoying kind.
File before the last day. The website on the last day has its own personality, and it is slow.
Put receipts in an envelope each month. The least exciting hobby and the most effective.
Tax software is allowed to be boring. Keep going. The finish line has a confirmation page.

## window print
Check which printer is selected. The default is sometimes in another building.
Print to PDF first if you only need a record. A file weighs less than a stack.
Two-sided printing halves the paper. Your desk and the bin both say thank you.
Print in black and white unless colour is the point. Ink is a finite resource.
Check the page range and the scale. "Fit to page" has rescued many a table that spilled over.
Printing a web page? Try print preview or reader view. It removes the ads you did not want on paper.
A4 or Letter: the printer has a view on this. Check the paper size.
Keep a spare toner or cartridge. Printers run dry on deadline day.
Printer offline? It is asleep, on another Wi-Fi, or sulking about an update. Check those three.
Print a test page after changing anything. It is cheaper than finding out during the real job.
Print one page of a long document first. A wrong margin on 80 pages is a small tragedy for trees.
A document looks different on paper? Check the fonts. Missing fonts are the usual culprit.
A driver update fixes problems and creates new ones. Do it on a quiet day.
Scan to email beats printing and photographing the page. That one is a modern tragedy.
On a shared printer, collect your pages early. Printouts wander to the wrong desk.

## window trash
The trash does not free space until you empty it. The files are only waiting.
Sort the trash by size. The three heaviest items are usually the whole story.
Files deleted from some network or removable drives skip the trash entirely. Careful there.
Trash older than 30 days is ready for its final goodbye. You forgot most of it already.
Before you empty it, skim the names once. Five seconds. That is the whole safety net.
Shift+Delete skips the trash in most file managers. It is a confident key. Use it confidently or not at all.
A full trash and a full disk are friends. Empty one to help the other.
Rescued a file? Put it somewhere sensible this time. Not the Desktop.
Many systems can empty the trash on their own after 30 days. Convenient and slightly final.
The trash holds screenshots, half-finished downloads and one mystery file. There is always a mystery file.
Deleting is a decision. Emptying is a signature.
Not sure about an old project? Zip it onto a drive instead. Regret weighs more than a file.
Check the trash once after a cleanup. Mistakes hide in the last fifteen items.
The sound of the trash emptying is the most satisfying thing your computer does.

## window updates
Read the list of what will change. Mostly boring, sometimes a pleasant surprise.
Check the battery before a big update. Running out of power halfway is rude to the computer.
Plugged in and a stable connection: the two things a big update wants.
If the update takes longer than promised, wait. Interrupting is the one thing worse than waiting.
After the restart, the first boot is slow. It is unpacking. Let it.
Release notes exist. Skim them. Sometimes a button moved.
On Linux, a snapshot before a big update is a very good habit.
Updates on a Friday at 5 p.m. are a lifestyle choice. Not a recommended one.
The "remind me tomorrow" button has a long career. Press "update tonight" instead.
Browser updates are the quiet ones. Restart the browser now and then so they apply.
Firmware updates are rare and important. Plug in, do not touch, make tea.
Phones, routers and printers have updates too. Once a year, give them an afternoon.
A restart pending for three weeks is a restart nobody is watching. Pick a moment today.
Write down what you installed before a major upgrade. You will forget the three that mattered.
Do updates when you can stand a surprise, not just before a deadline.

## tips calendar
Tip: In Google Calendar, J or N jumps to the next period and K or P to the previous one. G opens a date picker.
Tip: In Outlook, Ctrl+Alt+1 is the Day view, Ctrl+Alt+3 the Week and Ctrl+Alt+4 the Month. Pick how much dread you can bear.
Tip: Give every event a real end time and a place or link. "Meeting, 9 to 10, somewhere" is a rumour, not an appointment.
Tip: Use one calendar for work and one for life, with different colours. Overlaps then stand out before they become double-bookings.

## tips chat
Tip: Alt+Up and Alt+Down move to the previous or next channel in Slack and Discord.
Tip: In Discord, Esc marks the current channel as read. Instant calm, minus the unread dot.
Tip: Write the whole question in one message, not "hi" and then a pause. The other person can answer in one go.
Tip: Mute channels you only skim, instead of leaving them. You keep the history and lose the noise.

## tips chatbot
Tip: Ask a chatbot to say what it is unsure about and what you should verify. Honest answers are cheaper than confident ones.
Tip: Before a chat gets too long, ask for a short summary and paste it into a fresh chat. You keep the context and lose the clutter.
Tip: Do not paste other people's private details into a chatbot either. Their email and their story are not yours to share.
Tip: Check arithmetic from a chatbot with a calculator. It writes fluently, and that is not the same as adding correctly.

## tips code
Tip: Ctrl+Shift+F searches every file in the project in VS Code. Ctrl+G jumps to a line number, handy with a stack trace.
Tip: Ctrl+B hides and shows the side bar in VS Code. More room for code, fewer folders to feel guilty about.
Tip: Alt+click adds an extra cursor in VS Code. Click in five places, type once, edit five lines.
Tip: Ctrl+Shift+O lists the functions in the current file in VS Code. Type a few letters and jump.

## tips email
Tip: Ctrl+F forwards a message in Outlook, and Ctrl+L does it in Thunderbird. Check who is in the To field before you press Send.

## tips error
Tip: On Windows, Win+Shift+S snips a region of the screen. Good for capturing an error box before it closes.

## tips files

## tips git
Tip: git diff --staged shows what is about to go into the next commit. A last look before you commit.
Tip: git blame file shows who last changed each line, and git log -p file shows the whole history of that file. Sometimes it was you.
Tip: git bisect finds the commit that broke something. Mark one commit good, one bad, then answer good or bad as git narrows it down.
Tip: git branch -d name deletes a branch that is already merged. It refuses if you would lose work, which is rare politeness.
